sources.title: Fitbit Edge is Google’s middle ground between Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch - TechCrunch
passages: Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch.

It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.)
The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals.
Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather.
Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.

extraction.body: Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch. Priced at $179.99, it combines the Fitbit Air’s slim band with an OLED display for checking map directions, notifications, weather, and music controls. Like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, the Edge works with Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini. (You’ll need a Google Health Premium subscription to use it.) The coach can use your fitness, health, and medical information to put together weekly routines and workout plans, then adjust them around your schedule. It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.) Google says the Fitbit Edge can automatically recognize and log up to 100 activities, including runs, bike rides, and walks. The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather. The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips. Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters. The Fitbit Edge is available to preorder through the Google Store, with store availability set for October 27. Color choices include Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon. There’s also a Stephen Curry Special Edition, priced at $219.99. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. sources.title: Thought the future of fitness tracking was screenless? Think again, as Google debuts the Google Fitbit Edge with 46% more screen than previous Fitbit - TechRadar
passages: If you thought the Google Fitbit Air spelled the end of the 'old style' screen-bearing Fitbits, think again — Google has dropped the Google Fitbit Edge, a slim tracker with Google's 'largest and brightest tracker screen yet', and according to Google, it sits in between the 'quiet simplicity' of a Google Fitbit Air and a Google Pixel Watch .
Thought the future of fitness tracking was screenless?
It costs costs $179.99 / £159.99 / AU$269, and features a powerful 'hybrid OLED ' screen delivering 46% more viewing area than previous Fitbits, designed for direct sunlight visibility.
The chassis is 11.5mm thick, features metal touchpoints 'everywhere' across the device, and a 'satisfying' physical button.
This is terrific news for me, because I love the buttons on the best Garmin watches and older Fitbits.

The screen offers an improved browsing experience based on Tiles that, while not sporting full Wear OS, seems to take cues from Google's Materia 3 Expressive design language it uses on its best Android watches .
It sports call and notification management, as well as — surprisingly — Google Maps support, so it really is like a smartwatch-lite.
Matt is TechRadar's expert on all things fitness, wellness and wearable tech.
TechRadar is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.

Menstrual cycle tracking, sleep tracking, and all of Google Health's usual tools (including the AI fitness coach) are present and correct here, as are the new Health Guardian features like Insulin Resistance Trends and an ECG scan functionality.

If you thought the Google Fitbit Air spelled the end of the 'old style' screen-bearing Fitbits, think again — Google has dropped the Google Fitbit Edge, a slim tracker with Google's 'largest and brightest tracker screen yet', and according to Google, it sits in between the 'quiet simplicity' of a Google Fitbit Air and a Google Pixel Watch . It costs costs $179.99 / £159.99 / AU$269, and features a powerful 'hybrid OLED ' screen delivering 46% more viewing area than previous Fitbits, designed for direct sunlight visibility. The screen offers an improved browsing experience based on Tiles that, while not sporting full Wear OS, seems to take cues from Google's Materia 3 Expressive design language it uses on its best Android watches . It sports call and notification management, as well as — surprisingly — Google Maps support, so it really is like a smartwatch-lite. The exercise app features improved automatic activity tracking that can automatically detect up to 100 workout types, without you needing to manually start a workout. This will also be rolled out to the Google Fitbit Air. It's also packing onboard GPS, unlike the Fitbit Air, so Fitbit Edge users can run, cycle, swim or hike and track their routes and speeds without piggybacking off your phone. Menstrual cycle tracking, sleep tracking, and all of Google Health's usual tools (including the AI fitness coach) are present and correct here, as are the new Health Guardian features like Insulin Resistance Trends and an ECG scan functionality. The chassis is 11.5mm thick, features metal touchpoints 'everywhere' across the device, and a 'satisfying' physical button. This is terrific news for me, because I love the buttons on the best Garmin watches and older Fitbits. It's nice that Google is bringing some of that old-school Fitbit heritage back — even though it's axed the old Fitbit app and migrated all users to Google Health. The Fitbit Edge sports a long-lasting battery life that will go for a week, and a 90-minute charge can bring it back to 100%. The battery is also replaceable, extending the life of your hardware. Like the Google Fitbit Air, and previous Fitbits before it, bands are swappable: you can choose an Active Sport band, a micro-adjustable, flexible Performance Loop, or more stylish Metal Links for a watch aesthetic. This 'middle ground' Fitbit, situated between a Google Fitbit Air and full Pixel Watch, looks terrific. I'm not the biggest fan of Google's new Health app due to its reliance on the AI coach, but Google absolutely nails its wearable hardware, and the Fitbit Edge looks like another winner, reinventing the classic Fitbit pebble design. I love the form factor of the Pixel Watch and the Fitbit Air alike, and a halfway-house featuring a tactile button (my favorite feature on the Garmin Cirqa , and something I missed on the Fitbit Air), week-long battery life and the repairability of a replaceable battery for under $180 / £160 / AU$280 sounds like a slam-dunk. I look forward to testing it. What do you think of the Fitbit Edge? Let us know in the comments. sources.title: Google announces the Fitbit Edge, a middle ground between Pixel Watch 5 and Fitbit Air
passages: The Fitbit Edge is essentially a new Charge 6, but it has more of a Pixel Watch aesthetic.
Squish Google’s smartwatch from the sides, and you’ve got the Edge.
It has a pill-shaped 1.34-inch OLED touch display inside a slender aluminum frame that is rated IP68 (5 ATM) for water and dust protection.
Google says the screen has 46 percent more viewable area compared to the Charge 6.
It’s very close in overall size to the Fitbit Air and uses the same magnetic charging puck.
Google is releasing its second Fitbit tracker of 2026, offering fans of the aging Charge 6 a more refined option.
Like the Air, this tracker is not an island within Google’s ecosystem.
You can pair multiple Google wearables with the Health app and wear whichever one you want.
There’s no need to re-pair or manually switch your health tracking over.
The app collects stats from the device you wear at any given time, changing as often as necessary.
So you could sport the Pixel Watch 5 during the day and the Edge when you hit the gym, for example.
You can use that to wake the device or start/pause workouts.
Most interactions will be handled with the touchscreen, though.
This allows you to track an outdoor activity without bringing your phone along for the ride.
The Edge also has an altimeter, optical heart rate sensor, and skin temperature sensor.
It comes in matte black, polished silver, satin pyrite (between silver and gold), and champagne gold.
If the tracker is away from your phone, it can still follow your activity all week with support for seven days of full health data storage (or 30 days of basic data).
However, the generous weeklong battery life does not include always-on display mode.
There is also a Stephen Curry Special Edition available for $220.

While there will eventually be third-party options, Google plans to have a line of add-on bands at launch, including the Active Sport (silicone with holes) for $40, Performance Loop (polyester fabric) for $50, Magnet Band (leather-ish but still silicone) at $60, and a Metal Links Band for a whopping $150.
So responses are limited to pre-defined quick replies.
Google also notes the Edge can stay with you for the long haul.
This is the company’s first repairable fitness tracker, which has been designed with a replaceable battery.
There will be service options to swap the battery, but Google still doesn’t recommend you open up the tracker yourself.
All this data is beamed over Bluetooth 5.4 to the Google Health app (previously Fitbit), feeding all your data into the Gemini-powered Health Coach chatbot.

extraction.body: The Fitbit Edge offers more than the Air, but it’s not a real smartwatch. Google is releasing its second Fitbit tracker of 2026, offering fans of the aging Charge 6 a more refined option. The new Fitbit Edge slots right in between the Pixel Watch 5 and the Fitbit Air , featuring a compact screen and more health sensors than the Air. You won’t get all the apps and features of the Pixel Watch 5, but the Edge is only about half as expensive. The Fitbit Edge is essentially a new Charge 6, but it has more of a Pixel Watch aesthetic. Squish Google’s smartwatch from the sides, and you’ve got the Edge. It has a pill-shaped 1.34-inch OLED touch display inside a slender aluminum frame that is rated IP68 (5 ATM) for water and dust protection. Google says the screen has 46 percent more viewable area compared to the Charge 6. It’s very close in overall size to the Fitbit Air and uses the same magnetic charging puck. The Edge works with Android or iPhones via the Google Health app, and it can run for about seven days on a charge. If the tracker is away from your phone, it can still follow your activity all week with support for seven days of full health data storage (or 30 days of basic data). However, the generous weeklong battery life does not include always-on display mode. If you turn it on, battery life drops to about two days, barely longer than the Pixel Watch 5. The Fitbit Edge plays it right down the middle in Google’s wearable lineup, and not just in price and size—button count also splits the difference. The Pixel Watch has two buttons, the Air has none, and the Edge sports a single tactile side button. You can use that to wake the device or start/pause workouts. Most interactions will be handled with the touchscreen, though. The Edge will ship with a collection of fitness-focused experiences and watch faces, and you won’t be able to download more. While this looks a lot like the Pixel Watch’s software, it’s not a full version of WearOS. It can mirror notifications from your phone, but there’s no microphone or speaker. So responses are limited to pre-defined quick replies. Likewise, there’s no support for Gemini interactions. The Edge also lacks NFC, so there’s no Google Wallet tap-to-pay. One notable upgrade over the Fitbit Air is on-device GPS. This allows you to track an outdoor activity without bringing your phone along for the ride. However, Google says it’s not as accurate as the dual-band GPS radio in the Pixel Watch. The Edge does retain the ECG and blood oxygen sensor from the Pixel Watch, which you don’t get on the Air. The Edge also has an altimeter, optical heart rate sensor, and skin temperature sensor. All this data is beamed over Bluetooth 5.4 to the Google Health app (previously Fitbit), feeding all your data into the Gemini-powered Health Coach chatbot. The device comes with three months of Google Health Premium, without which you won’t get the AI features. Of course, some would probably prefer to skip the AI. The Premium subscription is $10 per month. It’s included with Google AI Pro, but you can disable the Health Coach if you want. Like the Pixel Watch, the Edge will come with the basic silicone Active Band for $180. There is also a Stephen Curry Special Edition available for $220. The Edge has a custom band connector similar to the Pixel Watch, but the plug is a different size. While there will eventually be third-party options, Google plans to have a line of add-on bands at launch, including the Active Sport (silicone with holes) for $40, Performance Loop (polyester fabric) for $50, Magnet Band (leather-ish but still silicone) at $60, and a Metal Links Band for a whopping $150. The Fitbit Edge is available for preorder today and will ship on October 27. It comes in matte black, polished silver, satin pyrite (between silver and gold), and champagne gold. While this is a much more expensive tracker compared to the $100 Fitbit Air, it’s only a little more than the Charge 6’s 2023 launch price of $160. The Pixel Watch 5 starts at $350. Like the Air, this tracker is not an island within Google’s ecosystem. You can pair multiple Google wearables with the Health app and wear whichever one you want. There’s no need to re-pair or manually switch your health tracking over. The app collects stats from the device you wear at any given time, changing as often as necessary. So you could sport the Pixel Watch 5 during the day and the Edge when you hit the gym, for example. Google also notes the Edge can stay with you for the long haul. This is the company’s first repairable fitness tracker, which has been designed with a replaceable battery. Note that does not mean user-replaceable . While this looks a lot like the Pixel Watch’s software, it’s not a full version of WearOS. It can mirror notifications from your phone, but there’s no microphone or speaker. So responses are limited to pre-defined quick replies. Likewise, there’s no support for Gemini interactions. The Edge also lacks NFC, so there’s no Google Wallet tap-to-pay.

One notable upgrade over the Fitbit Air is on-device GPS. This allows you to track an outdoor activity without bringing your phone along for the ride. However, Google says it’s not as accurate as the dual-band GPS radio in the Pixel Watch. The Edge does retain the ECG and blood oxygen sensor from the Pixel Watch, which you don’t get on the Air. The Edge also has an altimeter, optical heart rate sensor, and skin temperature sensor.

All this data is beamed over Bluetooth 5.4 to the Google Health app (previously Fitbit), feeding all your data into the Gemini-powered Health Coach chatbot. The device comes with three months of Google Health Premium, without which you won’t get the AI features. Of course, some would probably prefer to skip the AI. The Premium subscription is $10 per month. It’s included with Google AI Pro, but you can disable the Health Coach if you want.

Like the Pixel Watch, the Edge will come with the basic silicone Active Band for $180. There is also a Stephen Curry Special Edition available for $220. The Edge has a custom band connector similar to the Pixel Watch, but the plug is a different size. While there will eventually be third-party options, Google plans to have a line of add-on bands at launch, including the Active Sport (silicone with holes) for $40, Performance Loop (polyester fabric) for $50, Magnet Band (leather-ish but still silicone) at $60, and a Metal Links Band for a whopping $150.

The Fitbit Edge is available for preorder today and will ship on October 27. It comes in matte black, polished silver, satin pyrite (between silver and gold), and champagne gold. While this is a much more expensive tracker compared to the $100 Fitbit Air, it’s only a little more than the Charge 6’s 2023 launch price of $160. The Pixel Watch 5 starts at $350.

Like the Air, this tracker is not an island within Google’s ecosystem. You can pair multiple Google wearables with the Health app and wear whichever one you want. There’s no need to re-pair or manually switch your health tracking over. The app collects stats from the device you wear at any given time, changing as often as necessary. So you could sport the Pixel Watch 5 during the day and the Edge when you hit the gym, for example.

Google also notes the Edge can stay with you for the long haul. This is the company’s first repairable fitness tracker, which has been designed with a replaceable battery. Note that does not mean user-replaceable . There will be service options to swap the battery, but Google still doesn’t recommend you open up the tracker yourself.

extraction.body: If you’ve been following our wearable coverage on G Style , you know Google has spent the past couple of years leaning heavily into the Pixel Watch lineup. But for plenty of folks out there, a full-blown smartwatch that needs charging every day or two isn’t always the goal. Some people want something sleek, featherweight, and focused on wellness without the bulk on their wrist. Today, Google officially takes the wraps off its latest hardware entry: the Fitbit Edge . Google’s vision for bridging the gap between basic fitness bands and top-tier smartwatches. Alongside the new hardware, Google also announces some major AI-driven upgrades coming to the broader Google Health ecosystem. Here is everything you need to know about the announcement. The centerpiece is the Fitbit Edge , a dedicated fitness tracker built around an ultra-slim 11.5mm profile. Google clearly prioritized wrist feel here—the case design is 46% lighter than typical competitor devices in this bracket, making it practically unnoticeable when you’re sleeping or putting in work at the gym. Google isn’t just updating the shell; they are significantly retooling how the backend interprets your biometric data. Under their expanding Health Guardian umbrella, Fitbit devices are gaining deeper proactive health tracking. Using large sensor models trained on trillions of minutes of health data from more than 500,000 users, the system can now surface monthly trend reports for insulin resistance , plus blood pressure trends on the Pixel Watch 3, 4 and 5 and the Fitbit Air. Rather than simply throwing raw numbers at you, the goal is contextual pattern tracking that surfaces potential flags before they become major problems. Google also reiterates its privacy guardrails, confirming that all personal health data remains protected by multi-layered encryption and is strictly not used for targeted advertising . If you work out across multiple disciplines, you know automated workout detection can be hit or miss on wristbands. Google is tackling this with an upgraded motion model that now automatically recognizes over 100 activities . By deploying LLM-based reasoning directly against motion sensor inputs, Google claims a 2x improvement in activity tracking accuracy during internal testing. The wearable can better differentiate nuanced movements—like separating high-intensity interval sets from basic weight training—giving users a genuine “set-it-and-forget-it” workout tracking experience without requiring manual start and stop taps on the screen. On the software and research side, Google announced a multi-year strategic partnership with Flo Health , one of the leading platforms in the women’s health space. The collaboration aims to deepen menstrual cycle tracking, symptom analysis, and clinical research insights across Google’s health ecosystem, giving users more actionable correlation between cycle phases, sleep quality, and daily athletic performance. The Fitbit Edge feels like a very smart, calculated move by Google. The wearable market has split into two extremes: either basic silicone fitness bands that don’t do much, or $350+ smartwatches packed with LTE and speakers that demand daily wall power. By delivering a slim 11.5mm chassis, a week of battery life, improved GPS, and deeper AI trend analysis, the Edge gives fitness-first enthusiasts the exact metrics they want without the smartwatch baggage. We’re expecting review units to hit the home base soon, so stay tuned for our full hands-on review once we put the new tracking models and battery claims to the test. What are your thoughts? Does this feel like the just right in the middle device for you? Let us know in the comments.

coreStoryFacts.text: Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch.

It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.)
The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals.
Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather.
Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips.
Lauren covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch.

If you thought the Google Fitbit Air spelled the end of the 'old style' screen-bearing Fitbits, think again — Google has dropped the Google Fitbit Edge, a slim tracker with Google's 'largest and brightest tracker screen yet', and according to Google, it sits in between the 'quiet simplicity' of a Google Fitbit Air and a Google Pixel Watch .
Thought the future of fitness tracking was screenless?
It costs costs $179.99 / £159.99 / AU$269, and features a powerful 'hybrid OLED ' screen delivering 46% more viewing area than previous Fitbits, designed for direct sunlight visibility.
The chassis is 11.5mm thick, features metal touchpoints 'everywhere' across the device, and a 'satisfying' physical button.
This is terrific news for me, because I love the buttons on the best Garmin watches and older Fitbits.

The screen offers an improved browsing experience based on Tiles that, while not sporting full Wear OS, seems to take cues from Google's Materia 3 Expressive design language it uses on its best Android watches .
It sports call and notification management, as well as — surprisingly — Google Maps support, so it really is like a smartwatch-lite.
Matt is TechRadar's expert on all things fitness, wellness and wearable tech.

Menstrual cycle tracking, sleep tracking, and all of Google Health's usual tools (including the AI fitness coach) are present and correct here, as are the new Health Guardian features like Insulin Resistance Trends and an ECG scan functionality.

extraction.body: If you’ve been following our wearable coverage on G Style , you know Google has spent the past couple of years leaning heavily into the Pixel Watch lineup. But for plenty of folks out there, a full-blown smartwatch that needs charging every day or two isn’t always the goal. Some people want something sleek, featherweight, and focused on wellness without the bulk on their wrist. Today, Google officially takes the wraps off its latest hardware entry: the Fitbit Edge . Google’s vision for bridging the gap between basic fitness bands and top-tier smartwatches. Alongside the new hardware, Google also announces some major AI-driven upgrades coming to the broader Google Health ecosystem. Here is everything you need to know about the announcement. The centerpiece is the Fitbit Edge , a dedicated fitness tracker built around an ultra-slim 11.5mm profile. Google clearly prioritized wrist feel here—the case design is 46% lighter than typical competitor devices in this bracket, making it practically unnoticeable when you’re sleeping or putting in work at the gym. Google isn’t just updating the shell; they are significantly retooling how the backend interprets your biometric data. Under their expanding Health Guardian umbrella, Fitbit devices are gaining deeper proactive health tracking. Using large sensor models trained on trillions of minutes of health data from more than 500,000 users, the system can now surface monthly trend reports for insulin resistance , plus blood pressure trends on the Pixel Watch 3, 4 and 5 and the Fitbit Air. Rather than simply throwing raw numbers at you, the goal is contextual pattern tracking that surfaces potential flags before they become major problems. Google also reiterates its privacy guardrails, confirming that all personal health data remains protected by multi-layered encryption and is strictly not used for targeted advertising . If you work out across multiple disciplines, you know automated workout detection can be hit or miss on wristbands. Google is tackling this with an upgraded motion model that now automatically recognizes over 100 activities . By deploying LLM-based reasoning directly against motion sensor inputs, Google claims a 2x improvement in activity tracking accuracy during internal testing. The wearable can better differentiate nuanced movements—like separating high-intensity interval sets from basic weight training—giving users a genuine “set-it-and-forget-it” workout tracking experience without requiring manual start and stop taps on the screen. On the software and research side, Google announced a multi-year strategic partnership with Flo Health , one of the leading platforms in the women’s health space. The collaboration aims to deepen menstrual cycle tracking, symptom analysis, and clinical research insights across Google’s health ecosystem, giving users more actionable correlation between cycle phases, sleep quality, and daily athletic performance. The Fitbit Edge feels like a very smart, calculated move by Google. The wearable market has split into two extremes: either basic silicone fitness bands that don’t do much, or $350+ smartwatches packed with LTE and speakers that demand daily wall power. By delivering a slim 11.5mm chassis, a week of battery life, improved GPS, and deeper AI trend analysis, the Edge gives fitness-first enthusiasts the exact metrics they want without the smartwatch baggage. We’re expecting review units to hit the home base soon, so stay tuned for our full hands-on review once we put the new tracking models and battery claims to the test. What are your thoughts? Does this feel like the just right in the middle device for you? Let us know in the comments.

According to the social media giant, the models, which are available today, are designed to provide "state-of-the-art" performance across personal and professional AI agents and put the company squarely in the conversation for frontier-level AI. The software will eventually power more of the company's Muse AI agent, which Meta launched early last month and has exploded in popularity . The company says Muse Wonder and Wonder Full come with Active Memory and Active Focus. According to Meta, Active Memory allows AI models to bring information you need from across conversations, so you don't have to start from scratch each time you chat with the AI. Active Focus ensures the AI continues working on a task even if it encounters errors or roadblocks. Meta says it will also ask you for clarification or permission to perform tasks. The company claims that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full can take on the likes of Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) high-powered Fable 5.1, OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) GPT-6 Astra, and Google's ( GOOG , GOOGL ) Gemini 4 Argon in certain benchmarks. That's a massive swing in the right direction for Meta, which was seen as an also-ran in the AI race this time last year. It's also come at a high cost, though. The company has invested tens of billions of dollars, including $14 billion in Scale AI to acquire and hire co-founder and CEO Alexandr Wang, who now serves as Meta's chief AI officer. The spending spree, which also saw Meta poach AI workers and experts from its fellow tech behemoths, put serious pressure on the company's stock price. Shares of Meta are up just 6% over the last 12 months, slightly better than Microsoft, which has climbed a paltry 5%. The companies' hyperscaler rivals Amazon and Google, meanwhile, have jumped roughly 20% and 45%, respectively, in the same period. But with the debut of Meta's Muse agent and the unveiling of its Muse Charm device , which hits the market later this year, the company has managed to turn around the narrative that it can't hang with the leading AI firms. extraction.body: Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model. Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding. According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card ), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads. That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5. Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent. In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.” To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark , which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra. “We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch. The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year . Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for. According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio , which came online earlier this year. In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”

To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark , which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.

“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.

The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year . Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.
According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio , which came online earlier this year.

passages: In a Facebook post, Zuckerberg said that Muse Spark now powers an updated version of Meta AI, which users can access online at meta.ai or in the Meta AI app."Muse Spark is the first step on our scaling ladder and the first product of a ground-up overhaul of our AI efforts," a Meta announcement stated.Spark is designed to be particularly capable in areas tied to everyday personal use — tasks like visual understanding, health, shopping, and social content.
Mark Zuckerberg announced Wednesday that Meta Superintelligence Labs has reached its first major milestone: a new family of AI models called Muse, with the debut model, Spark, available now.

These scores could not be independently verified at this time, but Meta did release information on its testing methodology for Muse Spark.Overall, Meta reported mixed results when comparing Muse Spark to frontier models such as Claude Opus 4.6 Max, Gemini 3.1 Pro High, GPT 5.4 Xhigh, and Grok 4.2, with Muse Spark outperforming on some benchmarks and underperforming on others.Meta released a table comparing benchmark performance for Muse Spark.

When Zuckerberg first laid out his vision for "personal superintelligence" in a July 2025 manifesto, the ambition was an AI that helps people pursue their own goals rather than one controlled from the top down.To build it, Meta went on one of the most aggressive hiring sprees in recent memory, personally recruiting more than 50 researchers from rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, and bringing in former Scale AI chief Alexandr Wang to lead its new superintelligence research group.Then, just as quickly, Meta froze hiring altogether — citing routine budget planning — and restructured the team into four smaller units focused on research, superintelligence development, products, and infrastructure.

An MIT study circulating at the time found the vast majority of companies deploying AI were seeing no financial return.In his original manifesto, Zuckerberg drew a sharp philosophical line between Meta and its competitors, arguing that some AI labs want to concentrate superintelligence and pipe its output to humanity like a utility.
Meta released this benchmark comparison table.

Meta's ( META ) vast investments in its Meta Superintelligence Labs continue to pay dividends as the company unveiled its AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, on Monday. According to the social media giant, the models, which are available today, are designed to provide "state-of-the-art" performance across personal and professional AI agents and put the company squarely in the conversation for frontier-level AI. The software will eventually power more of the company's Muse AI agent, which Meta launched early last month and has exploded in popularity . The company says Muse Wonder and Wonder Full come with Active Memory and Active Focus. According to Meta, Active Memory allows AI models to bring information you need from across conversations, so you don't have to start from scratch each time you chat with the AI. Active Focus ensures the AI continues working on a task even if it encounters errors or roadblocks. Meta says it will also ask you for clarification or permission to perform tasks. The company claims that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full can take on the likes of Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) high-powered Fable 5.1, OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) GPT-6 Astra, and Google's ( GOOG , GOOGL ) Gemini 4 Argon in certain benchmarks. That's a massive swing in the right direction for Meta, which was seen as an also-ran in the AI race this time last year. It's also come at a high cost, though. The company has invested tens of billions of dollars, including $14 billion in Scale AI to acquire and hire co-founder and CEO Alexandr Wang, who now serves as Meta's chief AI officer. The spending spree, which also saw Meta poach AI workers and experts from its fellow tech behemoths, put serious pressure on the company's stock price. Shares of Meta are up just 6% over the last 12 months, slightly better than Microsoft, which has climbed a paltry 5%. The companies' hyperscaler rivals Amazon and Google, meanwhile, have jumped roughly 20% and 45%, respectively, in the same period. But with the debut of Meta's Muse agent and the unveiling of its Muse Charm device , which hits the market later this year, the company has managed to turn around the narrative that it can't hang with the leading AI firms. Next, the company will have to show if its software successes are paying off for its bottom line. Email Daniel Howley at dhowley@yahoofinance.com. Follow him on X at @DanielHowley . extraction.body: Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model. Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding. According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card ), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads. That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5. Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent. In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.” To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark , which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra. “We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch. The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year . Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for. According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio , which came online earlier this year. passages: The Fitbit Edge is essentially a new Charge 6, but it has more of a Pixel Watch aesthetic.
Squish Google’s smartwatch from the sides, and you’ve got the Edge.
It has a pill-shaped 1.34-inch OLED touch display inside a slender aluminum frame that is rated IP68 (5 ATM) for water and dust protection.
Google says the screen has 46 percent more viewable area compared to the Charge 6.
It’s very close in overall size to the Fitbit Air and uses the same magnetic charging puck.
Google is releasing its second Fitbit tracker of 2026, offering fans of the aging Charge 6 a more refined option.
Like the Air, this tracker is not an island within Google’s ecosystem.
You can pair multiple Google wearables with the Health app and wear whichever one you want.
There’s no need to re-pair or manually switch your health tracking over.
The app collects stats from the device you wear at any given time, changing as often as necessary.
So you could sport the Pixel Watch 5 during the day and the Edge when you hit the gym, for example.
You can use that to wake the device or start/pause workouts.
Most interactions will be handled with the touchscreen, though.
This allows you to track an outdoor activity without bringing your phone along for the ride.
The Edge also has an altimeter, optical heart rate sensor, and skin temperature sensor.
It comes in matte black, polished silver, satin pyrite (between silver and gold), and champagne gold.
If the tracker is away from your phone, it can still follow your activity all week with support for seven days of full health data storage (or 30 days of basic data).
However, the generous weeklong battery life does not include always-on display mode.
There is also a Stephen Curry Special Edition available for $220.

While there will eventually be third-party options, Google plans to have a line of add-on bands at launch, including the Active Sport (silicone with holes) for $40, Performance Loop (polyester fabric) for $50, Magnet Band (leather-ish but still silicone) at $60, and a Metal Links Band for a whopping $150.

Google also notes the Edge can stay with you for the long haul.
This is the company’s first repairable fitness tracker, which has been designed with a replaceable battery.

extraction.body: The Fitbit Edge offers more than the Air, but it’s not a real smartwatch. Google is releasing its second Fitbit tracker of 2026, offering fans of the aging Charge 6 a more refined option. The new Fitbit Edge slots right in between the Pixel Watch 5 and the Fitbit Air , featuring a compact screen and more health sensors than the Air. You won’t get all the apps and features of the Pixel Watch 5, but the Edge is only about half as expensive. The Fitbit Edge is essentially a new Charge 6, but it has more of a Pixel Watch aesthetic. Squish Google’s smartwatch from the sides, and you’ve got the Edge. It has a pill-shaped 1.34-inch OLED touch display inside a slender aluminum frame that is rated IP68 (5 ATM) for water and dust protection. Google says the screen has 46 percent more viewable area compared to the Charge 6. It’s very close in overall size to the Fitbit Air and uses the same magnetic charging puck. The Edge works with Android or iPhones via the Google Health app, and it can run for about seven days on a charge. If the tracker is away from your phone, it can still follow your activity all week with support for seven days of full health data storage (or 30 days of basic data). However, the generous weeklong battery life does not include always-on display mode. If you turn it on, battery life drops to about two days, barely longer than the Pixel Watch 5. The Fitbit Edge plays it right down the middle in Google’s wearable lineup, and not just in price and size—button count also splits the difference. The Pixel Watch has two buttons, the Air has none, and the Edge sports a single tactile side button. You can use that to wake the device or start/pause workouts. Most interactions will be handled with the touchscreen, though. The Edge will ship with a collection of fitness-focused experiences and watch faces, and you won’t be able to download more. While this looks a lot like the Pixel Watch’s software, it’s not a full version of WearOS. It can mirror notifications from your phone, but there’s no microphone or speaker. So responses are limited to pre-defined quick replies. Likewise, there’s no support for Gemini interactions. The Edge also lacks NFC, so there’s no Google Wallet tap-to-pay. One notable upgrade over the Fitbit Air is on-device GPS. This allows you to track an outdoor activity without bringing your phone along for the ride. However, Google says it’s not as accurate as the dual-band GPS radio in the Pixel Watch. The Edge does retain the ECG and blood oxygen sensor from the Pixel Watch, which you don’t get on the Air. The Edge also has an altimeter, optical heart rate sensor, and skin temperature sensor. All this data is beamed over Bluetooth 5.4 to the Google Health app (previously Fitbit), feeding all your data into the Gemini-powered Health Coach chatbot. The device comes with three months of Google Health Premium, without which you won’t get the AI features. Of course, some would probably prefer to skip the AI. The Premium subscription is $10 per month. It’s included with Google AI Pro, but you can disable the Health Coach if you want. Like the Pixel Watch, the Edge will come with the basic silicone Active Band for $180. There is also a Stephen Curry Special Edition available for $220. The Edge has a custom band connector similar to the Pixel Watch, but the plug is a different size. The Fitbit Edge is available for preorder today and will ship on October 27. It comes in matte black, polished silver, satin pyrite (between silver and gold), and champagne gold. So you could sport the Pixel Watch 5 during the day and the Edge when you hit the gym, for example. Google also notes the Edge can stay with you for the long haul. extraction.body: Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch. Priced at $179.99, it combines the Fitbit Air’s slim band with an OLED display for checking map directions, notifications, weather, and music controls. Like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, the Edge works with Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini. (You’ll need a Google Health Premium subscription to use it.) The coach can use your fitness, health, and medical information to put together weekly routines and workout plans, then adjust them around your schedule. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.) The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather. The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips. Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters. The Fitbit Edge is available to preorder through the Google Store, with store availability set for October 27. Color choices include Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon. There’s also a Stephen Curry Special Edition, priced at $219.99. Stuff / News / Fitbit Edge is Google’s mysterious wearable and may be a great Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5 middle ground
Leaked images and web page reveals Fitbit Edge as the successor to the Fitbit Charge

When Google released the next-generation Pixel line back in August, the marketing materials showed an unreleased wearable device hiding in plain sight alongside the Pixel 11, Pixel Watch 5 and others.
But what was it? Was it a Pixel Watch A-Series? A Fitbit Charge 7? Or something else entirely? Now, almost two months on. we may know a little more.
Android Headlines has published purported images of the unconfirmed device dubbed the Fitbit Edge, calling it a successor to the current Fitbit Charge 6 model last updated all the way back in 2023.

The ‘exclusive’ images appear to be press renders for the wearable with an oval-shaped display that could bridge the gap between the Pixel Watch 5 and the screen-free Fitbit Air . If you don’t want to go the full smartwatch and be bombarded with notifications, but still want to view your stats on a screen and get music and directions on a screen, this sounds like the best option.
Also, unlike the Pixel Watch 5, it’ll be compatible with both Android and iOS according to the report, but won’t have access to Wi-Fi or Cellular connectivity, or the Play Store.

According to the report, the ‘Fitbit Edge’ would have week-long battery life access to apps like Google Maps, YouTube Music, and Find My Phone, as well as a heart-rate sensor, step and activity tracker and built-in GPS and elevation tracking. We’d certainly imagine Google Pay will be available too, although the report doesn’t mention that.

The report adds that the colours will match the Pixel 11 Pro, with the Obsidian, Olive, and Canyon shades launching things, with other colours to follow. Swapping out the band will be as easy as pinching the mechanisms on the rear, the report says.
The Fitbit Edge may be out “very soon” and by the end of this month, according to the report. Pricing may be up to $200. We await the official announcement.

Prefer distinct sections with concrete evidence over generic context.

coreStoryFacts.text: The Fitbit Edge is essentially a new Charge 6, but it has more of a Pixel Watch aesthetic.
Squish Google’s smartwatch from the sides, and you’ve got the Edge.
It has a pill-shaped 1.34-inch OLED touch display inside a slender aluminum frame that is rated IP68 (5 ATM) for water and dust protection.
Google says the screen has 46 percent more viewable area compared to the Charge 6.
It’s very close in overall size to the Fitbit Air and uses the same magnetic charging puck.
Google is releasing its second Fitbit tracker of 2026, offering fans of the aging Charge 6 a more refined option.
Like the Air, this tracker is not an island within Google’s ecosystem.
You can pair multiple Google wearables with the Health app and wear whichever one you want.
There’s no need to re-pair or manually switch your health tracking over.
The app collects stats from the device you wear at any given time, changing as often as necessary.
So you could sport the Pixel Watch 5 during the day and the Edge when you hit the gym, for example.
You can use that to wake the device or start/pause workouts.
Most interactions will be handled with the touchscreen, though.
This allows you to track an outdoor activity without bringing your phone along for the ride.
The Edge also has an altimeter, optical heart rate sensor, and skin temperature sensor.
It comes in matte black, polished silver, satin pyrite (between silver and gold), and champagne gold.
If the tracker is away from your phone, it can still follow your activity all week with support for seven days of full health data storage (or 30 days of basic data).
However, the generous weeklong battery life does not include always-on display mode.
There is also a Stephen Curry Special Edition available for $220.

While there will eventually be third-party options, Google plans to have a line of add-on bands at launch, including the Active Sport (silicone with holes) for $40, Performance Loop (polyester fabric) for $50, Magnet Band (leather-ish but still silicone) at $60, and a Metal Links Band for a whopping $150.
So responses are limited to pre-defined quick replies.
Google also notes the Edge can stay with you for the long haul.
This is the company’s first repairable fitness tracker, which has been designed with a replaceable battery.
There will be service options to swap the battery, but Google still doesn’t recommend you open up the tracker yourself.

extraction.body: The Fitbit Edge offers more than the Air, but it’s not a real smartwatch. Google is releasing its second Fitbit tracker of 2026, offering fans of the aging Charge 6 a more refined option. The new Fitbit Edge slots right in between the Pixel Watch 5 and the Fitbit Air , featuring a compact screen and more health sensors than the Air. You won’t get all the apps and features of the Pixel Watch 5, but the Edge is only about half as expensive. The Fitbit Edge is essentially a new Charge 6, but it has more of a Pixel Watch aesthetic. Squish Google’s smartwatch from the sides, and you’ve got the Edge. It has a pill-shaped 1.34-inch OLED touch display inside a slender aluminum frame that is rated IP68 (5 ATM) for water and dust protection. Google says the screen has 46 percent more viewable area compared to the Charge 6. It’s very close in overall size to the Fitbit Air and uses the same magnetic charging puck. The Edge works with Android or iPhones via the Google Health app, and it can run for about seven days on a charge. If the tracker is away from your phone, it can still follow your activity all week with support for seven days of full health data storage (or 30 days of basic data). However, the generous weeklong battery life does not include always-on display mode. If you turn it on, battery life drops to about two days, barely longer than the Pixel Watch 5. The Fitbit Edge plays it right down the middle in Google’s wearable lineup, and not just in price and size—button count also splits the difference. The Pixel Watch has two buttons, the Air has none, and the Edge sports a single tactile side button. You can use that to wake the device or start/pause workouts. Most interactions will be handled with the touchscreen, though. The Edge will ship with a collection of fitness-focused experiences and watch faces, and you won’t be able to download more. While this looks a lot like the Pixel Watch’s software, it’s not a full version of WearOS. It can mirror notifications from your phone, but there’s no microphone or speaker. So responses are limited to pre-defined quick replies. Likewise, there’s no support for Gemini interactions. The Edge also lacks NFC, so there’s no Google Wallet tap-to-pay. One notable upgrade over the Fitbit Air is on-device GPS. This allows you to track an outdoor activity without bringing your phone along for the ride. However, Google says it’s not as accurate as the dual-band GPS radio in the Pixel Watch. The Edge does retain the ECG and blood oxygen sensor from the Pixel Watch, which you don’t get on the Air. The Edge also has an altimeter, optical heart rate sensor, and skin temperature sensor. All this data is beamed over Bluetooth 5.4 to the Google Health app (previously Fitbit), feeding all your data into the Gemini-powered Health Coach chatbot. The device comes with three months of Google Health Premium, without which you won’t get the AI features. Of course, some would probably prefer to skip the AI. The Premium subscription is $10 per month. It’s included with Google AI Pro, but you can disable the Health Coach if you want. Like the Pixel Watch, the Edge will come with the basic silicone Active Band for $180. There is also a Stephen Curry Special Edition available for $220. The Edge has a custom band connector similar to the Pixel Watch, but the plug is a different size. While there will eventually be third-party options, Google plans to have a line of add-on bands at launch, including the Active Sport (silicone with holes) for $40, Performance Loop (polyester fabric) for $50, Magnet Band (leather-ish but still silicone) at $60, and a Metal Links Band for a whopping $150. The Fitbit Edge is available for preorder today and will ship on October 27. It comes in matte black, polished silver, satin pyrite (between silver and gold), and champagne gold. While this is a much more expensive tracker compared to the $100 Fitbit Air, it’s only a little more than the Charge 6’s 2023 launch price of $160. The Pixel Watch 5 starts at $350. Like the Air, this tracker is not an island within Google’s ecosystem. You can pair multiple Google wearables with the Health app and wear whichever one you want. There’s no need to re-pair or manually switch your health tracking over. The app collects stats from the device you wear at any given time, changing as often as necessary. So you could sport the Pixel Watch 5 during the day and the Edge when you hit the gym, for example. Google also notes the Edge can stay with you for the long haul. This is the company’s first repairable fitness tracker, which has been designed with a replaceable battery. Note that does not mean user-replaceable . There will be service options to swap the battery, but Google still doesn’t recommend you open up the tracker yourself. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather. The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips. Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters. Stuff / News / Fitbit Edge is Google’s mysterious wearable and may be a great Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5 middle ground
Leaked images and web page reveals Fitbit Edge as the successor to the Fitbit Charge

When Google released the next-generation Pixel line back in August, the marketing materials showed an unreleased wearable device hiding in plain sight alongside the Pixel 11, Pixel Watch 5 and others.
But what was it? Was it a Pixel Watch A-Series? A Fitbit Charge 7? Or something else entirely? Now, almost two months on. we may know a little more.
Android Headlines has published purported images of the unconfirmed device dubbed the Fitbit Edge, calling it a successor to the current Fitbit Charge 6 model last updated all the way back in 2023.

The ‘exclusive’ images appear to be press renders for the wearable with an oval-shaped display that could bridge the gap between the Pixel Watch 5 and the screen-free Fitbit Air . If you don’t want to go the full smartwatch and be bombarded with notifications, but still want to view your stats on a screen and get music and directions on a screen, this sounds like the best option.
Also, unlike the Pixel Watch 5, it’ll be compatible with both Android and iOS according to the report, but won’t have access to Wi-Fi or Cellular connectivity, or the Play Store.

According to the report, the ‘Fitbit Edge’ would have week-long battery life access to apps like Google Maps, YouTube Music, and Find My Phone, as well as a heart-rate sensor, step and activity tracker and built-in GPS and elevation tracking. We’d certainly imagine Google Pay will be available too, although the report doesn’t mention that.

The report adds that the colours will match the Pixel 11 Pro, with the Obsidian, Olive, and Canyon shades launching things, with other colours to follow. Swapping out the band will be as easy as pinching the mechanisms on the rear, the report says.
The Fitbit Edge may be out “very soon” and by the end of this month, according to the report. Pricing may be up to $200. We await the official announcement.

extraction.body: Most startups fail. A new industry is giving their data an afterlife in AI. When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.” Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker , this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left. Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore. Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. The underlying models had been rewarded for cheating and communicating with each other, a new OpenAI report finds. Discover special offers, top stories, upcoming events, and more.

Here’s how it works . Spirit Airlines collapsed in May this year, but its data is set for a new lease of life after Google acquired it in an auction. The tech giant recently outbid AI company Mercor to acquire the de-identified data, according to court documents . Google bid $10 million, versus Mercor's $7.5 million, though reports note the bidding started around the $5 million mark. A third bidder also took part but was not named. A spokesperson for Google told ITPro the aim behind acquiring the defunct airline’s data lies in its potential use for AI training and product refinement. "We acquired part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines, which can be helpful in improving our products and AI models,” the spokesperson said. That same sentiment was highlighted by a spokesperson for Mercor, per reports from Business Insider . "Companies are sitting on decades of records that show how real work gets done, and that data is now some of the most valuable material for training and evaluating AI," the spokesperson said. "We partner with leading companies to license their operational data to the labs building the next generation of models. Spirit was that same process applied to a bankruptcy estate." The data bought by Google includes all productivity and collaboration data, which the filing notes includes everything from emails to chats, spreadsheets to calendars, as well as "core business systems and business applications data". This includes data on employee behavior and productivity, aircraft operations, and inventory, among other topics. Beyond that, Google has purchased workflow and process data from departments such as HR and marketing. In total, Google is picking up 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams chats, 30 million lines of code – but not records of loyalty program members or other customer data. Indeed, the data set does not include any consumer data or personal data, the filing noted, or any other information that could fall under data protection laws. The buyer was required to agree to not attempt to re-identify the data and link it to any person. The buyer is allowed to transfer the data set to third parties, however. "We will not receive any personal information from this dataset," the Google spokesperson added. "Any data we receive will be rigorously scrubbed of any personally identifiable information by a third party before receipt." Alongside the data, Google's $10 million also buys it all of Spirit's internally developed software and applications, including all the source code , plugins, data files, libraries, APIs and documentation. The battle for the business data reveals how desperate AI developers are for fresh material to feed AI, in particular for training models, though Google didn't specifically say that was the purpose of the data set. Anthropic has raised eyebrows via a campaign of buying up pre-2022 books to scan for training data, while Google was reportedly trying to buy code from Google Play Store app developers. SimpleClosure helps failed startups sell their old code, chats, and emails to AI companies, and Meta had to pause plans to track its own employees for AI training purposes amid internal backlash. All of this is to avoid issues like data exhaustion or hitting a data wall, in which they lack enough good quality data to build bigger models, and to avoid model collapse , when training data isn't of good enough quality — or is full of AI generated content. extraction.body: Can’t-miss innovations from the bleeding edge of science and tech Traditionally, books have been good for two things: reading, and looking nice on a shelf. To those building large language models, books are nothing more than fodder to be devoured en masse before being spit out like fishbone. Often, they’re happy to use digital books — or even better, pirated digital books, as Meta has been accused of doing, and as Anthropic was forced to pay a $1.5 billion settlement to authors for also doing. But many companies, including Anthropic, have turned to ingesting physical books instead, which they can buy countless used copies of on the cheap. According to the settled lawsuit , Anthropic used a hydraulic powered cutting machine to neatly remove the pages from the books it procured from book resellers and then scanned them using industrial-grade imaging equipment. In other words, it was literally ripping off authors’ books to train its AI. This process took advantage of a legal concept known as first-sale doctrine, which allows a buyer to do what they want with a purchase without the original copyright holder’s say-so. And since Anthropic was turning the original physical texts into digital ones — rather than redistributing them as new copies — a judge found this to be “transformative,” and therefore protected by fair use. Now, as 404 Media reports , this practice has become prevalent enough that even well-established book sellers are looking to cash in on the AI boom. One called ISBNdb, which boasts the “world’s largest book database,” extolls that the “world’s best AI training data is setting on a shelf,” upholding these physical texts as uncorrupted by shoddy AI writing that’s already polluted so much of the internet (and indeed, newer books ). “Print books from the pre-LLM era are structurally guaranteed to be free of this contamination. That alone is a significant advantage,” it explains in an article on its website, as quoted by 404 . “Physical books published before this date [pre-2022] are structurally clean of modern poisoning tools.” Once focused on helping libraries, distributors, and book shops find and sell books, ISBNdb now helps AI companies bulk-buy anywhere between 1,000 to one million books per order, according to 404 . Traditionally, books have been good for two things: reading, and looking nice on a shelf.

To those building large language models, books are nothing more than fodder to be devoured en masse before being spit out like fishbone. Often, they’re happy to use digital books — or even better, pirated digital books, as Meta has been accused of doing, and as Anthropic was forced to pay a $1.5 billion settlement to authors for also doing.

But many companies, including Anthropic, have turned to ingesting physical books instead, which they can buy countless used copies of on the cheap. In late June, AI agent startup Warmly announced it would be acquired by HubSpot.

extraction.body: When a startup shuts down or gets acquired, its most valuable asset may no longer be its code, patents, or customer lists—but rather the communication records its employees used every day. As artificial intelligence (AI) evolves from chatbots into autonomous digital workers, AI data companies are aggressively acquiring internal datasets from defunct companies, including Slack chat logs, Google Drive files, emails, and Zoom meeting recordings, with individual offers reaching as high as $300,000 (approximately NT$9.6 million). AI data company Mercor has been actively targeting failed or acquired startups, seeking to purchase their internal datasets. Mercor is the data supplier behind AI giants such as OpenAI and Anthropic, and its reach has now extended from publicly available internet content into the most private communication trails within enterprises. In late June, AI agent startup Warmly announced it would be acquired by HubSpot. Just eight days later, Warmly founder and CEO Max Greenwald received an email from Mercor seeking to purchase or license Warmly's internal data—including Slack chat logs, GitHub records, Asana project management content, Google Drive files, and employee meeting transcripts—with offers reaching up to $300,000. In the days that followed, Warmly received multiple similar inquiries from Mercor and other AI data companies, but Greenwald ultimately turned them all down. AI data companies buying books and startup code is hardly news, but as AI giants accelerate development of autonomous AI agents, the nature of data demand is undergoing a fundamental shift. Public internet content, books, and code are no longer sufficient to support the training needs of next-generation AI models. Bobby Samuels, CEO of data company Protege, put it bluntly: AI labs have essentially "scraped the entire internet," and what they need now is real human-to-human interaction. Protege primarily helps companies assess whether their internal data qualifies for sale or licensing. This year alone, the company has processed at least $100 million (approximately NT$3 billion) in data transactions—a more than threefold increase from roughly $30 million (approximately NT$1 billion) in the same period last year. The following table shows the change in data transaction volume handled by Protege: Note: Figures disclosed by Protege CEO Bobby Samuels. When AI transitions from a chatbot that simply answers questions to a digital worker that can genuinely share the workload, it needs far more than just "what the answer is"—it needs to understand "how humans actually get work done." For example: how a human employee responds when a customer raises an issue; how an engineer troubleshoots step by step when an IT system fails; how a finance staffer handles an invoice discrepancy; how a salesperson updates customer records in a CRM system. Even the specific clicks and inputs an employee makes when software suddenly throws an error. These real-world work experiences are nearly impossible to find on the public internet. An IT ticket might record "employee unable to log into website," followed by Slack chat logs showing engineers discussing the root cause, emails containing the final resolution, and a GitHub commit documenting a related code fix. To a human, this is just routine troubleshooting. But to an AI agent, it is an entire set of highly valuable "on-the-job training"—precisely the material needed to train AI systems capable of autonomous task execution. This emerging business is far more complicated than it appears on the surface. Companies involved must navigate thorny issues around privacy and intellectual property. Slack conversations may contain customer information, emails may include employee names, meeting transcripts may reveal trade secrets, and data from healthcare companies may even involve patient privacy. All such data must undergo anonymization before it can be legally sold or licensed to AI companies. Warmly CEO Greenwald's decision to decline selling internal data reflects the reservations some entrepreneurs hold about such transactions. Even when a company is about to be acquired or has already shut down, internal communication records may still implicate the privacy of employees, customers, and partners. Yet the rapid expansion of the data trading market signals that the AI industry's demand for "real work data" is forming an irreversible wave. Protege's data transaction volume surging from $30 million to $100 million in a single year is the most direct quantitative proof of this trend. As the AI agent race heats up, the digital legacies of failed companies—those traces of human work scattered across Slack, email, and meeting recordings—are becoming the scarcest raw material for AI training. And how to strike a balance between data demand and privacy protection will be the core challenge this emerging industry must confront going forward. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups.
Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets.
In total, Google is picking up 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams chats, 30 million lines of code – but not records of loyalty program members or other customer data.
Spirit Airlines collapsed in May this year, but its data is set for a new lease of life after Google acquired it in an auction.

Alongside the data, Google's $10 million also buys it all of Spirit's internally developed software and applications, including all the source code , plugins, data files, libraries, APIs and documentation.
The tech giant recently outbid AI company Mercor to acquire the de-identified data, according to court documents .
Google bid $10 million, versus Mercor's $7.5 million, though reports note the bidding started around the $5 million mark.
"We acquired part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines, which can be helpful in improving our products and AI models,” the spokesperson said.
