extraction.body: Most startups fail. A new industry is giving their data an afterlife in AI. When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.” Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker , this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left. Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore. Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. The underlying models had been rewarded for cheating and communicating with each other, a new OpenAI report finds. Discover special offers, top stories, upcoming events, and more.

Google bid $10 million, versus Mercor's $7.5 million, though reports note the bidding started around the $5 million mark. A third bidder also took part but was not named. A spokesperson for Google told ITPro the aim behind acquiring the defunct airline’s data lies in its potential use for AI training and product refinement. "We acquired part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines, which can be helpful in improving our products and AI models,” the spokesperson said. That same sentiment was highlighted by a spokesperson for Mercor, per reports from Business Insider . "Companies are sitting on decades of records that show how real work gets done, and that data is now some of the most valuable material for training and evaluating AI," the spokesperson said. "We partner with leading companies to license their operational data to the labs building the next generation of models. Spirit was that same process applied to a bankruptcy estate." The data bought by Google includes all productivity and collaboration data, which the filing notes includes everything from emails to chats, spreadsheets to calendars, as well as "core business systems and business applications data". This includes data on employee behavior and productivity, aircraft operations, and inventory, among other topics. Beyond that, Google has purchased workflow and process data from departments such as HR and marketing. In total, Google is picking up 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams chats, 30 million lines of code – but not records of loyalty program members or other customer data. Indeed, the data set does not include any consumer data or personal data, the filing noted, or any other information that could fall under data protection laws. The buyer was required to agree to not attempt to re-identify the data and link it to any person. The buyer is allowed to transfer the data set to third parties, however. "We will not receive any personal information from this dataset," the Google spokesperson added. "Any data we receive will be rigorously scrubbed of any personally identifiable information by a third party before receipt." Alongside the data, Google's $10 million also buys it all of Spirit's internally developed software and applications, including all the source code , plugins, data files, libraries, APIs and documentation. The battle for the business data reveals how desperate AI developers are for fresh material to feed AI, in particular for training models, though Google didn't specifically say that was the purpose of the data set. SimpleClosure helps failed startups sell their old code, chats, and emails to AI companies, and Meta had to pause plans to track its own employees for AI training purposes amid internal backlash. All of this is to avoid issues like data exhaustion or hitting a data wall, in which they lack enough good quality data to build bigger models, and to avoid model collapse , when training data isn't of good enough quality — or is full of AI generated content. sources.title: AI Data Firm Offers Up to $300,000 for Internal Chat Logs of Defunct Startups - BigGo Finance
passages: When a startup shuts down or gets acquired, its most valuable asset may no longer be its code, patents, or customer lists—but rather the communication records its employees used every day.

As artificial intelligence (AI) evolves from chatbots into autonomous digital workers, AI data companies are aggressively acquiring internal datasets from defunct companies, including Slack chat logs, Google Drive files, emails, and Zoom meeting recordings, with individual offers reaching as high as $300,000 (approximately NT$9.6 million).
In late June, AI agent startup Warmly announced it would be acquired by HubSpot.

extraction.body: When a startup shuts down or gets acquired, its most valuable asset may no longer be its code, patents, or customer lists—but rather the communication records its employees used every day. As artificial intelligence (AI) evolves from chatbots into autonomous digital workers, AI data companies are aggressively acquiring internal datasets from defunct companies, including Slack chat logs, Google Drive files, emails, and Zoom meeting recordings, with individual offers reaching as high as $300,000 (approximately NT$9.6 million). AI data company Mercor has been actively targeting failed or acquired startups, seeking to purchase their internal datasets. Mercor is the data supplier behind AI giants such as OpenAI and Anthropic, and its reach has now extended from publicly available internet content into the most private communication trails within enterprises. In late June, AI agent startup Warmly announced it would be acquired by HubSpot. Just eight days later, Warmly founder and CEO Max Greenwald received an email from Mercor seeking to purchase or license Warmly's internal data—including Slack chat logs, GitHub records, Asana project management content, Google Drive files, and employee meeting transcripts—with offers reaching up to $300,000. In the days that followed, Warmly received multiple similar inquiries from Mercor and other AI data companies, but Greenwald ultimately turned them all down. AI data companies buying books and startup code is hardly news, but as AI giants accelerate development of autonomous AI agents, the nature of data demand is undergoing a fundamental shift. Public internet content, books, and code are no longer sufficient to support the training needs of next-generation AI models. Bobby Samuels, CEO of data company Protege, put it bluntly: AI labs have essentially "scraped the entire internet," and what they need now is real human-to-human interaction. Protege primarily helps companies assess whether their internal data qualifies for sale or licensing. This year alone, the company has processed at least $100 million (approximately NT$3 billion) in data transactions—a more than threefold increase from roughly $30 million (approximately NT$1 billion) in the same period last year. The following table shows the change in data transaction volume handled by Protege: Note: Figures disclosed by Protege CEO Bobby Samuels. When AI transitions from a chatbot that simply answers questions to a digital worker that can genuinely share the workload, it needs far more than just "what the answer is"—it needs to understand "how humans actually get work done." For example: how a human employee responds when a customer raises an issue; how an engineer troubleshoots step by step when an IT system fails; how a finance staffer handles an invoice discrepancy; how a salesperson updates customer records in a CRM system. Even the specific clicks and inputs an employee makes when software suddenly throws an error. These real-world work experiences are nearly impossible to find on the public internet. An IT ticket might record "employee unable to log into website," followed by Slack chat logs showing engineers discussing the root cause, emails containing the final resolution, and a GitHub commit documenting a related code fix. To a human, this is just routine troubleshooting. But to an AI agent, it is an entire set of highly valuable "on-the-job training"—precisely the material needed to train AI systems capable of autonomous task execution. This emerging business is far more complicated than it appears on the surface. Companies involved must navigate thorny issues around privacy and intellectual property. Slack conversations may contain customer information, emails may include employee names, meeting transcripts may reveal trade secrets, and data from healthcare companies may even involve patient privacy. All such data must undergo anonymization before it can be legally sold or licensed to AI companies. Warmly CEO Greenwald's decision to decline selling internal data reflects the reservations some entrepreneurs hold about such transactions. Even when a company is about to be acquired or has already shut down, internal communication records may still implicate the privacy of employees, customers, and partners. Yet the rapid expansion of the data trading market signals that the AI industry's demand for "real work data" is forming an irreversible wave. Protege's data transaction volume surging from $30 million to $100 million in a single year is the most direct quantitative proof of this trend. As the AI agent race heats up, the digital legacies of failed companies—those traces of human work scattered across Slack, email, and meeting recordings—are becoming the scarcest raw material for AI training. And how to strike a balance between data demand and privacy protection will be the core challenge this emerging industry must confront going forward. extraction.body: BANGKOK/WASHINGTON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday against "complacency" in global financial markets, citing risks from an artificial intelligence-driven selloff, rising government bond yields, or cyberattacks as potential threats facing still-resilient markets. The IMF said in its ‌Global Financial Stability Report that AI investments have so far helped offset economic drags from war in the Middle East and overall policy ‌uncertainty. But it noted "growing evidence" that AI capabilities may not require as much investment, or the potential economic gains may not be as large as expected. "An AI market correction will affect ​the real economy," Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director in the IMF's Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said at a press briefing in Bangkok. He said while global risk sentiment was very strong, underpinned by solid earnings and optimism about AI, such "resilience is not necessarily safety". An AI correction would have impacts on wealth and investment that could spill into broader markets, he said. The risk of such a selloff, as well as a spike in sovereign bond yields or a major cyberattack, were among "plausible near-term ‌catalysts" that policymakers should monitor, the IMF said ⁠in its report. While each of these risks might be manageable on its own, they also could trigger vulnerabilities with potential systemic implications, Vamvakidis said. Should the momentum in AI investment slow, the IMF noted growing leverage in the sector could exacerbate any shock ⁠by triggering forced selling and higher volatility. For example, hyperscalers now represent 10% of global investment-grade bond issuance, up from less than 1% in 2024. "The consequences of an AI correction could be global," the IMF warned, as it called on policymakers to curb leverage use, including derivatives and margin loans, where it is "excessive." The IMF said ​bond ​market risks have worsened since its April report, as higher energy prices have driven ​government bond yields up. Historically high sovereign debt levels and ‌unresolved fiscal deficits in major economies were adding to the pressure. "The market is concerned about absorption potential of the huge issuance that is coming from the sovereigns and increasingly also from the private sector, at the time that central banks are shrinking their balances, and we have to rely more on price-sensitive investors," Vamvakidis said. The IMF report said bond markets have so far dealt with the stress well, with hedge funds able to unwind some of their repurchase agreement borrowing without triggering turmoil in repo markets. The group called on policymakers to put public debt on a sustainable path. On cyber threats, the ‌IMF said that a lack of resources, particularly in emerging markets, and a growing reliance ​on a small number of critical providers was making cyber defense more difficult. In over 70% of ​cases so far in 2026, software providers have had almost no ​time to patch vulnerabilities before they were exploited, a 20 percentage point jump from a year ago, the IMF said. ‌It noted that while AI can help address some of these risks, ​models were also making cyberattacks more ​sophisticated. The IMF cautioned that a major attack affecting a critical service or financial institution could undermine confidence, which could quickly ripple throughout markets. It called on policymakers to boost cybersecurity capacity, including stricter oversight of third-party technology vendors. The IMF said its stress test models showed banks' ​capital cushions remained robust even in a hypothetical downturn ‌triggered by an AI slowdown and bond market fragility. But it warned of "pockets of weakness," with banks representing 22% of global ​banking assets found to have "weak" capital levels under the test, up from 18% under the 2025 test. (Reporting by Pete Schroeder in ​Washington and Selena Li in Bangkok; Editing by Andrea Ricci and John Mair)

extraction.body: BANGKOK/WASHINGTON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday against "complacency" in global financial markets, citing risks from an artificial intelligence-driven selloff, rising government bond yields, or cyberattacks as potential threats facing still-resilient markets. The IMF said in its ‌Global Financial Stability Report that AI investments have so far helped offset economic drags from war in the Middle East and overall policy ‌uncertainty. But it noted "growing evidence" that AI capabilities may not require as much investment, or the potential economic gains may not be as large as expected. "An AI market correction will affect ​the real economy," Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director in the IMF's Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said at a press briefing in Bangkok. He said while global risk sentiment was very strong, underpinned by solid earnings and optimism about AI, such "resilience is not necessarily safety". An AI correction would have impacts on wealth and investment that could spill into broader markets, he said. The risk of such a selloff, as well as a spike in sovereign bond yields or a major cyberattack, were among "plausible near-term ‌catalysts" that policymakers should monitor, the IMF said ⁠in its report. While each of these risks might be manageable on its own, they also could trigger vulnerabilities with potential systemic implications, Vamvakidis said. Should the momentum in AI investment slow, the IMF noted growing leverage in the sector could exacerbate any shock ⁠by triggering forced selling and higher volatility. For example, hyperscalers now represent 10% of global investment-grade bond issuance, up from less than 1% in 2024. "The consequences of an AI correction could be global," the IMF warned, as it called on policymakers to curb leverage use, including derivatives and margin loans, where it is "excessive." The IMF said ​bond ​market risks have worsened since its April report, as higher energy prices have driven ​government bond yields up. Historically high sovereign debt levels and ‌unresolved fiscal deficits in major economies were adding to the pressure. "The market is concerned about absorption potential of the huge issuance that is coming from the sovereigns and increasingly also from the private sector, at the time that central banks are shrinking their balances, and we have to rely more on price-sensitive investors," Vamvakidis said. The IMF report said bond markets have so far dealt with the stress well, with hedge funds able to unwind some of their repurchase agreement borrowing without triggering turmoil in repo markets. The group called on policymakers to put public debt on a sustainable path. On cyber threats, the ‌IMF said that a lack of resources, particularly in emerging markets, and a growing reliance ​on a small number of critical providers was making cyber defense more difficult. In over 70% of ​cases so far in 2026, software providers have had almost no ​time to patch vulnerabilities before they were exploited, a 20 percentage point jump from a year ago, the IMF said. ‌It noted that while AI can help address some of these risks, ​models were also making cyberattacks more ​sophisticated. The IMF cautioned that a major attack affecting a critical service or financial institution could undermine confidence, which could quickly ripple throughout markets. It called on policymakers to boost cybersecurity capacity, including stricter oversight of third-party technology vendors. The IMF said its stress test models showed banks' ​capital cushions remained robust even in a hypothetical downturn ‌triggered by an AI slowdown and bond market fragility. But it warned of "pockets of weakness," with banks representing 22% of global ​banking assets found to have "weak" capital levels under the test, up from 18% under the 2025 test. (Reporting by Pete Schroeder in ​Washington and Selena Li in Bangkok; Editing by Andrea Ricci and John Mair)

Such a sell-off, a spike in sovereign bond yields or a major cyberattack were among the "plausible near-term catalysts" policymakers should monitor, the fund said. "These risks by themselves do not necessarily threaten financial stability but could become systemic...if they are amplified by underlying vulnerabilities," the IMF said in the semi-annual report, adding that financial stability risks remain elevated. The IMF said AI investment had so far helped offset economic headwinds from the war in the Middle East and broader policy uncertainty. However, it noted "growing evidence" that AI capabilities might not require as much investment as previously expected, or that the potential economic gains might be smaller than anticipated. A slowdown in momentum could expose growing leverage in the AI sector, potentially exacerbating any shock through forced selling and increased volatility. For example, hyperscalers now account for 10% of global investment-grade bond issuance, up from less than 1% in 2024. The IMF said bond market risks had worsened since its April report, as higher energy prices pushed government bond yields upwards. Policymakers may need to raise interest rates to tackle inflation, potentially worsening debt burdens for countries refinancing short-term debt. In addition, more price-sensitive investors could put further upward pressure on yields, while market liquidity could deteriorate amid increased volatility. Each of these factors could trigger a sudden rise in bond yields, the IMF warned, adding that historically high sovereign debt levels and unresolved fiscal deficits in major economies were intensifying the pressure. However, bond markets had so far weathered the stress, with hedge funds able to unwind some of their borrowing through repurchase agreements without triggering turmoil in repo markets, it said. The IMF urged policymakers to put public debt on a sustainable path. The fund also warned that technological developments and growing reliance on a small number of critical service providers were making cyber defence more difficult. In more than 70% of cases so far in 2026, software providers had almost no time to patch vulnerabilities before they were exploited, a rise of 20 percentage points from a year earlier, the IMF said. The IMF said AI investment had so far helped offset economic headwinds from the war in the Middle East and broader policy uncertainty. However, it noted "growing evidence" that AI capabilities might not require as much investment as previously expected, or that the potential economic gains might be smaller than anticipated.

A slowdown in momentum could expose growing leverage in the AI sector, potentially exacerbating any shock through forced selling and increased volatility. For example, hyperscalers now account for 10% of global investment-grade bond issuance, up from less than 1% in 2024.
"The consequences of an AI correction could be global," the IMF warned, urging policymakers to curb excessive leverage, including through derivatives and margin loans.

The IMF said bond market risks had worsened since its April report, as higher energy prices pushed government bond yields upwards. Policymakers may need to raise interest rates to tackle inflation, potentially worsening debt burdens for countries refinancing short-term debt. In addition, more price-sensitive investors could put further upward pressure on yields, while market liquidity could deteriorate amid increased volatility.

Each of these factors could trigger a sudden rise in bond yields, the IMF warned, adding that historically high sovereign debt levels and unresolved fiscal deficits in major economies were intensifying the pressure.

However, bond markets had so far weathered the stress, with hedge funds able to unwind some of their borrowing through repurchase agreements without triggering turmoil in repo markets, it said. The IMF urged policymakers to put public debt on a sustainable path.

The fund also warned that technological developments and growing reliance on a small number of critical service providers were making cyber defence more difficult. In more than 70% of cases so far in 2026, software providers had almost no time to patch vulnerabilities before they were exploited, a rise of 20 percentage points from a year earlier, the IMF said.
AI could help address some of these risks, but AI models were also making cyberattacks more sophisticated.

A major attack affecting a critical service or financial institution could undermine confidence and quickly send shockwaves through financial markets, the IMF cautioned. It urged policymakers to strengthen cybersecurity capabilities, including through stricter oversight of third-party technology vendors.

The IMF said its stress-test models showed that banks' capital buffers remained robust even under a hypothetical downturn triggered by an AI slowdown and bond market fragility. However, it warned of "pockets of weakness", with banks accounting for 22% of global banking assets found to have weak capital levels under the test, up from 18% in the 2025 assessment.

Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from one ship, the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries, Radev said in a video posted to social media. The crew, which included seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijan citizens, reported the ship's deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. One crew member from the sunken vessel was rescued, Radev added, without providing details about the others aboard. The strikes on the two ships occurred 18 and 17 miles (29 and 27.5 kilometers) from the Bulgarian coast. During an emergency meeting of Bulgaria’s Security Council on Tuesday, Radev called the attacks “absolutely unacceptable” and said Bulgaria was seeking NATO and European Union assistance. While authorities do not possess clear evidence on who was responsible for the drone attacks, “logic, as I have already stated, indicates that the result is in favor of the Russian Federation,” Radev said. The attacks come exactly a week after sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. A Togo-flagged ship sank, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated the 18-member crew from a Pulau-flagged vessel. Ukraine’s military did not conduct any operations near the locations of last week's drone strikes, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who pointed the finger at Russia. A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said. Russia did not immediately comment on Tuesday's incident. Radev said he would summon the Russian ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, for a conversation Tuesday. SOFIA, Bulgaria (AP) — Drones struck two ships in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from one ship, the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries, Radev said in a video posted to social media.
The crew, which included seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijan citizens, reported the ship's deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones.

One crew member from the sunken vessel was rescued, Radev added, without providing details about the others aboard. The strikes on the two ships occurred 18 and 17 miles (29 and 27.5 kilometers) from the Bulgarian coast.
During an emergency meeting of Bulgaria’s Security Council on Tuesday, Radev called the attacks “absolutely unacceptable” and said Bulgaria was seeking NATO and European Union assistance.

While authorities do not possess clear evidence on who was responsible for the drone attacks, “logic, as I have already stated, indicates that the result is in favor of the Russian Federation,” Radev said.

The attacks come exactly a week after sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. A Togo-flagged ship sank, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated the 18-member crew from a Pulau-flagged vessel.
Ukraine’s military did not conduct any operations near the locations of last week's drone strikes, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who pointed the finger at Russia.

A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said.
Russia did not immediately comment on Tuesday's incident.
Radev said he would summon the Russian ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, for a conversation Tuesday.

extraction.body: LOS ANGELES , Oct. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR ), a U.S.-based Embodied AI ("EAI") robotics company that has proposed to acquire Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc.'s (NASDAQ: FFAI ) EAI Robotics business, today highlighted FFAI's announcement that this week's Investor Weekly Report from Faraday Future ("FF") Founder and Global CEO YT Jia has been rescheduled to October 14. Additionally, FFR and FFAI will host a joint new product launch event on October 14, 2026, featuring four major launches focused on embodied AI robotics, Physical AI education, and developer enablement. The event will feature FF Nova, FF's first embodied AI humanoid robot designed for developers and educational institutions, through an exclusive, invitation-only launch. FFAI has also announced that FF will introduce FF Nova Mini, a humanoid robot designed for foundational Physical AI education, along with the EAI Education Ecosystem Brain and Curriculum Skills 2.0. In addition, FF will launch the FF Nova Developer Reinforcement Learning Platform and open exclusive early access to the developer community. FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR ) is a U.S.-based Embodied AI (EAI) robotics company that is in the process of acquiring the FF EAI Robotics business. Upon completion of the acquisition, the Company will focus on the research and development, manufacturing, commercialization, and deployment of intelligent robotic technologies, products, and industry solutions. The Company is committed to building a "Four-Core Full-Stack" AI ecosystem covering the full lifecycle of robotics, consisting of EAI Brain & Developer Platform, EAI Devices, Industry Productivity Solutions, and EAI Data Factory. Guided by the technology and product philosophy of "One Brain, Multi-forms, Multi-capabilities," the Company aims to empower humanoid, biomimetic, and other robotic form factors through a unified EAI Brain, while continuously expanding their multi-task and multi-scenario capabilities. The ecosystem is designed to support the full robotics lifecycle, including R&D, deployment, data collection and training, operations, and commercial applications. The FF EAI Robotics business has already achieved commercial deliveries of humanoid and biomimetic robotic products. Through its multi-form-factor robotic products, EAI technology platform, closed-loop data capabilities, and industry solutions, the business continues to advance the scaled adoption of robotics across real-world applications. The Company also operates RoboShare, a robot-sharing and services platform designed to connect robotic assets, service capabilities, customer demand, and ecosystem partners, further strengthening its robotics commercialization and service ecosystem. Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from one ship, the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries, Radev said in a video posted to social media. The crew, which included seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijan citizens, reported the ship's deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. One crew member from the sunken vessel was rescued, Radev added, without providing details about the others aboard. The strikes on the two ships occurred 18 and 17 miles (29 and 27.5 kilometers) from the Bulgarian coast. During an emergency meeting of Bulgaria’s Security Council on Tuesday, Radev called the attacks “absolutely unacceptable” and said Bulgaria was seeking NATO and European Union assistance. While authorities do not possess clear evidence on who was responsible for the drone attacks, “logic, as I have already stated, indicates that the result is in favor of the Russian Federation,” Radev said. The attacks come exactly a week after sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. A Togo-flagged ship sank, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated the 18-member crew from a Pulau-flagged vessel. Ukraine’s military did not conduct any operations near the locations of last week's drone strikes, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who pointed the finger at Russia. A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said. Russia did not immediately comment on Tuesday's incident. Radev said he would summon the Russian ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, for a conversation Tuesday. extraction.body: IonQ will acquire Zero Trust security firm Elisity in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion, pairing IonQ’s quantum cryptography with Elisity’s enterprise security platform. The acquisition aims to address current cyber threats and prepare customers for the approaching quantum era, a transition highlighted by recent White House directives. Elisity has demonstrated significant growth, “doubling its revenue and its customer base year-over-year,” and brings a strong foothold in the more than $10 billion microsegmentation market. “With Elisity and its team as part of IonQ, we will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure,” said Niccolo de Masi , Chairman and CEO of IonQ. IonQ’s acquisition of Elisity directly addresses the escalating need for layered cybersecurity, integrating Zero Trust principles with emerging quantum defenses. This move aligns with a recent White House executive order from June 22, 2026, which prioritizes quantum innovation and the federal government’s transition to PQC standards. Elisity’s core offering, IdentityGraph, correlates identity, asset and risk information to enforce least-privilege access policies for users, devices and increasingly, AI agents. Teams can simulate these policies before implementation, reducing attack surfaces and limiting the spread of potential breaches. By integrating IdentityGraph with IonQ’s cryptographic protections, the companies aim to offer a solution that not only safeguards sensitive data with PQC and QKD but also controls who and what can access it, creating a multi-layered defense. The combined roadmap will extend IdentityGraph with cryptographic inventory and risk information, enhancing its capabilities for quantum-era security. The urgency of this integration is highlighted by the dual challenges enterprises currently face: containing attacks operating at machine speed and preparing for the long-term threat posed by quantum computers. “Our customers need to prioritize cryptography initiatives while securing existing assets to keep essential operations running,” said James Winebrenner, CEO of Elisity. “With IonQ, we will be optimally positioned to partner with them to modernize their crypto-agility programs, accelerate cryptography capabilities while advancing their holistic Zero Trust posture and deploy hybrid-cybersecurity solutions today that are prepared for the quantum future.” Elisity’s existing customer base, exceeding 100 global deployments and including deep relationships with Chief Information Security Officers, provides IonQ with an expanded channel to market its quantum security offerings to both enterprise and government networks. IonQ anticipates significant cross-selling opportunities, using Elisity’s established enterprise presence to introduce its PQC, QKD and broader quantum computing services. This acquisition builds upon IonQ’s existing momentum in quantum security, having already deployed quantum-safe national communications networks in Switzerland, Poland, Romania and Slovakia, and serving global customers with quantum-safe defense-in-depth solutions. In the second quarter of 2026, IonQ reported 40 percent year-over-year growth in multiproduct revenue, demonstrating customer demand for integrated quantum solutions. The strategic rationale behind the acquisition extends beyond immediate security enhancements. As de Masi first stated, the arrival of Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted. He drew a parallel to the acquisition of SkyWater Technology , noting that Elisity will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to IonQ’s quantum security strategy, establishing a strong growth platform for serving customers and creating shareholder value. Elisity will continue operating under its current leadership, including CEO James Winebrenner, ensuring continuity for existing customers and partners. The company, founded in 2019, has a global employee footprint and a growing number of Fortune 500 clients, IonQ says. IonQ’s approach of investing in acquired technologies suggests a commitment to supporting innovation and building upon Elisity’s existing strengths, creating a synergistic relationship that addresses the evolving landscape of cybersecurity threats. The transaction, expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, remains subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approval. As I said first, Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted. By continuing to use our website you agree to our policies COLLEGE PARK, Maryland, October 12, 2026 — Quantum computing company IonQ Inc. has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire enterprise cybersecurity firm Elisity Inc. in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion , expanding its enterprise security business and strengthening its strategy to address emerging cybersecurity challenges associated with advances in quantum computing. The proposed transaction includes up to $150 million in performance-based earn-outs linked to specified business milestones. The number of IonQ common shares to be issued will be calculated using a volume-weighted average price, subject to a collar ranging from $33.07 to $49.61 per share . The acquisition is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to required regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. The agreement remains pending until the transaction is completed. Founded in 2019, Elisity develops an identity-based microsegmentation platform that helps organizations manage network access across information technology (IT), operational technology (OT), Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and enterprise workloads. According to the companies’ transaction announcement, Elisity has more than 100 customer deployments worldwide, providing IonQ with an established enterprise cybersecurity presence. The acquisition comes as organizations assess the long-term implications of quantum computing for existing encryption systems. One major concern is the harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL) threat, in which attackers collect and store encrypted information today in the hope of decrypting it in the future using more powerful computing capabilities. Widely deployed public-key cryptographic systems, including those based on RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC), could be vulnerable to sufficiently capable quantum computers. However, the timeline for developing machines capable of breaking these systems at scale remains uncertain. IonQ intends to combine its quantum security technologies with Elisity’s zero-trust capabilities to address complementary aspects of enterprise cybersecurity. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is designed to protect information against attacks from future quantum computers, while identity-based microsegmentation restricts unauthorized communications within enterprise networks. Microsegmentation can reduce the ability of attackers to move laterally after compromising an initial device or system. It does not, however, independently prevent the future decryption of encrypted data that has already been intercepted. Organizations facing HNDL risks must also assess their cryptographic systems, protect sensitive information, and plan migrations to appropriate post-quantum standards. IonQ Chief Executive Officer Niccolo de Masi has positioned the transaction as part of the company’s broader effort to expand its security offerings and help customers prepare for the quantum era. The acquisition could provide IonQ with additional enterprise relationships through which to introduce complementary cybersecurity and cryptographic products. The proposed Elisity acquisition complements IonQ’s broader strategy to expand beyond quantum computing hardware into quantum networking, cybersecurity, and semiconductor manufacturing. IonQ’s earlier acquisition of SkyWater Technology expanded its capabilities in semiconductor manufacturing and related technologies. Elisity would add an established enterprise security platform, creating opportunities to connect quantum security offerings with network access controls used by corporate and government customers. The combined strategy has three principal components: Quantum hardware and manufacturing: IonQ develops trapped-ion quantum computing systems and has expanded its semiconductor manufacturing capabilities through SkyWater Technology. Cryptographic protection: IonQ’s quantum networking and security initiatives include technologies intended to support secure communications and the transition toward quantum-resistant protection. Enterprise network enforcement: Elisity’s identity-based microsegmentation platform helps security teams apply least-privilege access policies to users, devices, applications, workloads, and other network entities. The companies expect the combination to create opportunities for cross-selling, strengthen relationships with enterprise security teams, and support the development of integrated security products. Potential applications include improving visibility into cryptographic dependencies and helping organizations prioritize security upgrades. These benefits remain prospective. Their realization will depend on regulatory approval, successful integration, customer adoption, and the technical and commercial execution of the combined product strategy. Elisity develops an enterprise zero-trust security platform based on identity-aware microsegmentation. Its technology helps organizations manage communications between users, devices, applications, and workloads, reducing unnecessary network access and limiting the potential spread of cyberattacks. The transaction includes up to $150 million in additional payments tied to Elisity’s future performance, executives told The Wall Street Journal . IonQ Chairman and CEO Niccolo de Masi told the newspaper that the acquisition reflects his expectation that companies will need stronger defenses as both technologies become more powerful. “With Elisity and its team as part of IonQ , we will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure and enterprise networks throughout the transition to the quantum era. As I said first, Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted. IonQ is offering its customers a vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform across quantum computing, networking, sensing and cybersecurity. Just as adding SkyWater Technology expanded IonQ’s capabilities in chip design, fabrication and packaging, Elisity will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to our quantum security strategy and will give IonQ a strong growth platform to serve customers and create value for our shareholders,” Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ, said in a statement . Elisity, founded in 2019, provides software designed to stop attackers and ransomware from spreading through an organization’s network. Its major customers include health care companies and hospitals, according to the WSJ. “Our customers need to prioritize post-quantum cryptography initiatives while securing existing assets to keep essential operations running,” James Winebrenner, CEO of Elisity, said in the release. “With IonQ, we will be optimally positioned to partner with them to modernize their crypto-agility programs, accelerate post-quantum cryptography capabilities while advancing their holistic Zero Trust posture and deploy hybrid-cybersecurity solutions today that are prepared for the quantum future.” The purchase would bring that business into IonQ , which develops quantum computers and has been buying companies to offer customers a broader range of technology. Winebrenner is expected to remain after the transaction closes, the WSJ reported. De Masi told the Journal that the combined companies would seek to help customers address growing security risks, including threats involving AI agents. These are software systems that can carry out tasks with some degree of independence, rather than simply respond to individual questions. The acquisition brings together businesses addressing different parts of the computing and security market. IonQ is developing machines intended to tackle certain problems beyond the practical reach of conventional computers. Elisity focuses on limiting the damage attackers can cause after entering an organization’s network. Preventing an intrusion from spreading is a central part of that defense. An attacker who gains access to one system may try to reach other computers and sensitive information. Ransomware can compound the damage by locking organizations out of their files or systems. Elisity’s platform aims to contain that movement, according to the WSJ. The proposed acquisition would give IonQ an established cybersecurity offering and customers with immediate security needs. The WSJ also reported growing concern among businesses and government officials about unauthorized activity involving AI systems. De Masi presented those risks as part of the rationale for combining the companies. De Masi told the WSJ that American companies and the federal government must prepare for “Q-Day,” the point at which quantum computers become powerful enough to defeat widely used public-key cryptography. “The bad guys are going to keep taking advantage of new technology,” De Masi told the WSJ. “Unfortunately, we are entering the most dangerous years, vis-à-vis cybersecurity risks.” Public-key cryptography helps protect information and verify identities online. The concern is that sufficiently capable quantum computers could undermine some of the mathematical methods supporting those protections. That potential threat differs from the spread of an attacker through a network, which Elisity’s software is designed to address. De Masi’s comments place the acquisition within a broader effort to help customers manage security risks associated with increasingly capable computing systems. IonQ specializes in trapped-ion quantum computers, which use electrically charged atoms to store and process quantum information. The company is pursuing applications ranging from drug discovery to national defense. The newspaper reported that the Trump administration’s support for quantum technology has helped the business. Over the summer, President Donald Trump signed executive orders promoting the development of a powerful quantum computer and protection of government systems against related cyber threats. The Elisity agreement follows IonQ ’s $1.8 billion deal earlier this year to acquire chipmaker SkyWater Technology, likely its largest acquisition to date. IonQ , which works closely with the Defense Department, has pursued acquisitions to become a broader technology supplier for its customers, the newspaper reported. Under the Elisity agreement, the number of IonQ shares issued will be calculated using a share price between $33.07 and $49.61, executives told the WSJ. IonQ shares closed Friday at $39.89, giving the company a market value of nearly $16 billion. Currently, the company is trading down 2% in pre-market trading. The proposed transaction includes up to $150 million in performance-based earn-outs linked to specified business milestones. The number of IonQ common shares to be issued will be calculated using a volume-weighted average price, subject to a collar ranging from $33.07 to $49.61 per share . According to the companies’ transaction announcement, Elisity has more than 100 customer deployments worldwide, providing IonQ with an established enterprise cybersecurity presence. The acquisition comes as organizations assess the long-term implications of quantum computing for existing encryption systems. One major concern is the harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL) threat, in which attackers collect and store encrypted information today in the hope of decrypting it in the future using more powerful computing capabilities. Widely deployed public-key cryptographic systems, including those based on RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC), could be vulnerable to sufficiently capable quantum computers. However, the timeline for developing machines capable of breaking these systems at scale remains uncertain. IonQ intends to combine its quantum security technologies with Elisity’s zero-trust capabilities to address complementary aspects of enterprise cybersecurity. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is designed to protect information against attacks from future quantum computers, while identity-based microsegmentation restricts unauthorized communications within enterprise networks. Microsegmentation can reduce the ability of attackers to move laterally after compromising an initial device or system. It does not, however, independently prevent the future decryption of encrypted data that has already been intercepted. Organizations facing HNDL risks must also assess their cryptographic systems, protect sensitive information, and plan migrations to appropriate post-quantum standards. IonQ Chief Executive Officer Niccolo de Masi has positioned the transaction as part of the company’s broader effort to expand its security offerings and help customers prepare for the quantum era. Enterprise network enforcement: Elisity’s identity-based microsegmentation platform helps security teams apply least-privilege access policies to users, devices, applications, workloads, and other network entities. COLLEGE PARK, Maryland, October 12, 2026 — Quantum computing company IonQ Inc. has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire enterprise cybersecurity firm Elisity Inc. in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion , expanding its enterprise security business and strengthening its strategy to address emerging cybersecurity challenges associated with advances in quantum computing.

The proposed transaction includes up to $150 million in performance-based earn-outs linked to specified business milestones. The number of IonQ common shares to be issued will be calculated using a volume-weighted average price, subject to a collar ranging from $33.07 to $49.61 per share .

The acquisition is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to required regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. The agreement remains pending until the transaction is completed.

Founded in 2019, Elisity develops an identity-based microsegmentation platform that helps organizations manage network access across information technology (IT), operational technology (OT), Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and enterprise workloads. According to the companies’ transaction announcement, Elisity has more than 100 customer deployments worldwide, providing IonQ with an established enterprise cybersecurity presence.

The acquisition comes as organizations assess the long-term implications of quantum computing for existing encryption systems. One major concern is the harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL) threat, in which attackers collect and store encrypted information today in the hope of decrypting it in the future using more powerful computing capabilities.

Widely deployed public-key cryptographic systems, including those based on RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC), could be vulnerable to sufficiently capable quantum computers. However, the timeline for developing machines capable of breaking these systems at scale remains uncertain.

IonQ intends to combine its quantum security technologies with Elisity’s zero-trust capabilities to address complementary aspects of enterprise cybersecurity. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is designed to protect information against attacks from future quantum computers, while identity-based microsegmentation restricts unauthorized communications within enterprise networks.

Microsegmentation can reduce the ability of attackers to move laterally after compromising an initial device or system. It does not, however, independently prevent the future decryption of encrypted data that has already been intercepted. Organizations facing HNDL risks must also assess their cryptographic systems, protect sensitive information, and plan migrations to appropriate post-quantum standards.

IonQ Chief Executive Officer Niccolo de Masi has positioned the transaction as part of the company’s broader effort to expand its security offerings and help customers prepare for the quantum era. The acquisition could provide IonQ with additional enterprise relationships through which to introduce complementary cybersecurity and cryptographic products.
The proposed Elisity acquisition complements IonQ’s broader strategy to expand beyond quantum computing hardware into quantum networking, cybersecurity, and semiconductor manufacturing.

IonQ’s earlier acquisition of SkyWater Technology expanded its capabilities in semiconductor manufacturing and related technologies. Elisity would add an established enterprise security platform, creating opportunities to connect quantum security offerings with network access controls used by corporate and government customers.
The combined strategy has three principal components:
Quantum hardware and manufacturing: IonQ develops trapped-ion quantum computing systems and has expanded its semiconductor manufacturing capabilities through SkyWater Technology.
Cryptographic protection: IonQ’s quantum networking and security initiatives include technologies intended to support secure communications and the transition toward quantum-resistant protection.

Enterprise network enforcement: Elisity’s identity-based microsegmentation platform helps security teams apply least-privilege access policies to users, devices, applications, workloads, and other network entities.

The companies expect the combination to create opportunities for cross-selling, strengthen relationships with enterprise security teams, and support the development of integrated security products. Potential applications include improving visibility into cryptographic dependencies and helping organizations prioritize security upgrades.

These benefits remain prospective. Their realization will depend on regulatory approval, successful integration, customer adoption, and the technical and commercial execution of the combined product strategy.

Its technology helps organizations manage communications between users, devices, applications, and workloads, reducing unnecessary network access and limiting the potential spread of cyberattacks.

extraction.body: The localization race: From language to experience The widespread impact of artificial intelligence (AI), especially generative models like ChatGPT, has dramatically transformed industries, and education is among the first to feel the change. While grappling with challenges around effectiveness, the sector is also seeing unprecedented opportunities for expansion. Global edtech is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 13.6%, reaching $348 billion by 2030. This surge is fueled not only by the digital transformation of education but also by remote work trends and the need for lifelong learning in the face of rapidly evolving labor market demands. According to a World Economic Forum (WEF) report, 44% of today’s workforce skills will become obsolete within five years. The rise of AI makes competencies like data science, coding, and big data essential. Meanwhile, irreplaceable human skills such as critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, and analysis are becoming top priorities for corporate training programs. Victory will only go to those who truly “speak Vietnamese” – both literally and figuratively. Amid this shift, Coursera, a global online learning platform, has emerged as a leader in adapting to Vietnam’s rapidly changing tech landscape. Greg Hart, CEO of Coursera, noted that the platform currently has about 1.8 million learners in Vietnam, ranking third in Southeast Asia behind the Philippines (2.8 million) and Indonesia (2.1 million). Vietnamese users are particularly drawn to data science, AI, and Chinese language courses. Local edtech start-ups like Vuihoc.vn, Edupia, Moon.vn, and Topica are also accelerating, investing in AI and adaptive learning models that personalize learning progress for individual students. Many have integrated livestream classes, support teachers, 24/7 learning chatbots, and exam prep content aligned with Vietnam’s national education curriculum. These domestic players have a deep understanding of local student and parent psychology – a decisive advantage in a cost-sensitive and trust-driven market. Despite its vast potential, Vietnam’s edtech market faces hurdles such as affordability, users’ preference for free or partially paid models, and the challenge of retaining learners long-term. However, national digital transformation policies, AI development commitments, and efforts to popularize digital skills in education are creating tangible growth opportunities for market participants. The race for experience and content, not just tech Vietnam’s online education sector is shifting from a “tech pilot” phase to a “content and experience strategy” phase. Localization now means more than translating content - it involves a deep understanding of Vietnamese learners: their learning styles, parental expectations, classroom culture, curricula, and spending capacity. The battle between international platforms and local start-ups is playing out across multiple dimensions: technology, culture, and trust. While technology offers an advantage, it is no longer a barrier. Victory will go to those who truly “speak Vietnamese,” in every sense. Though promising, online learning still faces the paradox of high accessibility but low effectiveness. Studies show that completion rates for massive open online courses (MOOCs) remain low. However, the integration of AI is beginning to change that. Tools like Coach offer instant feedback, allow learners to ask questions, practice, and track personalized progress - features previously available only in low student-teacher ratio classrooms. The combination of human and AI interaction is creating a more effective, immersive learning experience. Edtech’s story cannot be separated from global employment trends. According to WEF’s 2023 report, around 83 million jobs will disappear over the next five years, while only 69 million new ones will be created - resulting in a net loss of 14 million. Repetitive, low-skill roles are likely to be the first replaced by technology. Conversely, new roles are emerging rapidly, requiring a flexible workforce committed to lifelong learning and adaptation. Interdisciplinary skills such as digital-era critical thinking, cross-cultural literacy, and fluency in AI tools are becoming essential survival credentials.

Greg Hart, CEO of Coursera, noted that the platform currently has about 1.8 million learners in Vietnam, ranking third in Southeast Asia behind the Philippines (2.8 million) and Indonesia (2.1 million). Vietnamese users are particularly drawn to data science, AI, and Chinese language courses.
Local edtech start-ups like Vuihoc.vn, Edupia, Moon.vn, and Topica are also accelerating, investing in AI and adaptive learning models that personalize learning progress for individual students.

Many have integrated livestream classes, support teachers, 24/7 learning chatbots, and exam prep content aligned with Vietnam’s national education curriculum. These domestic players have a deep understanding of local student and parent psychology – a decisive advantage in a cost-sensitive and trust-driven market.

Despite its vast potential, Vietnam’s edtech market faces hurdles such as affordability, users’ preference for free or partially paid models, and the challenge of retaining learners long-term. However, national digital transformation policies, AI development commitments, and efforts to popularize digital skills in education are creating tangible growth opportunities for market participants.
The race for experience and content, not just tech

Vietnam’s online education sector is shifting from a “tech pilot” phase to a “content and experience strategy” phase. Localization now means more than translating content - it involves a deep understanding of Vietnamese learners: their learning styles, parental expectations, classroom culture, curricula, and spending capacity.

The battle between international platforms and local start-ups is playing out across multiple dimensions: technology, culture, and trust. While technology offers an advantage, it is no longer a barrier. Victory will go to those who truly “speak Vietnamese,” in every sense.

Though promising, online learning still faces the paradox of high accessibility but low effectiveness. Studies show that completion rates for massive open online courses (MOOCs) remain low. However, the integration of AI is beginning to change that.

Tools like Coach offer instant feedback, allow learners to ask questions, practice, and track personalized progress - features previously available only in low student-teacher ratio classrooms. The combination of human and AI interaction is creating a more effective, immersive learning experience.

Edtech’s story cannot be separated from global employment trends. According to WEF’s 2023 report, around 83 million jobs will disappear over the next five years, while only 69 million new ones will be created - resulting in a net loss of 14 million. Repetitive, low-skill roles are likely to be the first replaced by technology.

Conversely, new roles are emerging rapidly, requiring a flexible workforce committed to lifelong learning and adaptation. Interdisciplinary skills such as digital-era critical thinking, cross-cultural literacy, and fluency in AI tools are becoming essential survival credentials.

The rise of AI makes competencies like data science, coding, and big data essential. Meanwhile, irreplaceable human skills such as critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, and analysis are becoming top priorities for corporate training programs. Victory will only go to those who truly “speak Vietnamese” – both literally and figuratively. However, national digital transformation policies, AI development commitments, and efforts to popularize digital skills in education are creating tangible growth opportunities for market participants. The race for experience and content, not just tech Vietnam’s online education sector is shifting from a “tech pilot” phase to a “content and experience strategy” phase. Localization now means more than translating content - it involves a deep understanding of Vietnamese learners: their learning styles, parental expectations, classroom culture, curricula, and spending capacity. While technology offers an advantage, it is no longer a barrier. Victory will go to those who truly “speak Vietnamese,” in every sense. Though promising, online learning still faces the paradox of high accessibility but low effectiveness. Studies show that completion rates for massive open online courses (MOOCs) remain low. However, the integration of AI is beginning to change that. According to WEF’s 2023 report, around 83 million jobs will disappear over the next five years, while only 69 million new ones will be created - resulting in a net loss of 14 million. Repetitive, low-skill roles are likely to be the first replaced by technology. Conversely, new roles are emerging rapidly, requiring a flexible workforce committed to lifelong learning and adaptation. Interdisciplinary skills such as digital-era critical thinking, cross-cultural literacy, and fluency in AI tools are becoming essential survival credentials.

extraction.body: BEIJING, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Nvidia's share of China's market for data-centre AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters. Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China from January through June, down 44% from a year earlier, IDC data showed. AI accelerators are specialised chips used to train and run AI models. Washington has restricted China's access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, limiting the range of products the US chipmaker can sell in the world's second-largest economy. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington's export curbs, saying the policy forced a US company to cede China's $50 billion AI chip market to Huawei. IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said. Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%. Total AI-accelerator shipments reached 2.008 million units in the first half. Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs -- the chips most widely used to train AI models -- fell 26% to 991,000 units, as supplies eligible for sale in mainland China remained limited, IDC said. Shipments of other AI accelerators rose nearly 80% to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs by volume. This category includes chips designed for specific AI tasks, such as running trained models. Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95% of the non-GPU segment, which IDC said was being adopted by government agencies, internet companies and telecoms providers. IDC said competition was shifting from the performance of a single chip to system-level capabilities, including how well chips work in a larger computing cluster. IDC expects total accelerator shipments in China to grow 19% this year, even as GPU shipments fall 9%. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista and Che Pan; Editing by Jamie Freed)

extraction.body: BEIJING, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Nvidia's share of China's market for data-centre AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters. Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China from January through June, down 44% from a year earlier, IDC data showed. AI accelerators are specialised chips used to train and run AI models. Washington has restricted China's access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, limiting the range of products the US chipmaker can sell in the world's second-largest economy. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington's export curbs, saying the policy forced a US company to cede China's $50 billion AI chip market to Huawei. IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said. Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%. Total AI-accelerator shipments reached 2.008 million units in the first half. Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs -- the chips most widely used to train AI models -- fell 26% to 991,000 units, as supplies eligible for sale in mainland China remained limited, IDC said. Shipments of other AI accelerators rose nearly 80% to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs by volume. This category includes chips designed for specific AI tasks, such as running trained models. Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95% of the non-GPU segment, which IDC said was being adopted by government agencies, internet companies and telecoms providers. IDC said competition was shifting from the performance of a single chip to system-level capabilities, including how well chips work in a larger computing cluster. IDC expects total accelerator shipments in China to grow 19% this year, even as GPU shipments fall 9%. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista and Che Pan; Editing by Jamie Freed)

(AP Photo/Adam Gray, File) Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed scrutiny to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid . The Justice Department confirmed that a judicially authorized search warrant of Omar’s home was executed by Homeland Security Investigations but provided no other details. Trump administration officials have repeatedly hinted at the existence of an inquiry targeting the Minnesota representative. Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” A senior U.S. official said President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. And a bipartisan group of senators is calling on the Trump administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia despite a U.S. sanctions law. Trump used his rally in Youngstown, Ohio, to defend his administration’s investigation into the Democratic congresswoman. Federal agents on Monday searched Omar’s home in Washington. She is a Somali immigrant and an outspoken Trump critic. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military,” Trump said. “All they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right.’ She’s got a constitutional right. She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.” The crowd responded to the president by shouting, “Deport,” suggesting that the sitting member of Congress be removed from the U.S. Trump slams Sherrod Brown as he stumps in Ohio The president said the former Democratic senator, who lost his seat in 2024 and is running for another seat this time, is “the candidate of the Marxists, the communists.” He tied Brown to what he described as an out-of-control border and runaway inflation under former President Joe Biden. And he urged the crowd to vote for Sen. Jon Husted, whom he noted, with a colorful anatomical description of his athletic build, was a college football player. Omar supporters turn out for her at Minnesota rally More than 100 people chanted “Ilhan! Ilhan!” at an afternoon rally in Minneapolis in support of Omar. Speakers addressed the crowd from the bed of a pickup truck behind a large sign that said, “We Stand With Ilhan.” “This administration is a violent authoritative regime. Take it from us: We would know. We have been experiencing this for generations,” said Rachel Dionne-Thunder, a member of the Big Stone Cree Nation. Trump, in response to another question about the Houthis, said “they are misbehaving very badly. No good.” But he didn’t say anything about whether the U.S. would respond to the Houthis. Trump says there’s an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia because he said so Trump is insisting that an energy ceasefire is in place for Ukraine and Russia, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that Moscow struck his country’s energy sites. When pressed about the attacks by Russia, Trump said: “Well, I’d have to look at it and see, because there’s been violations on both sides.” Trump says he has ‘nothing to do’ with search of Omar’s Washington home “I understand they’re looking at it very carefully,” the president said of an investigation that sparked federal agents to search the home of the Democratic representative. Trump said he’d found the congresswoman to “be totally crooked, personally.” But even after the judge’s 6:45 p.m. deadline , a few of the spots labeled as paid for by the U.S. government aired on television, data from AdImpact shows. The Department of Homeland Security did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel those final ad buys, the White House said in an email. The White House said the ads, which it refers to as public service announcements, will be paid for by outside groups going forward. Trump says he’ll have a rally in Kansas to boost Sen. Roger Marshall Trump said last week he struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, reversing years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine. After touring an ethanol plant in Dyersville, Iowa, Hinson told reporters that fuel prices are a priority for her. But she also said the U.S. should be “strong” on Russia, noting her support for a sanctions package that the House passed last month. Top of the ticket in Georgia will share the stage with Trump The screen grab wasn’t dated, but Omar posted that phrase on social media as the House debated Trump’s first impeachment case in 2019. Debbie Dingell wrote that Trump had “repeatedly targeted Congresswoman Omar with hateful rhetoric, contributing to death threats and violence.” Arizona Rep. Adellita Grijalva said it represented “the latest — and darkest — chapter of Trump’s racist political persecution against Ilhan Omar and the entire Somali-American community.” Saying Trump was “weaponizing our government against his perceived political opponents,” Colorado Rep. The search was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of the Department of Homeland Security that manages criminal investigations, and, according to a Justice Department spokesperson, “executed a judicially authorized search warrant” the agency secured. An anonymous source reportedly “familiar with the situation” alleged to NBC News that the raid was part of a yearslong investigation involving whistleblowers. CNN also reported that a federal judge approved the search warrant but did not name the judge. White House border czar Tom Homan, the acting head of ICE, stated on Fox News last month that Homeland Security was investigating Omar for alleged unspecified “criminal” conduct, but claimed he couldn’t “give the specifics of what’s happening.” “If someone committed an immigration violation, if someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law,” Homan said at the time. “So, I’ll leave it at that. We’ll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations, continue the investigation.” In a Monday morning Fox interview, Homan confirmed that the search had taken place.
