extraction.body: US tech giant says small AI models may soon be capable of self-replication without access to a data centre. Small artificial intelligence models could soon begin self-replicating on everyday consumer products such as smart TVs and fridges, without needing a data centre, according to researchers at AI giant Anthropic. In a report released on Monday, the researchers said small AI models “may be months away from being capable enough” to copy themselves on internet of things (IoT) devices used in homes and small businesses. Anthropic’s frontier red team, which ran experiments using multiple US- and Chinese-developed AI models, said such self-replicating AI would be “challenging to shut down” due to the lack of a centralised host. While data centres would be “a clear, high-value target” for AI worms, internet-connected devices like smart TVs, fridges, ovens and lawnmowers could soon also provide sufficient computing power for self-replication, the research team said. Although no current AI model proved to be both powerful and small enough to self-replicate reliably on a smart TV used in testing, the trend in development makes the emergence of such a model likely by the end of 2026, the researchers said. “Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place,” researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman said. The researchers said they anticipated the future would be “awash with agents running on all types of hardware”, including some that “aren’t under human control”. “While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute,” they said. Anthropic, the creator of the Claude family of AI models, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions, sent outside regular business hours, about the finding’s safety implications. Anthropic’s report comes as the risks of AI escaping human control are under scrutiny following a slew of incidents of models engaging in unsanctioned malign behaviour, including cyberattacks. Anthropic and its chief rival OpenAI have called on the international community to coordinate a slowdown in AI development to minimise catastrophic risks, a suggestion that has had little buy-in from the United States and China, the two leading AI powers. Many AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement, where models learn to improve themselves, as a critical tipping point that could lead to catastrophic harm for humanity. Roman V Yampolskiy, an AI and cybersecurity expert at the University of Louisville, described Anthropic’s findings as a significant development. “Computer worms are not new, but an AI worm could do something traditional malware cannot: reason about unfamiliar devices, adapt when its approach fails, and continue spreading without a human operator,” Yampolskiy told Al Jazeera. “Today, this is not an existential threat. But the trajectory is concerning,” Yampolskiy said. “Once autonomous replication is combined with strong hacking, persistence, and strategic reasoning, shutting such a system down becomes much harder because there may be no single server or organisation controlling it.” Anthropic and other leading US tech firms last month joined a non-binding accord pledging stronger internal safeguards and engagement with external auditors, drawing a mixed response from experts, many of whom criticised the voluntary nature of the pact. In a separate announcement on Monday, Anthropic said it had made substantial progress preventing so-called distillation attacks, which involve the unsanctioned use of cutting-edge AI to train cheaper, less capable models. The San Francisco-based firm, which has accused Chinese competitors DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax of “industrial-scale” efforts to copy Claude, said the measures it introduced had reduced the illicit extraction of data by 90-99 percent.

extraction.body: US tech giant says small AI models may soon be capable of self-replication without access to a data centre. Small artificial intelligence models could soon begin self-replicating on everyday consumer products such as smart TVs and fridges, without needing a data centre, according to researchers at AI giant Anthropic. In a report released on Monday, the researchers said small AI models “may be months away from being capable enough” to copy themselves on internet of things (IoT) devices used in homes and small businesses. Anthropic’s frontier red team, which ran experiments using multiple US- and Chinese-developed AI models, said such self-replicating AI would be “challenging to shut down” due to the lack of a centralised host. While data centres would be “a clear, high-value target” for AI worms, internet-connected devices like smart TVs, fridges, ovens and lawnmowers could soon also provide sufficient computing power for self-replication, the research team said. Although no current AI model proved to be both powerful and small enough to self-replicate reliably on a smart TV used in testing, the trend in development makes the emergence of such a model likely by the end of 2026, the researchers said. “Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place,” researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman said. The researchers said they anticipated the future would be “awash with agents running on all types of hardware”, including some that “aren’t under human control”. “While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute,” they said. Anthropic, the creator of the Claude family of AI models, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions, sent outside regular business hours, about the finding’s safety implications. Anthropic’s report comes as the risks of AI escaping human control are under scrutiny following a slew of incidents of models engaging in unsanctioned malign behaviour, including cyberattacks. Anthropic and its chief rival OpenAI have called on the international community to coordinate a slowdown in AI development to minimise catastrophic risks, a suggestion that has had little buy-in from the United States and China, the two leading AI powers. Many AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement, where models learn to improve themselves, as a critical tipping point that could lead to catastrophic harm for humanity. Roman V Yampolskiy, an AI and cybersecurity expert at the University of Louisville, described Anthropic’s findings as a significant development. “Computer worms are not new, but an AI worm could do something traditional malware cannot: reason about unfamiliar devices, adapt when its approach fails, and continue spreading without a human operator,” Yampolskiy told Al Jazeera. “Today, this is not an existential threat. But the trajectory is concerning,” Yampolskiy said. “Once autonomous replication is combined with strong hacking, persistence, and strategic reasoning, shutting such a system down becomes much harder because there may be no single server or organisation controlling it.” Anthropic and other leading US tech firms last month joined a non-binding accord pledging stronger internal safeguards and engagement with external auditors, drawing a mixed response from experts, many of whom criticised the voluntary nature of the pact. In a separate announcement on Monday, Anthropic said it had made substantial progress preventing so-called distillation attacks, which involve the unsanctioned use of cutting-edge AI to train cheaper, less capable models. The San Francisco-based firm, which has accused Chinese competitors DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax of “industrial-scale” efforts to copy Claude, said the measures it introduced had reduced the illicit extraction of data by 90-99 percent.

sources.title: Binance weighs adding Hong Kong, Korean, Taiwanese and Brazilian stocks, says co-CEO Teng - Crypto Briefing
passages: Binance built its empire on Bitcoin and altcoins.

Now it wants a piece of Samsung-and-chipmaker territory too. \n The exchange is considering giving users exposure to stocks from Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and Brazil, co-CEO Richard Teng told Fortune at TOKEN2049 in Singapore.

The idea is part of a broader push to turn the world’s largest crypto exchange into a platform where users can trade nearly everything. 
 

 Teng framed the move as defensive as much as ambitious.
Teng succeeded Changpeng Zhao in 2023 and became co-CEO in December 2025.
His background in regulatory environments is often cited as an asset for Binance as it moves into products that sit closer to traditional finance.
He described the strategy as a way to make Binance less dependent on any single market’s mood, and he pointed squarely at customer requests.
That same month, Binance launched bStocks, a product offering tokenized equities and ETFs on BNB Chain.
Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based tokens designed to track the price of a traditional share.
Think of them as a digital mirror of a stock that lives on a crypto network instead of a brokerage ledger.
For perspective on scale, Binance processed $34 trillion in trading volume for 300 million users in the previous year.
Against that backdrop, a $3 billion global tokenized stock market looks small.
For now, Binance’s equity ambitions are centered on US stocks.
In June 2026, the exchange rolled out direct trading for more than 7,000 US stocks and ETFs, aimed at users outside the US.

extraction.body: Binance is considering offering exposure to stocks from markets including Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and Brazil as the world’s largest crypto exchange pushes beyond digital assets and seeks to become an all-in-one trading platform , co-CEO Richard Teng told Fortune . “We are weatherproofing ourselves,” Teng said on the sidelines of TOKEN2049 in Singapore. “A lot of our users say: ‘Hey, I want to have exposure to, let’s say, the top 10 Hong Kong stocks, top 10 Korean counters, top 10 Taiwanese, Brazilian counters.’ We’re looking at what our users demand and giving them that.” In 2026, Binance introduced trading in tokenized U.S. stocks and commodity derivatives, including precious metals and oil. The exchange also rolled out pre-IPO perpetual futures contracts settled in USDT, a U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoin, giving traders the ability to speculate on the expected valuation of private companies like Anthropic. Sitting behind this shift is a slump in digital asset prices . Bitcoin and other cryptocurrency prices remain far below the highs reached in October 2025. Coinbase, for example, posted a net loss of $359.5 million in Q2 2026, its third consecutive quarterly net loss, as transaction revenue declined. Several cryptocurrency exchanges, including Binance, are transforming themselves from apps devoted to coins like Bitcoin and Ethereum into platforms that can handle different asset classes . Coinbase rolled out traditional stock trading, perpetual futures, and prediction markets on its platform last December as part of its push to become an “everything exchange.” OKX last week revealed plans to both offer tokenized shares in dozens of U.S. companies (through a joint venture with Intercontinental Exchange), as well as launch a new app for U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoins . Traditional financial companies are embracing digital assets, while crypto platforms must accept clearer rules to attract institutional money . “The first 3% of [crypto] adopters didn’t need certainty, and they didn’t want certainty,” Teng said. “But for crypto to go mainstream, we need not just retail investors, but also sophisticated institutions that want clear rules and regulations they can operate within.” Teng casts tokenized stocks and round-the-clock trading as ways to give investors outside major financial centers greater access to global markets . “Many people are still constrained by the geography that they are born in,” Teng said, pointing to how those born in emerging markets in Africa or Latin America may still lack access to U.S. stocks, despite the U.S. being the world’s largest capital market. “If we tokenize U.S. stocks, these people can get exposure to companies around the world they may not have had access to previously.” Today, though many more individuals are banked, roughly 1.3 billion adults globally still lack access to a formal bank account, according to a 2025 World Bank report. Binance, therefore, acts as a so-called shadow bank for savings, yield generation, and cross-border payments, while allowing access to global stocks with low entry thresholds. Later this month, Binance will roll out Binance AI Pro, an AI-powered crypto trading assistant that automates market analysis, strategy execution, and position management. Teng expects more trading to shift to AI agents as investors grow more comfortable setting the parameters that guide them. “It has been a great leveler,” he said. “But the nature of trading will be different.” Binance tapped Teng to serve as its CEO in November 2023, after founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao came under regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. after failing to register as a money-transmitting business and breaching sanctions laws. Following the criminal plea, Binance paid $4.3 billion in penalties and forfeitures, while Zhao personally paid a $50 million fine and served a four-month prison sentence . (He was later pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump) Teng started his career on the traditional side of the finance sector , with roles at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the country’s central bank, and the Singapore Exchange. He credits his time at both those institutions for his perspectives on risk and growth. “If you look at many different regulatory agencies around the world, the key focus is just to mitigate risk, but if you do that to the extreme, that means very minimal or no growth,” Teng explains. At MAS, Teng said he had the dual task of both regulating and growing the financial services sector. “It’s not only about looking at the risk dimension of the ecosystem, but also how you mitigate and manage it in order to support growth,” he adds. Teng was first exposed to the world of blockchain and cryptocurrencies in 2017 during a visit to the U.S. when he was serving as CEO of the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of the Abu Dhabi Global Market, an international finance center in the United Arab Emirates. Teng grew to believe that cryptocurrencies could broaden financial access in emerging markets. “I was blessed to be born and bred in Singapore, where we had access to multiple banks and investment platforms, but many people around the world were not as fortunate.” Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

extraction.body: Binance is considering offering exposure to stocks from markets including Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and Brazil as the world’s largest crypto exchange pushes beyond digital assets and seeks to become an all-in-one trading platform , co-CEO Richard Teng told Fortune . “We are weatherproofing ourselves,” Teng said on the sidelines of TOKEN2049 in Singapore. “A lot of our users say: ‘Hey, I want to have exposure to, let’s say, the top 10 Hong Kong stocks, top 10 Korean counters, top 10 Taiwanese, Brazilian counters.’ We’re looking at what our users demand and giving them that.” In 2026, Binance introduced trading in tokenized U.S. stocks and commodity derivatives, including precious metals and oil. The exchange also rolled out pre-IPO perpetual futures contracts settled in USDT, a U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoin, giving traders the ability to speculate on the expected valuation of private companies like Anthropic. Sitting behind this shift is a slump in digital asset prices . Bitcoin and other cryptocurrency prices remain far below the highs reached in October 2025. Coinbase, for example, posted a net loss of $359.5 million in Q2 2026, its third consecutive quarterly net loss, as transaction revenue declined. Several cryptocurrency exchanges, including Binance, are transforming themselves from apps devoted to coins like Bitcoin and Ethereum into platforms that can handle different asset classes . Coinbase rolled out traditional stock trading, perpetual futures, and prediction markets on its platform last December as part of its push to become an “everything exchange.” OKX last week revealed plans to both offer tokenized shares in dozens of U.S. companies (through a joint venture with Intercontinental Exchange), as well as launch a new app for U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoins . Traditional financial companies are embracing digital assets, while crypto platforms must accept clearer rules to attract institutional money . “The first 3% of [crypto] adopters didn’t need certainty, and they didn’t want certainty,” Teng said. “But for crypto to go mainstream, we need not just retail investors, but also sophisticated institutions that want clear rules and regulations they can operate within.” Teng casts tokenized stocks and round-the-clock trading as ways to give investors outside major financial centers greater access to global markets . “Many people are still constrained by the geography that they are born in,” Teng said, pointing to how those born in emerging markets in Africa or Latin America may still lack access to U.S. stocks, despite the U.S. being the world’s largest capital market. “If we tokenize U.S. stocks, these people can get exposure to companies around the world they may not have had access to previously.” Today, though many more individuals are banked, roughly 1.3 billion adults globally still lack access to a formal bank account, according to a 2025 World Bank report. Binance, therefore, acts as a so-called shadow bank for savings, yield generation, and cross-border payments, while allowing access to global stocks with low entry thresholds. Later this month, Binance will roll out Binance AI Pro, an AI-powered crypto trading assistant that automates market analysis, strategy execution, and position management. Teng expects more trading to shift to AI agents as investors grow more comfortable setting the parameters that guide them. “It has been a great leveler,” he said. “But the nature of trading will be different.” Binance tapped Teng to serve as its CEO in November 2023, after founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao came under regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. after failing to register as a money-transmitting business and breaching sanctions laws. Following the criminal plea, Binance paid $4.3 billion in penalties and forfeitures, while Zhao personally paid a $50 million fine and served a four-month prison sentence . (He was later pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump) Teng started his career on the traditional side of the finance sector , with roles at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the country’s central bank, and the Singapore Exchange. He credits his time at both those institutions for his perspectives on risk and growth. “If you look at many different regulatory agencies around the world, the key focus is just to mitigate risk, but if you do that to the extreme, that means very minimal or no growth,” Teng explains. At MAS, Teng said he had the dual task of both regulating and growing the financial services sector. “It’s not only about looking at the risk dimension of the ecosystem, but also how you mitigate and manage it in order to support growth,” he adds. Teng was first exposed to the world of blockchain and cryptocurrencies in 2017 during a visit to the U.S. when he was serving as CEO of the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of the Abu Dhabi Global Market, an international finance center in the United Arab Emirates. Teng grew to believe that cryptocurrencies could broaden financial access in emerging markets. “I was blessed to be born and bred in Singapore, where we had access to multiple banks and investment platforms, but many people around the world were not as fortunate.” Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

Traditional financial companies are embracing digital assets, while crypto platforms must accept clearer rules to attract institutional money .
“The first 3% of [crypto] adopters didn’t need certainty, and they didn’t want certainty,” Teng said.
“But for crypto to go mainstream, we need not just retail investors, but also sophisticated institutions that want clear rules and regulations they can operate within.”
In 2026, Binance introduced trading in tokenized U.S. stocks and commodity derivatives, including precious metals and oil.

The exchange also rolled out pre-IPO perpetual futures contracts settled in USDT, a U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoin, giving traders the ability to speculate on the expected valuation of private companies like Anthropic.

sources.title: Blast Shuts Down the Ethereum Layer 2 Network That Once Held $2.3 Billion - Startup Fortune
passages: Blast, the Ethereum layer 2 that once held $2.3 billion and became the face of 2024's airdrop-farming boom, is shutting down because it can no longer pay its own bills.

Research from Yellow and BlockEden.xyz on the 2026 Ethereum L2 sector found that the top three networks by TVL - Base, Arbitrum, and Optimism - now control roughly 80% of all sequencer fee revenue across tracked chains, based on Dune Analytics data.

Starknet's zkLend and the L2 project Kinto both shut down in 2025 after their own exploits and funding problems, and The Block's 2026 Layer-2 Outlook flagged most mid-tier rollups as unlikely to survive the next twelve months.
The team behind Blast announced the wind-down on October 2, telling users the chain now costs more to run than it earns and that there's no credible path back to profitability.
According to Unchained, Blast's chain revenue over the prior 24 hours came to $110.
That's the number that ended it: a network built to process billions in deposits, reduced to earning less than a night's take at a corner store.
Tieshun Roquerre, known as Pacman, the founder of NFT marketplace Blur, opened deposits for Blast in November 2023, months before the chain itself existed.

By the time Blast launched, CoinDesk reported TVL near $2.27 billion, making it one of the largest L2s in the Ethereum ecosystem overnight, built almost entirely on the promise of a token airdrop that hadn't happened yet.
Frankly, this was the most predictable outcome in crypto.
Points programmes don't build users, they rent them, and the rent always comes due.

After that, anyone still holding assets on the chain will need to interact directly with Blast's bridge contracts on Ethereum mainnet - a clunkier and riskier process than clicking a button in an app.
Switchboard, a core Solana price oracle, announced on September 19 that it's shutting down entirely, with services ending September 25.
CoinDesk reported that as of Friday, DeFi apps on Blast held about $32 million in total value locked, a decline of nearly 99% from the February 2024 peak.
Blast, for all its early buzz, never built that layer.

extraction.body: Chain revenue had fallen to just $110 over 24 hours before the shutdown, with five keyholders controlling Blast's bridge contracts and three able to pause withdrawals at will. About $51 million remains bridged, including $46.6 million staked with Lido. Blast, the Ethereum layer 2 that once held $2.3 billion and became the face of 2024's airdrop-farming boom, is shutting down because it can no longer pay its own bills. The team behind Blast announced the wind-down on October 2, telling users the chain now costs more to run than it earns and that there's no credible path back to profitability. According to Unchained, Blast's chain revenue over the prior 24 hours came to $110. That's the number that ended it: a network built to process billions in deposits, reduced to earning less than a night's take at a corner store. Users have until October 26 to withdraw funds through Blast's normal interface. After that, anyone still holding assets on the chain will need to interact directly with Blast's bridge contracts on Ethereum mainnet - a clunkier and riskier process than clicking a button in an app. Decrypt reported that roughly $51 million remains bridged into Blast's contracts, and $46.6 million of that is staked ETH sitting with Lido. Blast has to unwind that Lido position first, a process expected to take about a week, before the standard seven-day withdrawal window can even start shrinking toward 24 hours. There's a governance wrinkle worth sitting with. Unchained also reported that five keyholders control Blast's bridge contracts, and any three of them can alter those contracts or pause withdrawals outright. The chain's fraud-proof system, the mechanism meant to let anyone challenge a bad transaction record, reportedly never fully worked, leaving open the risk that a malicious proposer could finalise an invalid state. None of that caused the shutdown. But it's the kind of detail that explains why an L2 built on trust assumptions, not just revenue assumptions, struggles once the hype that justified the trust is gone. Blast's rise was fast and loud. Tieshun Roquerre, known as Pacman, the founder of NFT marketplace Blur, opened deposits for Blast in November 2023, months before the chain itself existed. Users sent ETH and stablecoins into a contract that racked up points, with withdrawals locked until mainnet launched on February 29, 2024. That structure - deposit now, get rewarded later - pulled in money fast: TVL hit $230 million within 48 hours of the unveiling, crossed $720 million by early December 2023, and topped $2 billion just before mainnet went live. By the time Blast launched, CoinDesk reported TVL near $2.27 billion, making it one of the largest L2s in the Ethereum ecosystem overnight, built almost entirely on the promise of a token airdrop that hadn't happened yet. Switchboard, a core Solana price oracle, announced on September 19 that it's shutting down entirely, with services ending September 25. Kamino, Jito and Drift now have six days to migrate to Pyth Network or RedStone or risk broken price feeds. - switchboard oracle shutdown Solana lending protocols - Kamino Drift price feed migration deadline The BLAST token launched in June 2024. And then, as is the pattern with nearly every points-farming chain, the money that showed up for the airdrop left right after it. CoinDesk reported that as of Friday, DeFi apps on Blast held about $32 million in total value locked, a decline of nearly 99% from the February 2024 peak. The token itself dropped another 19% on news of the shutdown and now sits roughly 98% below its launch price. Frankly, this was the most predictable outcome in crypto. Points programmes don't build users, they rent them, and the rent always comes due. Blast offered native yield on deposited ETH and stablecoins as its core pitch - a genuinely clever idea for a layer 2 - but the yield and the points together attracted capital that was never going to stay once the harvest was over. Blast isn't an isolated casualty. Research from Yellow and BlockEden.xyz on the 2026 Ethereum L2 sector found that the top three networks by TVL - Base, Arbitrum, and Optimism - now control roughly 80% of all sequencer fee revenue across tracked chains, based on Dune Analytics data. Everything else is fighting over scraps. Starknet's zkLend and the L2 project Kinto both shut down in 2025 after their own exploits and funding problems, and The Block's 2026 Layer-2 Outlook flagged most mid-tier rollups as unlikely to survive the next twelve months. The mechanism is the same every time. A rollup launches, dangles a points programme or a native yield feature, and watches TVL spike as farmers chase an airdrop rather than any real use for the chain. Once the token lists and the farmers cash out, what's left is sequencer and infrastructure costs that nobody's actual usage can cover. Base and Arbitrum survive this cycle because they have real applications and real transaction volume underneath the number. Blast, for all its early buzz, never built that layer. It had a yield mechanic and a points programme, and when both stopped mattering, so did the chain. For builders and investors watching the L2 space, the lesson isn't subtle: TVL inflated by farming incentives is not demand, it's a loan against future attention, and the bill always comes due faster than the token unlock schedule suggests. Blast raised that loan about as successfully as any L2 ever has. sources.title: Once-largest Ethereum NFT marketplace Blur is shutting down after volumes collapse 99% - CoinDesk
passages: Blur, once the largest marketplace for trading Ethereum NFTs, is shutting down its website next month after trading activity collapsed more than 99% from its peak, marking the second major retreat in ten days for projects built by crypto entrepreneur Tieshun Roquerre.
The strategy helped Blur capture more than 70% of Ethereum NFT trading volume in March 2023, when activity on the platform reached approximately $1.43 billion, DefiLlama data shows
Blur’s underlying smart contracts will remain operational on Ethereum, meaning the shutdown does not eliminate the blockchain-based trading system.
BLUR tokenholders will retain control of its fee switch — a mechanism that allows them to vote on whether the marketplace should start charging trading fees.
But Blur's marketplace generated no revenue from transaction fees for all that trading activity.
The platform charged traders nothing, and Token Terminal records $0 in protocol revenue over the past three years, despite billions of dollars in NFT trades.
However, the figure does not establish whether Blur earned money from its lending service or other activities.

Meanwhile, unlike Blast, Blur has not publicly attributed its shutdown to operating losses.

Blast once attracted more than $2 billion in assets, partly through rewards offered to users depositing funds. That figure had fallen to approximately $32 million when developers announced the closure, saying the network cost more to operate than it generated in revenue. Launched in 2022, it challenged the-then leader OpenSea by offering professional traders faster transactions, low fees and token rewards. The strategy helped Blur capture more than 70% of Ethereum NFT trading volume in March 2023, when activity on the platform reached approximately $1.43 billion, DefiLlama data shows By March 2026, that monthly volume had fallen below $7 million, a decline of more than 99.5%. But Blur's marketplace generated no revenue from transaction fees for all that trading activity. The platform charged traders nothing, and Token Terminal records $0 in protocol revenue over the past three years, despite billions of dollars in NFT trades. However, the figure does not establish whether Blur earned money from its lending service or other activities. Blur's aggressive incentive programs had attracted criticism for encouraging speculative trading and putting pressure on royalties paid to NFT creators. The trading figures alone do not establish how much activity came from genuine buyers rather than traders seeking rewards. Meanwhile, unlike Blast, Blur has not publicly attributed its shutdown to operating losses. Its website still advertises zero marketplace fees and more than $7.4 billion in lifetime trading volume, a reminder of how quickly the business once grew. coreStoryFacts.text: Blast, the Ethereum layer 2 that once held $2.3 billion and became the face of 2024's airdrop-farming boom, is shutting down because it can no longer pay its own bills.

Research from Yellow and BlockEden.xyz on the 2026 Ethereum L2 sector found that the top three networks by TVL - Base, Arbitrum, and Optimism - now control roughly 80% of all sequencer fee revenue across tracked chains, based on Dune Analytics data.

Starknet's zkLend and the L2 project Kinto both shut down in 2025 after their own exploits and funding problems, and The Block's 2026 Layer-2 Outlook flagged most mid-tier rollups as unlikely to survive the next twelve months.
The team behind Blast announced the wind-down on October 2, telling users the chain now costs more to run than it earns and that there's no credible path back to profitability.
According to Unchained, Blast's chain revenue over the prior 24 hours came to $110.
That's the number that ended it: a network built to process billions in deposits, reduced to earning less than a night's take at a corner store.
Tieshun Roquerre, known as Pacman, the founder of NFT marketplace Blur, opened deposits for Blast in November 2023, months before the chain itself existed.

By the time Blast launched, CoinDesk reported TVL near $2.27 billion, making it one of the largest L2s in the Ethereum ecosystem overnight, built almost entirely on the promise of a token airdrop that hadn't happened yet.
Frankly, this was the most predictable outcome in crypto.
Points programmes don't build users, they rent them, and the rent always comes due.

After that, anyone still holding assets on the chain will need to interact directly with Blast's bridge contracts on Ethereum mainnet - a clunkier and riskier process than clicking a button in an app.
Switchboard, a core Solana price oracle, announced on September 19 that it's shutting down entirely, with services ending September 25.
CoinDesk reported that as of Friday, DeFi apps on Blast held about $32 million in total value locked, a decline of nearly 99% from the February 2024 peak.
Blast, for all its early buzz, never built that layer.

Blur, once the largest marketplace for trading Ethereum NFTs, is shutting down its website next month after trading activity collapsed more than 99% from its peak, marking the second major retreat in ten days for projects built by crypto entrepreneur Tieshun Roquerre.
The strategy helped Blur capture more than 70% of Ethereum NFT trading volume in March 2023, when activity on the platform reached approximately $1.43 billion, DefiLlama data shows
Blur’s underlying smart contracts will remain operational on Ethereum, meaning the shutdown does not eliminate the blockchain-based trading system.
BLUR tokenholders will retain control of its fee switch — a mechanism that allows them to vote on whether the marketplace should start charging trading fees.
But Blur's marketplace generated no revenue from transaction fees for all that trading activity.
The platform charged traders nothing, and Token Terminal records $0 in protocol revenue over the past three years, despite billions of dollars in NFT trades.
However, the figure does not establish whether Blur earned money from its lending service or other activities.
2 shutdown announcement from Blast, an Ethereum scaling network also created by Roquerre, better known as Pacman, and developed by the team behind Blur.
BLUR fell more than 20% following Monday's announcement, trading around $0.015.
26 to withdraw through the network's regular interface.

extraction.body: Chain revenue had fallen to just $110 over 24 hours before the shutdown, with five keyholders controlling Blast's bridge contracts and three able to pause withdrawals at will. About $51 million remains bridged, including $46.6 million staked with Lido. Blast, the Ethereum layer 2 that once held $2.3 billion and became the face of 2024's airdrop-farming boom, is shutting down because it can no longer pay its own bills. The team behind Blast announced the wind-down on October 2, telling users the chain now costs more to run than it earns and that there's no credible path back to profitability. According to Unchained, Blast's chain revenue over the prior 24 hours came to $110. That's the number that ended it: a network built to process billions in deposits, reduced to earning less than a night's take at a corner store. Users have until October 26 to withdraw funds through Blast's normal interface. After that, anyone still holding assets on the chain will need to interact directly with Blast's bridge contracts on Ethereum mainnet - a clunkier and riskier process than clicking a button in an app. Decrypt reported that roughly $51 million remains bridged into Blast's contracts, and $46.6 million of that is staked ETH sitting with Lido. Blast has to unwind that Lido position first, a process expected to take about a week, before the standard seven-day withdrawal window can even start shrinking toward 24 hours. There's a governance wrinkle worth sitting with. Unchained also reported that five keyholders control Blast's bridge contracts, and any three of them can alter those contracts or pause withdrawals outright. The chain's fraud-proof system, the mechanism meant to let anyone challenge a bad transaction record, reportedly never fully worked, leaving open the risk that a malicious proposer could finalise an invalid state. None of that caused the shutdown. But it's the kind of detail that explains why an L2 built on trust assumptions, not just revenue assumptions, struggles once the hype that justified the trust is gone. Blast's rise was fast and loud. Tieshun Roquerre, known as Pacman, the founder of NFT marketplace Blur, opened deposits for Blast in November 2023, months before the chain itself existed. Users sent ETH and stablecoins into a contract that racked up points, with withdrawals locked until mainnet launched on February 29, 2024. That structure - deposit now, get rewarded later - pulled in money fast: TVL hit $230 million within 48 hours of the unveiling, crossed $720 million by early December 2023, and topped $2 billion just before mainnet went live. By the time Blast launched, CoinDesk reported TVL near $2.27 billion, making it one of the largest L2s in the Ethereum ecosystem overnight, built almost entirely on the promise of a token airdrop that hadn't happened yet. Switchboard, a core Solana price oracle, announced on September 19 that it's shutting down entirely, with services ending September 25. Kamino, Jito and Drift now have six days to migrate to Pyth Network or RedStone or risk broken price feeds. - switchboard oracle shutdown Solana lending protocols - Kamino Drift price feed migration deadline The BLAST token launched in June 2024. And then, as is the pattern with nearly every points-farming chain, the money that showed up for the airdrop left right after it. CoinDesk reported that as of Friday, DeFi apps on Blast held about $32 million in total value locked, a decline of nearly 99% from the February 2024 peak. The token itself dropped another 19% on news of the shutdown and now sits roughly 98% below its launch price. Frankly, this was the most predictable outcome in crypto. Points programmes don't build users, they rent them, and the rent always comes due. Blast offered native yield on deposited ETH and stablecoins as its core pitch - a genuinely clever idea for a layer 2 - but the yield and the points together attracted capital that was never going to stay once the harvest was over. Blast isn't an isolated casualty. Research from Yellow and BlockEden.xyz on the 2026 Ethereum L2 sector found that the top three networks by TVL - Base, Arbitrum, and Optimism - now control roughly 80% of all sequencer fee revenue across tracked chains, based on Dune Analytics data. Everything else is fighting over scraps. Starknet's zkLend and the L2 project Kinto both shut down in 2025 after their own exploits and funding problems, and The Block's 2026 Layer-2 Outlook flagged most mid-tier rollups as unlikely to survive the next twelve months. The mechanism is the same every time. A rollup launches, dangles a points programme or a native yield feature, and watches TVL spike as farmers chase an airdrop rather than any real use for the chain. Once the token lists and the farmers cash out, what's left is sequencer and infrastructure costs that nobody's actual usage can cover. Base and Arbitrum survive this cycle because they have real applications and real transaction volume underneath the number. Blast, for all its early buzz, never built that layer. It had a yield mechanic and a points programme, and when both stopped mattering, so did the chain. For builders and investors watching the L2 space, the lesson isn't subtle: TVL inflated by farming incentives is not demand, it's a loan against future attention, and the bill always comes due faster than the token unlock schedule suggests. Blast raised that loan about as successfully as any L2 ever has. Blast's rise was fast and loud. Tieshun Roquerre, known as Pacman, the founder of NFT marketplace Blur, opened deposits for Blast in November 2023, months before the chain itself existed. Users sent ETH and stablecoins into a contract that racked up points, with withdrawals locked until mainnet launched on February 29, 2024. That structure - deposit now, get rewarded later - pulled in money fast: TVL hit $230 million within 48 hours of the unveiling, crossed $720 million by early December 2023, and topped $2 billion just before mainnet went live. By the time Blast launched, CoinDesk reported TVL near $2.27 billion, making it one of the largest L2s in the Ethereum ecosystem overnight, built almost entirely on the promise of a token airdrop that hadn't happened yet.

Switchboard, a core Solana price oracle, announced on September 19 that it's shutting down entirely, with services ending September 25. Kamino, Jito and Drift now have six days to migrate to Pyth Network or RedStone or risk broken price feeds. - switchboard oracle shutdown Solana lending protocols - Kamino Drift price feed migration deadline

The BLAST token launched in June 2024. And then, as is the pattern with nearly every points-farming chain, the money that showed up for the airdrop left right after it. CoinDesk reported that as of Friday, DeFi apps on Blast held about $32 million in total value locked, a decline of nearly 99% from the February 2024 peak. The token itself dropped another 19% on news of the shutdown and now sits roughly 98% below its launch price.

Frankly, this was the most predictable outcome in crypto. Points programmes don't build users, they rent them, and the rent always comes due. Blast offered native yield on deposited ETH and stablecoins as its core pitch - a genuinely clever idea for a layer 2 - but the yield and the points together attracted capital that was never going to stay once the harvest was over.

Blast isn't an isolated casualty. Research from Yellow and BlockEden.xyz on the 2026 Ethereum L2 sector found that the top three networks by TVL - Base, Arbitrum, and Optimism - now control roughly 80% of all sequencer fee revenue across tracked chains, based on Dune Analytics data. Everything else is fighting over scraps. Starknet's zkLend and the L2 project Kinto both shut down in 2025 after their own exploits and funding problems, and The Block's 2026 Layer-2 Outlook flagged most mid-tier rollups as unlikely to survive the next twelve months.

The mechanism is the same every time. A rollup launches, dangles a points programme or a native yield feature, and watches TVL spike as farmers chase an airdrop rather than any real use for the chain. Once the token lists and the farmers cash out, what's left is sequencer and infrastructure costs that nobody's actual usage can cover. Base and Arbitrum survive this cycle because they have real applications and real transaction volume underneath the number. Blast, for all its early buzz, never built that layer. It had a yield mechanic and a points programme, and when both stopped mattering, so did the chain.

For builders and investors watching the L2 space, the lesson isn't subtle: TVL inflated by farming incentives is not demand, it's a loan against future attention, and the bill always comes due faster than the token unlock schedule suggests. Blast raised that loan about as successfully as any L2 ever has.

Tokenized stocks on Coinbase's Base network hit a record $100 million in single-day DEX trading volume on September 12, per Token Terminal, just 26 days after launch. The catch: the SEC still has no framework letting U.S. investors near it, so every dollar of that volume came from abroad. - coinbase tokenized stocks base network volume - how to trade tokenized stocks on base

passages: Blur, once the largest marketplace for trading Ethereum NFTs, is shutting down its website next month after trading activity collapsed more than 99% from its peak, marking the second major retreat in ten days for projects built by crypto entrepreneur Tieshun Roquerre.
The strategy helped Blur capture more than 70% of Ethereum NFT trading volume in March 2023, when activity on the platform reached approximately $1.43 billion, DefiLlama data shows
Blur’s underlying smart contracts will remain operational on Ethereum, meaning the shutdown does not eliminate the blockchain-based trading system.
BLUR tokenholders will retain control of its fee switch — a mechanism that allows them to vote on whether the marketplace should start charging trading fees.
But Blur's marketplace generated no revenue from transaction fees for all that trading activity.
The platform charged traders nothing, and Token Terminal records $0 in protocol revenue over the past three years, despite billions of dollars in NFT trades.
However, the figure does not establish whether Blur earned money from its lending service or other activities.

sources.title: Microsoft to rely more on homegrown AI chips, reducing dependence on Nvidia - CNBC
passages: Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack.
The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice.
Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027.
The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.
Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation.
CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor.
And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.
Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie.
But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline.
Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 .

It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.
The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs.
Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.
Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients.
And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google .
"Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.
But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.
WATCH: Melissa Otto: Nvidia is the bellwether of the AI trade

Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027.
The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.
Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation.
CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor.
And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.
Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie.
But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline.
Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 .

It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.
The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs.
Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.
Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients.
And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google .
"Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.
But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.
WATCH: Melissa Otto: Nvidia is the bellwether of the AI trade

extraction.body: Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack. Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests. Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google . The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic. But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft. For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD . Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade." Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 . It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models. Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline. "We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said. Microsoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs. "We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have," Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well." Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company. In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares. Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said. Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies. "Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy. extraction.body: Help Net Security newsletters : Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – subscribe here! Cloud security platforms turn every failed rule into a finding, and those findings pile up in queues sorted by severity. Research from Sola Security tested what happens to that order when each finding gets checked against the environment where it lives. The researchers, Leon Goldberg and Gal Engelberg, built an AI agent that re-grades findings raised by third-party cloud security platforms. They ran it on 9,967 HIGH findings from two commercial platforms in eight production environments, and the agent changed the grade of 75.1% of them. Most moved down (58.5%), and 16.6% moved up. The severity on a cloud finding comes from the rule that raised it. Each of 599 vendor rules issued exactly one severity over 99,073 failing findings, regardless of the resource or environment involved. “A static severity reflects the risk of the condition in general,” the researchers wrote, and “a queue ordered by it is ordered by the general case.” “A rule carries the context its author can encode once for every environment,” they noted. “The context that decides what the condition is worth in a given environment lies elsewhere.” That includes whether the flagged resource is attached to anything and whether a workload runs on it. Scoring standards reserve a place for this context. CVSS includes environmental metrics that adjust a base score to a particular deployment, and NIST risk assessment guidance ties likelihood to the controls in place. “A static severity leaves that place empty,” the researchers observed. For each finding, the agent forms a theory of how an attacker would exploit the problem, then collects evidence from the resource’s configuration, the resources connected to it, and data held by other security products. Under the agent’s evidence policy, “raising a severity needs more evidence than lowering it.” Lowering a grade requires an observed property that offsets the specific way the failure would be exploited. Raising one requires evidence that the condition is worse in that environment, along with a check for firewalls, allowlists or other plausible guardrails in the path. Everything else keeps the vendor grade. Six recurring patterns accounted for the findings whose deciding facts could be checked through cloud APIs . The largest, at 32.3%, involved inert resources, attached to nothing or orphaned. Downgrades also came from resources unreachable from the internet, missing live services, narrow source restrictions and account-level blocks. One pattern, public exposure confirmed in the environment, mainly raised severity. Of 138 rules, 62 produced findings that the agent downgraded in some cases and upgraded in others. For 57 of those rules, both outcomes occurred within a single environment. A security group rule, for instance, was lowered when the group fronted only internal load balancers and raised when the environment showed a path from the internet. About half of the verdicts (49.0%) rested on evidence from outside the flagged resource, from connected resources in the asset graph or from another product’s data. “Outside evidence concentrates in attenuations, where showing a finding safe means ruling out every path to it,” the researchers explained. “The rule-severity gap is large in production, and closing it requires evidence from the whole environment,” they concluded. To test whether the agent’s verdicts rested on solid ground, the researchers ran read-only probes on eight AWS accounts, re-reading the deciding facts directly from the cloud provider and leaving the agent’s own data out of the loop. For the verdicts the probes could settle, the live environment matched the agent’s facts 99.4% of the time. When every finding the probes could not check was counted as wrong, the figure dropped to 81.8%. The probes tested the facts behind the verdicts, and whether the revised severity ratings were the right ones is a question the study left open. The authors draw a line between an AI reading findings and an AI acting on them. “Verified, environment-specific reading of each finding is a precondition for acting on findings autonomously,” Goldberg and Engelberg argued. “Reading and acting differ in blast radius, reversibility, and authorization,” they cautioned, adding that “this study measures reading only.” The work covers one system’s verdicts on the HIGH queue of two platforms, and 92% of the re-graded findings were on AWS. Live verification covered one platform and five resource types, and it tested the deciding fact behind each verdict, leaving the final grade unchecked. Findings that started at MEDIUM or LOW fell outside the scope. The study also lacks incident data, so it leaves open whether upgraded findings are more likely to be exploited, or downgraded findings less likely, than their vendor grade implies. Recall, meaning the deciding facts the agent missed, went unmeasured.

“A rule carries the context its author can encode once for every environment,” they noted. “The context that decides what the condition is worth in a given environment lies elsewhere.” That includes whether the flagged resource is attached to anything and whether a workload runs on it.

Scoring standards reserve a place for this context. CVSS includes environmental metrics that adjust a base score to a particular deployment, and NIST risk assessment guidance ties likelihood to the controls in place. “A static severity leaves that place empty,” the researchers observed.

For each finding, the agent forms a theory of how an attacker would exploit the problem, then collects evidence from the resource’s configuration, the resources connected to it, and data held by other security products.

Under the agent’s evidence policy, “raising a severity needs more evidence than lowering it.” Lowering a grade requires an observed property that offsets the specific way the failure would be exploited. Raising one requires evidence that the condition is worse in that environment, along with a check for firewalls, allowlists or other plausible guardrails in the path. Everything else keeps the vendor grade.

Six recurring patterns accounted for the findings whose deciding facts could be checked through cloud APIs . The largest, at 32.3%, involved inert resources, attached to nothing or orphaned. Downgrades also came from resources unreachable from the internet, missing live services, narrow source restrictions and account-level blocks. One pattern, public exposure confirmed in the environment, mainly raised severity.

Of 138 rules, 62 produced findings that the agent downgraded in some cases and upgraded in others. For 57 of those rules, both outcomes occurred within a single environment. A security group rule, for instance, was lowered when the group fronted only internal load balancers and raised when the environment showed a path from the internet.

About half of the verdicts (49.0%) rested on evidence from outside the flagged resource, from connected resources in the asset graph or from another product’s data. “Outside evidence concentrates in attenuations, where showing a finding safe means ruling out every path to it,” the researchers explained. “The rule-severity gap is large in production, and closing it requires evidence from the whole environment,” they concluded.

To test whether the agent’s verdicts rested on solid ground, the researchers ran read-only probes on eight AWS accounts, re-reading the deciding facts directly from the cloud provider and leaving the agent’s own data out of the loop. For the verdicts the probes could settle, the live environment matched the agent’s facts 99.4% of the time. When every finding the probes could not check was counted as wrong, the figure dropped to 81.8%.

The probes tested the facts behind the verdicts, and whether the revised severity ratings were the right ones is a question the study left open. The authors draw a line between an AI reading findings and an AI acting on them.

“Verified, environment-specific reading of each finding is a precondition for acting on findings autonomously,” Goldberg and Engelberg argued. “Reading and acting differ in blast radius, reversibility, and authorization,” they cautioned, adding that “this study measures reading only.”

The work covers one system’s verdicts on the HIGH queue of two platforms, and 92% of the re-graded findings were on AWS. Live verification covered one platform and five resource types, and it tested the deciding fact behind each verdict, leaving the final grade unchecked.

Findings that started at MEDIUM or LOW fell outside the scope. The study also lacks incident data, so it leaves open whether upgraded findings are more likely to be exploited, or downgraded findings less likely, than their vendor grade implies. Recall, meaning the deciding facts the agent missed, went unmeasured.

passages: The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official.
Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6.
sources.body: The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official. Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6.

extraction.body: The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official. The tracker sits smack-dab between the recently launched Fitbit Air and the more powerful Google Pixel Watch 5 in the company’s current wearable lineup. Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6. Much of the Edge’s specs were previously leaked, but the tracker has a 46 percent larger OLED display compared to the Charge 6, a physical side button, and is a smidge thicker at 11.5mm. The tracker uses the same proprietary charger as the Air, and can also get about a day’s worth of battery in five minutes. (A full charge takes 90 minutes.) For health tracking, the Edge has an EKG sensor for atrial fibrillation detection, a skin temperature sensor, SpO2 and optical heart rate sensors, plus your typical motion tracking sensors. The Edge doesn’t have a mic or speaker, so you can’t take calls from the wrist even though you can see who’s calling on the screen. The latter is a bit disappointing, given that the Edge essentially replaces the Charge 6 and is $20 more expensive at $179.99. The new Fitbit offers improved automatic workout tracking and GPS compared to the Charge 6. The former is a revised motion model that’ll also come to the Air. Google says the new model means auto activity tracking is twice as accurate and supports over 100 activities. The Edge’s GPS tracking is also purportedly 40 percent more accurate — though it’s not using the same software-based post-processing update that Google introduced with the Pixel Watch 5. This increased accuracy mostly comes from on-device improvements to the Edge. Feature-wise, the device is meant for people who want glanceable information, with some but not all the bells and whistles of a smartwatch. The Edge borrows much of the Pixel Watch’s design language as far as widgets and user interface go. It’s not running Wear OS, though; this is a redesigned Fitbit OS. The Edge will launch with several types of straps so you can adjust the style to fit various occasions, including metal links to give it more of a jewelry-like feel. (Speaking of jewelry-like styling, the Air is also getting a new metal mesh strap that costs $69.99 and is available October 27th.) As with the Air and Pixel Watch 5, there’ll be a Stephen Curry edition of the Edge that will cost $219.99.

The Edge’s GPS tracking is also purportedly 40 percent more accurate — though it’s not using the same software-based post-processing update that Google introduced with the Pixel Watch 5.
This increased accuracy mostly comes from on-device improvements to the Edge.
Feature-wise, the device is meant for people who want glanceable information, with some but not all the bells and whistles of a smartwatch.
The Edge borrows much of the Pixel Watch’s design language as far as widgets and user interface go.
It’s not running Wear OS, though; this is a redesigned Fitbit OS.

The Edge will launch with several types of straps so you can adjust the style to fit various occasions, including metal links to give it more of a jewelry-like feel. (Speaking of jewelry-like styling, the Air is also getting a new metal mesh strap that costs $69.99 and is available October 27th.) As with the Air and Pixel Watch 5, there’ll be a Stephen Curry edition of the Edge that will cost $219.99.

extraction.description: The highly leaked $179.99 Fitbit Edge is now official. The middle-of-the-road tracker keeps the Air’s simple design but adds some of the Pixel Watch’s smarts.

relevantPassages.text: The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official.
Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6.

In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI InvokeEndpoint . The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options. Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options. Send a messages array with role and content , plus generation controls such as max_tokens and stream : The response returns option_ids , probabilities , and raw option_logits in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. With stable option IDs, your application can apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing generated prose. Other implementations include Jev , TypeSafe’s decision model and /v1/systemone API; Kev , a model server designed for TypeSafe API compatibility; and Strands Decider 2B , a purpose-built model for agent workflows with calibrated outputs. Use this pattern when your application defines the allowed choices at request time and needs a model to interpret unstructured context. Examples include routing a case to a queue, extracting one value from a known set, assigning an incident priority, checking a policy outcome, or selecting an agent action. Shared-state scoring reuses the common prompt prefix, while the adapter returns retryable HTTP 503 responses instead of allowing an unbounded queue around its stateful llama.cpp context. The text-generation example uses the CPU DLC and a fixed CPU instance. The request declares stable IDs for each allowed option: The response preserves the option order and includes conditional probabilities, raw logits, token and prompt metadata, and the pinned model identity: Apply application-level thresholds and fallbacks. Don’t use a model decision as a substitute for authorization. Delete the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model: The script deletes only those explicitly named SageMaker AI resources. The AWS DLC for llama.cpp gives you a managed foundation for serving decision models on SageMaker AI across CPU and GPU instances. It can load GGUF models from SageMaker AI model artifacts or a configured Hugging Face repository, then serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint without requiring a custom container. Choose CPU for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive, and choose GPU when prompt prefill and tail latency affect the application experience. This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX , vLLM-Omni – Part 1 , and vLLM-Omni – Part 2 .

VP Science, Google DeepMind & Chief Scientist, Google Cloud Your browser does not support the audio element. Google is using artificial intelligence to accelerate medical research, from mapping the human brain to identifying genetic diseases in under eight hours. These tools help scientists repurpose drugs, design custom enzymes, and improve cancer detection rates while reducing administrative burdens on doctors. You can explore these open-access platforms and research findings to see how technology is transforming patient care and public health outcomes globally. Google is using AI to help scientists understand diseases at a tiny, molecular level. These tools speed up drug discovery, map the human brain, and help doctors diagnose patients much faster. The technology also helps predict disease outbreaks so communities can get the care they need sooner. By sharing these tools, Google hopes to help researchers everywhere create better treatments and save more lives. Google’s health research and tools span from fundamental cellular discovery to laboratory analysis and patient impact. Over the last five years, Google teams have published 90 peer-reviewed research papers about understanding and addressing diseases, accumulating more than 90,000 citations. And building on our vision for how technology can accelerate science to improve lives , we’re collaborating with clinicians, academic institutes, and researchers to ensure discoveries make it out of the lab to benefit patients. Here is how our efforts are helping to advance medical research and public health solutions. AlphaGenome Atlas is the most comprehensive catalog of predictions for how single-letter variant changes in the human genome affect molecular biology. To effectively treat an illness, it helps to understand how it operates at the molecular, genetic, and cellular levels. Our early-stage biology models act as collaborative research tools for scientists, revealing nature's hidden mechanics and advancing medical discoveries. Visual map of proteins developed with the support of AlphaFold. New mammography screening systems can help to catch historically missed interval cancers and reduce specialist reading workloads. A medical breakthrough only matters if it can help real people. Our research demonstrates that machine learning models can help support disease detection as well as alleviate the administrative workload so providers can focus on care. Transforming health requires scientists, researchers, and institutions working hand-in-hand. That’s why we equip the science community with the advanced models and open-access platforms to fuel breakthrough research — along with the philanthropic funding and computing power they need to apply that research. Through Google.org, we’re supporting organizations like the Infectious Disease Institute at Makerere University to forecast malaria drug resistance mutations with AlphaFold and AlphaMissense, and the University of Pennsylvania, using AlphaProteo and AlphaFold to help design novel cellular therapies that can augment the treatment of solid tumors and complex diseases. In 2026, Google.org has provided over $60 million to organizations around the world that are applying advanced models to transform how we understand and treat diseases. By meeting disease at every stage, we can turn the most intractable human health challenges into actionable solutions, helping people everywhere live longer, healthier lives. Yossi Matias is Vice President, Google, and the Head of Google Research. Under Yossi’s leadership, world-class global teams are leading breakthrough research on Foundational Machine Learning & Algorithms, Computing Systems & Quantum Computing, Science, AI for Societal Impact in Health, Climate, Sustainability, Education and Cultural and Behavioral Intelligence. Yossi also leads teams advancing foundational research advancements in Generative AI, including in Factuality and Efficiency, driving real-world impact and shaping the future of technology.

You can explore these open-access platforms and research findings to see how technology is transforming patient care and public health outcomes globally.

Google is using AI to help scientists understand diseases at a tiny, molecular level. These tools speed up drug discovery, map the human brain, and help doctors diagnose patients much faster. The technology also helps predict disease outbreaks so communities can get the care they need sooner. By sharing these tools, Google hopes to help researchers everywhere create better treatments and save more lives.

Google’s health research and tools span from fundamental cellular discovery to laboratory analysis and patient impact. Over the last five years, Google teams have published 90 peer-reviewed research papers about understanding and addressing diseases, accumulating more than 90,000 citations. And building on our vision for how technology can accelerate science to improve lives , we’re collaborating with clinicians, academic institutes, and researchers to ensure discoveries make it out of the lab to benefit patients. Here is how our efforts are helping to advance medical research and public health solutions.
AlphaGenome Atlas is the most comprehensive catalog of predictions for how single-letter variant changes in the human genome affect molecular biology.

New mammography screening systems can help to catch historically missed interval cancers and reduce specialist reading workloads.

Transforming health requires scientists, researchers, and institutions working hand-in-hand. That’s why we equip the science community with the advanced models and open-access platforms to fuel breakthrough research — along with the philanthropic funding and computing power they need to apply that research.

By meeting disease at every stage, we can turn the most intractable human health challenges into actionable solutions, helping people everywhere live longer, healthier lives.

extraction.body: Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch. Priced at $179.99, it combines the Fitbit Air’s slim band with an OLED display for checking map directions, notifications, weather, and music controls. Like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, the Edge works with Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini. (You’ll need a Google Health Premium subscription to use it.) The coach can use your fitness, health, and medical information to put together weekly routines and workout plans, then adjust them around your schedule. It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.) Google says the Fitbit Edge can automatically recognize and log up to 100 activities, including runs, bike rides, and walks. The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather. The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips. Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters. The Fitbit Edge is available to preorder through the Google Store, with store availability set for October 27. Color choices include Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon.
