coreStoryFacts.text: The global AI in education market size was calculated at USD 7.05 billion in 2025 and is predicted to surpass around USD 136.79 billion by 2035, expanding at a strong CAGR of 34.52% from 2026 to 2035.
The growing penetration of high-speed internet and the strong development of customized learning paths increases adoption of EdTech.

The U.S. market is growing rapidly, with strong demand for personalized learning and adaptive platforms that tailor content to individual student needs, driving investments and adoption in K-12 and higher education institutions.

Market forecasts show significant expansion in market value over the coming decade, supported by robust growth rates as schools and EdTech companies integrate AI-driven tools for analytics, tutoring, and automated assessments.
The learning platform and virtual facilitators segment held the largest revenue share in the market in 2025.

It offers benefits like automated assessment, administrative efficiency, immersive learning experiences, boosts engagement, 24/7 support, enhanced accessibility, improves educational material, and 24/7 tutoring.

National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 (India) : This policy mandates the integration of AI-related subjects like digital literacy and coding across all school levels to prepare students for a tech-driven economy.
Major technology companies, including Tencent, Alibaba Group, and Baidu, are investing heavily in AI-powered tutoring platforms, adaptive learning systems, and intelligent assessment tools.
Amid this shift, Coursera, a global online learning platform, has emerged as a leader in adapting to Vietnam’s rapidly changing tech landscape.

Greg Hart, CEO of Coursera, noted that the platform currently has about 1.8 million learners in Vietnam, ranking third in Southeast Asia behind the Philippines (2.8 million) and Indonesia (2.1 million).
Vietnamese users are particularly drawn to data science, AI, and Chinese language courses.
Despite its vast potential, Vietnam’s edtech market faces hurdles such as affordability, users’ preference for free or partially paid models, and the challenge of retaining learners long-term.

However, national digital transformation policies, AI development commitments, and efforts to popularize digital skills in education are creating tangible growth opportunities for market participants.
Many have integrated livestream classes, support teachers, 24/7 learning chatbots, and exam prep content aligned with Vietnam’s national education curriculum.
These domestic players have a deep understanding of local student and parent psychology – a decisive advantage in a cost-sensitive and trust-driven market.
Vietnam’s online education sector is shifting from a “tech pilot” phase to a “content and experience strategy” phase.
This surge is fueled not only by the digital transformation of education but also by remote work trends and the need for lifelong learning in the face of rapidly evolving labor market demands.
Local edtech start-ups like Vuihoc.vn, Edupia, Moon.vn, and Topica are also accelerating, investing in AI and adaptive learning models that personalize learning progress for individual students.
The widespread impact of artificial intelligence (AI), especially generative models like ChatGPT, has dramatically transformed industries, and education is among the first to feel the change.

facts.text: The global AI in education market size was calculated at USD 7.05 billion in 2025 and is predicted to surpass around USD 136.79 billion by 2035, expanding at a strong CAGR of 34.52% from 2026 to 2035.
The growing penetration of high-speed internet and the strong development of customized learning paths increases adoption of EdTech.

The U.S. market is growing rapidly, with strong demand for personalized learning and adaptive platforms that tailor content to individual student needs, driving investments and adoption in K-12 and higher education institutions.

Market forecasts show significant expansion in market value over the coming decade, supported by robust growth rates as schools and EdTech companies integrate AI-driven tools for analytics, tutoring, and automated assessments.
The learning platform and virtual facilitators segment held the largest revenue share in the market in 2025.

It offers benefits like automated assessment, administrative efficiency, immersive learning experiences, boosts engagement, 24/7 support, enhanced accessibility, improves educational material, and 24/7 tutoring.

National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 (India) : This policy mandates the integration of AI-related subjects like digital literacy and coding across all school levels to prepare students for a tech-driven economy.
Major technology companies, including Tencent, Alibaba Group, and Baidu, are investing heavily in AI-powered tutoring platforms, adaptive learning systems, and intelligent assessment tools.
Amid this shift, Coursera, a global online learning platform, has emerged as a leader in adapting to Vietnam’s rapidly changing tech landscape.

Greg Hart, CEO of Coursera, noted that the platform currently has about 1.8 million learners in Vietnam, ranking third in Southeast Asia behind the Philippines (2.8 million) and Indonesia (2.1 million).
Vietnamese users are particularly drawn to data science, AI, and Chinese language courses.
Despite its vast potential, Vietnam’s edtech market faces hurdles such as affordability, users’ preference for free or partially paid models, and the challenge of retaining learners long-term.

However, national digital transformation policies, AI development commitments, and efforts to popularize digital skills in education are creating tangible growth opportunities for market participants.
Many have integrated livestream classes, support teachers, 24/7 learning chatbots, and exam prep content aligned with Vietnam’s national education curriculum.
These domestic players have a deep understanding of local student and parent psychology – a decisive advantage in a cost-sensitive and trust-driven market.
Vietnam’s online education sector is shifting from a “tech pilot” phase to a “content and experience strategy” phase.
This surge is fueled not only by the digital transformation of education but also by remote work trends and the need for lifelong learning in the face of rapidly evolving labor market demands.
Local edtech start-ups like Vuihoc.vn, Edupia, Moon.vn, and Topica are also accelerating, investing in AI and adaptive learning models that personalize learning progress for individual students.
The widespread impact of artificial intelligence (AI), especially generative models like ChatGPT, has dramatically transformed industries, and education is among the first to feel the change.

Market Size and Projected Expansion of the AI-Powered Personalized Learning and EdTech Tutoring Platforms Market The market for AI-driven personalized learning and EdTech tutoring platforms has experienced remarkable expansion recently.
It is projected to grow from $8.08 billion in 2025 to $10.03 billion in 2026, reflecting a strong compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 24.0%.

This surge is largely attributed to widespread adoption of digital education tools, improved internet access facilitating online learning, heightened demand for customized educational experiences, the expansion of e-learning offerings in academic institutions, and growing investments in education technology solutions.

LONDON, GREATER LONDON, UNITED KINGDOM, October 12, 2026 / EINPresswire.com / -- The landscape of education technology is rapidly evolving, with artificial intelligence (AI) playing a pivotal role in transforming personalized learning experiences.
This overview delves into the current market status, growth drivers, regional dynamics, and key trends shaping this innovative sector.
These systems dynamically adjust instructional materials, learning speed, and assessments to suit individual needs while offering intelligent guidance and feedback.
By leveraging data-driven insights and automated support, these platforms enhance educational outcomes through continuous optimization of the learning process.
Personalized learning involves crafting educational paths, content, and assessments tailored to each learner’s unique preferences, abilities, and progress.
This demand has surged alongside the rapid integration of digital learning technologies that support adaptive, student-centered education models.

AI-powered platforms harness machine learning algorithms to provide customized lessons, intelligent tutoring, performance monitoring, and immediate feedback, catering to individual learner requirements.

The market analysis encompasses various geographical areas including Asia-Pacific, South East Asia, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, North America, South America, the Middle East, and Africa, offering a detailed global perspective on market trends and expansion opportunities.

Key trends anticipated during the forecast period involve the adoption of personalized learning path generation, real-time learner performance analytics, adaptive assessment technologies, intelligent student engagement and feedback mechanisms, as well as platforms designed to automate learning outcome optimization.
Such evidence highlights the growing appreciation and demand for personalized education solutions, which in turn fuels market growth.

passages: BEIJING, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Nvidia's share of China's market for data-centre AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters.

IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country.
Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said.
Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%.
Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country. Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said. Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

extraction.body: BEIJING, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Nvidia's share of China's market for data-centre AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters. Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China from January through June, down 44% from a year earlier, IDC data showed. AI accelerators are specialised chips used to train and run AI models. Washington has restricted China's access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, limiting the range of products the US chipmaker can sell in the world's second-largest economy. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington's export curbs, saying the policy forced a US company to cede China's $50 billion AI chip market to Huawei. IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said. Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%. Total AI-accelerator shipments reached 2.008 million units in the first half. Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs -- the chips most widely used to train AI models -- fell 26% to 991,000 units, as supplies eligible for sale in mainland China remained limited, IDC said. Shipments of other AI accelerators rose nearly 80% to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs by volume. This category includes chips designed for specific AI tasks, such as running trained models. Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95% of the non-GPU segment, which IDC said was being adopted by government agencies, internet companies and telecoms providers. IDC said competition was shifting from the performance of a single chip to system-level capabilities, including how well chips work in a larger computing cluster. IDC expects total accelerator shipments in China to grow 19% this year, even as GPU shipments fall 9%. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista and Che Pan; Editing by Jamie Freed)

Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China from January through June, down 44% from a year earlier, IDC data showed. AI accelerators are specialised chips used to train and run AI models. Washington has restricted China's access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, limiting the range of products the US chipmaker can sell in the world's second-largest economy. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington's export curbs, saying the policy forced a US company to cede China's $50 billion AI chip market to Huawei. IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said. Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%. Total AI-accelerator shipments reached 2.008 million units in the first half. Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs -- the chips most widely used to train AI models -- fell 26% to 991,000 units, as supplies eligible for sale in mainland China remained limited, IDC said. Shipments of other AI accelerators rose nearly 80% to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs by volume. This category includes chips designed for specific AI tasks, such as running trained models. Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95% of the non-GPU segment, which IDC said was being adopted by government agencies, internet companies and telecoms providers. IDC said competition was shifting from the performance of a single chip to system-level capabilities, including how well chips work in a larger computing cluster. IDC expects total accelerator shipments in China to grow 19% this year, even as GPU shipments fall 9%. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista and Che Pan; Editing by Jamie Freed)

The Justice Department confirmed that a judicially authorized search warrant of Omar’s home was executed by Homeland Security Investigations but provided no other details. And a bipartisan group of senators is calling on the Trump administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia despite a U.S. sanctions law. Trump used his rally in Youngstown, Ohio, to defend his administration’s investigation into the Democratic congresswoman. Federal agents on Monday searched Omar’s home in Washington. She is a Somali immigrant and an outspoken Trump critic. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military,” Trump said. “All they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right.’ She’s got a constitutional right. She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.” The crowd responded to the president by shouting, “Deport,” suggesting that the sitting member of Congress be removed from the U.S. Trump slams Sherrod Brown as he stumps in Ohio The president said the former Democratic senator, who lost his seat in 2024 and is running for another seat this time, is “the candidate of the Marxists, the communists.” He tied Brown to what he described as an out-of-control border and runaway inflation under former President Joe Biden. And he urged the crowd to vote for Sen. Jon Husted, whom he noted, with a colorful anatomical description of his athletic build, was a college football player. Omar supporters turn out for her at Minnesota rally More than 100 people chanted “Ilhan! Ilhan!” at an afternoon rally in Minneapolis in support of Omar. Speakers addressed the crowd from the bed of a pickup truck behind a large sign that said, “We Stand With Ilhan.” “This administration is a violent authoritative regime. Take it from us: We would know. We have been experiencing this for generations,” said Rachel Dionne-Thunder, a member of the Big Stone Cree Nation. Roger Marshall Trump said last week he struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, reversing years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine. After touring an ethanol plant in Dyersville, Iowa, Hinson told reporters that fuel prices are a priority for her. extraction.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) takes questions at the Capitol, January 13, 2026. J. Scott Applewhite/AP Federal officers raided Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home early Monday morning, reportedly related to an investigation into the lawmaker’s immigration paperwork, filed by a relative when Omar was a child. The search was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of the Department of Homeland Security that manages criminal investigations, and, according to a Justice Department spokesperson, “executed a judicially authorized search warrant” the agency secured. An anonymous source reportedly “familiar with the situation” alleged to NBC News that the raid was part of a yearslong investigation involving whistleblowers. CNN also reported that a federal judge approved the search warrant but did not name the judge. White House border czar Tom Homan, the acting head of ICE, stated on Fox News last month that Homeland Security was investigating Omar for alleged unspecified “criminal” conduct, but claimed he couldn’t “give the specifics of what’s happening.” “If someone committed an immigration violation, if someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law,” Homan said at the time. “So, I’ll leave it at that. We’ll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations, continue the investigation.” In a Monday morning Fox interview, Homan confirmed that the search had taken place. Omar immigrated to the US from Somalia in 1995, when she was 12, amid the ongoing civil war in the country. She became a naturalized US citizen in 2000. President Donald Trump and his administration have regularly racially targeted Omar —a progressive Democrat and frequent critic of the administration’s policies—fueling further violent threats against her and other lawmakers of color, and people from Somalia living in Minnesota . Trump and other White House officials have repeatedly cited the Feeding Our Future fraud scandal that involved members of the state’s Somali American community to justify the mass violence by immigration officers in the area as part of ICE’s Operation Metro Surge in late 2025. The timing of the raid on Omar’s Washington-area home—22 days before the November midterms, in which she is a heavy favorite for reelection—adds additional scrutiny, as Justice Department policy prohibits federal prosecutors and agents from timing investigations or charges to affect election outcomes. While not a binding rule, the Justice Department has historically complied by pausing all related actions in the 60 days before an election. (Trump and the wider MAGA movement have repeatedly targeted former FBI head James Comey, and that agency as a whole, in part over the timing and supposed political motivations of the FBI’s own investigations under Comey into both Trump and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.) “Americans see this for what it is,” Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat who the Trump administration has also targeted , wrote on social media. “President ​Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.” “I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar posted on social media Monday afternoon. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.” I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. passages: Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) takes questions at the Capitol, January 13, 2026. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Federal officers raided Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home early Monday morning, reportedly related to an investigation into the lawmaker’s immigration paperwork, filed by a relative when Omar was a child.

The search was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of the Department of Homeland Security that manages criminal investigations, and, according to a Justice Department spokesperson, “executed a judicially authorized search warrant” the agency secured. An anonymous source reportedly “familiar with the situation” alleged to NBC News that the raid was part of a yearslong investigation involving whistleblowers. CNN also reported that a federal judge approved the search warrant but did not name the judge.

White House border czar Tom Homan, the acting head of ICE, stated on Fox News last month that Homeland Security was investigating Omar for alleged unspecified “criminal” conduct, but claimed he couldn’t “give the specifics of what’s happening.”

“If someone committed an immigration violation, if someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law,” Homan said at the time. “So, I’ll leave it at that. We’ll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations, continue the investigation.”
In a Monday morning Fox interview, Homan confirmed that the search had taken place.

Omar immigrated to the US from Somalia in 1995, when she was 12, amid the ongoing civil war in the country. She became a naturalized US citizen in 2000. President Donald Trump and his administration have regularly racially targeted Omar —a progressive Democrat and frequent critic of the administration’s policies—fueling further violent threats against her and other lawmakers of color, and people from Somalia living in Minnesota .

Trump and other White House officials have repeatedly cited the Feeding Our Future fraud scandal that involved members of the state’s Somali American community to justify the mass violence by immigration officers in the area as part of ICE’s Operation Metro Surge in late 2025.

The timing of the raid on Omar’s Washington-area home—22 days before the November midterms, in which she is a heavy favorite for reelection—adds additional scrutiny, as Justice Department policy prohibits federal prosecutors and agents from timing investigations or charges to affect election outcomes. While not a binding rule, the Justice Department has historically complied by pausing all related actions in the 60 days before an election. (Trump and the wider MAGA movement have repeatedly targeted former FBI head James Comey, and that agency as a whole, in part over the timing and supposed political motivations of the FBI’s own investigations under Comey into both Trump and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.)

“Americans see this for what it is,” Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat who the Trump administration has also targeted , wrote on social media. “President ​Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.”

“I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar posted on social media Monday afternoon. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

Ilhan Omar, a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed scrutiny to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid . The Justice Department confirmed that a judicially authorized search warrant of Omar’s home was executed by Homeland Security Investigations but provided no other details. Trump administration officials have repeatedly hinted at the existence of an inquiry targeting the Minnesota representative. Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” A senior U.S. official said President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. And a bipartisan group of senators is calling on the Trump administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia despite a U.S. sanctions law. Trump used his rally in Youngstown, Ohio, to defend his administration’s investigation into the Democratic congresswoman. Federal agents on Monday searched Omar’s home in Washington. She is a Somali immigrant and an outspoken Trump critic. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military,” Trump said. “All they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right.’ She’s got a constitutional right. She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.” The crowd responded to the president by shouting, “Deport,” suggesting that the sitting member of Congress be removed from the U.S. Trump slams Sherrod Brown as he stumps in Ohio The president said the former Democratic senator, who lost his seat in 2024 and is running for another seat this time, is “the candidate of the Marxists, the communists.” He tied Brown to what he described as an out-of-control border and runaway inflation under former President Joe Biden. And he urged the crowd to vote for Sen. Jon Husted, whom he noted, with a colorful anatomical description of his athletic build, was a college football player. Omar supporters turn out for her at Minnesota rally More than 100 people chanted “Ilhan! Ilhan!” at an afternoon rally in Minneapolis in support of Omar. Speakers addressed the crowd from the bed of a pickup truck behind a large sign that said, “We Stand With Ilhan.” “This administration is a violent authoritative regime. Take it from us: We would know. We have been experiencing this for generations,” said Rachel Dionne-Thunder, a member of the Big Stone Cree Nation. Trump, in response to another question about the Houthis, said “they are misbehaving very badly. No good.” But he didn’t say anything about whether the U.S. would respond to the Houthis. Trump says there’s an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia because he said so Trump is insisting that an energy ceasefire is in place for Ukraine and Russia, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that Moscow struck his country’s energy sites. When pressed about the attacks by Russia, Trump said: “Well, I’d have to look at it and see, because there’s been violations on both sides.” Trump says he has ‘nothing to do’ with search of Omar’s Washington home “I understand they’re looking at it very carefully,” the president said of an investigation that sparked federal agents to search the home of the Democratic representative. Trump said he’d found the congresswoman to “be totally crooked, personally.” But even after the judge’s 6:45 p.m. deadline , a few of the spots labeled as paid for by the U.S. government aired on television, data from AdImpact shows. The Department of Homeland Security did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel those final ad buys, the White House said in an email. The White House said the ads, which it refers to as public service announcements, will be paid for by outside groups going forward. Trump says he’ll have a rally in Kansas to boost Sen. After touring an ethanol plant in Dyersville, Iowa, Hinson told reporters that fuel prices are a priority for her. But she also said the U.S. should be “strong” on Russia, noting her support for a sanctions package that the House passed last month. extraction.body: SPARTANBURG — The 200,000-square-foot, 60-megawatt proposed data center at 300 Jones Road has appealed county planning staff's rejection of its development application and is on the agenda for the Board of Zoning Appeals meeting Aug. 25. The hearing comes after Spartanburg County Council declined to pass a proposed data center moratorium on third reading, which would have stopped new data centers from coming to the county for at least a year. Council member Monier Abusaft told The Post and Courier afterward that the county wanted to get more input before passing the data center ban. The delay also came after executives from Pacolet Milliken and its subsidiary, Lockhart Power, lobbied against an expansive pause, advocating instead for a moratorium only on larger data centers. They argued that small data centers were good for the power grid and lower electricity rates. It was the Lightstone Group's proposed data center at 300 Jones Road — then referred to as Project Lighthouse — that prompted council to vote for a moratorium in the first place . Following a public uprising against another project — the Tiger DC data center — county council voted not to award it the same kind of tax deal it gave to the NorthMark and Valara data center on Pine Street. Their thinking at the time was that without tax incentives , data centers would look elsewhere. But when the Lightstone Group decided to move forward anyway, council passed the first reading of an ordinance to pause all data centers, regardless of size. The vote on June 22 came shortly before the Republican primary runoff election in which two incumbents faced strong challengers. After it passed two of three readings, council on Aug. 17 delayed final approval of the moratorium to gather more information. In the meantime, the Lightstone Group's data center has worked its way through the planning department. Engineering firm Thomas and Hutton submitted a development application April 28 for the site. County staff rejected it June 26 for not complying with the county's unified land management ordinance, according to background information included in the BZA agenda. On June 29, Thomas and Hutton submitted revised plans, but county staff on July 10 told them that since their prior application was denied, a new one would be required. By that time, county council was considering the new moratorium. Lightstone Group executive vice president and general counsel Joseph E. Teichman then appealed the denial of their application, which brings it before the board of zoning appeals. County spokesperson Scottie Kay Blackwell said in an email that the pending ordinance doctrine — the legal principle that governments may deny zoning and permit applications if they violate pending rule changes — still applies. She noted that the BZA appeal was administrative and that the county would still deny any new applications for data centers while the moratorium was under consideration. "Accordingly, no data center subject to the proposed moratorium — including the 300 Jones Road application — will be approved during that period," she said. "The Board of Zoning Appeals hearing is an administrative appeal; it is not a hearing to approve the data center. Council's postponement of third reading did not authorize the underlying development application to proceed." The property on Jones Road has been in limbo. In 2021, Greenidge Generation Holdings bought 175 acres at 300 Jones Road for $15 million, and in 2023 sold 23 acres and a 44-megawatt bitcoin mining facility, according to a news release. In 2024, it planned to sell the remaining 152 acres to Data Journey LLC for $12.1 million and an 8 percent stake in the profits of a data center planned for the site. But the deal fell through. Last December, Greenidge announced a new sale, this time for $18 million to an affiliate of The Lightstone Group and LightHouse Data Centers. According to the Lightstone Group , the data center is "designed to provide secure, reliable computing infrastructure for businesses and organizations that rely on cloud services, enterprise applications, digital communications, and emerging technologies. Data centers are essential infrastructure supporting the digital services people use every day." It will use 60 megawatts of power from the grid that was already permitted for the site, and the Lightstone Group said in a statement that all necessary infrastructure upgrades had already been paid for. The group said the data center will use about 12 million gallons of water a year — or around 33,000 gallons per day. That's less than many other industrial users, including the NorthMark data center , which is projected to use 460,000 gallons of water per day. Spartanburg Water said because it was so early in the process, it had not yet "received any information regarding their anticipated water and/or wastewater needs." The board of zoning appeals is scheduled to meet at 4:30 p.m. Aug. 25 in the Spartanburg County Council chambers. SPARTANBURG —A former cryptocurrency mining facility in the Tiger River Industrial Park is being converted into a data center. The company hopes it’s operational by the end of 2027. Officials hold a ground-breaking ceremony for BV Power Alpha in Spartanburg. The company is now called AIB Data Center and is converting its cryptocurrency mining site into a data center. SPARTANBURG —A former cryptocurrency mining facility in the Tiger River Industrial Park is being converted into a data center. The company hopes it’s operational by the end of 2027. BV Power Alpha previously received a fee-in-lieu-of-tax agreement for its crypto mining facility that started up in 2022. The company, owned by Jerry Tang, is now called AIB Data Centers . In February, Tang abandoned efforts to build a new data center in the Tyger River Industrial Park after Spartanburg County Council declined to offer tax incentives in the wake of community criticism over the project. Since then, county council passed a data center moratorium that could prevent new data centers that have an IT electrical load of 65 megawatts or more . Council voted to include the caveat after lobbying from William Crawford, president of Pacolet Milliken, and Bryan Stone, president of Pacolet Milliken subsidiary Lockhart Power, who argued that small data centers create revenue that helps keep costs down for ratepayers. Pacolet Milliken developed the Tyger River Industrial Park and Lockhart supplies much of the power there. The new AIB data center will have an electrical load of only 50 megawatts, falling below that 65-megawatt threshold, according to the company. It will buy power from a utility instead of producing it, meaning it won’t create the type of air pollution that the NorthMark data center will generate. Company spokesperson Pierre DuBois said in an email that the planned data center would exist on the same land footprint as the bitcoin mining facility. “Essentially, the same equipment moves inside the walls, with other equipment added within those walls,” he added. DuBois also said the water use in the data center would be a fraction of what the crypto mining facility used. “Since the site began operating, it has used about 14,000 gallons a day,” said DuBois. “We estimate the data center will use about 165 gallons a day.” For comparison, the NorthMark data center projects to use more than 1 million gallons a day . In an email, DuBois said the new data center wouldn’t be a “hyperscale mega-project,” and that the company “offered to give up incentives awarded to the crypto mining facility in 2022, which would otherwise have carried over to the data center. The county accepted.” According to a news release, AIB has already signed a 12-year agreement with Dutch AI company Nebius . It includes two potential five-year renewal periods. extraction.body: Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebecca Bellan, and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one-year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms of how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried. It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step. Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc. And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. But we’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them. And that’s because, a lot of time, the [technological] ability’s not there, and in part because they’re just not explaining it well. I wrote a story last week about how it’s been a year since we’ve really heard Tesla beating its own drum about building towards what it originally was calling “sustainable abundance” and is now “amazing abundance” as its mission statement. It’s just wild to me that we’re a year into that, and the company still doesn’t have a very good definition of it, especially considering that they released this whole multi-page PDF laying it out when they announced this, and even Tesla’s biggest fans criticized Elon Musk and Tesla for how unspecific it was. It read like LLM nonsense. Anthony: One of the things this has made me think about is just the narrative and this sense that for a while, it really felt like it was being pushed down our throats — this idea of, “This is inevitable, this AI-driven future, and get on board or you’re just going to be left behind.” Obviously that future is barreling ahead in a lot of ways, but in a few key ways, there have been these obstacles. What I’ve really liked about that is this sense of “No, you actually have to make the case for it.” You can’t just say, “This is the future, shut up.” And then specifically about Tesla and the abundance thing, what was shocking to me is not so much that they haven’t come up with a definition of abundance, but that that was a promise that they were making in the first place. I think [that] speaks to how strange our relationship to Tesla, and particularly the people who are invested and ride-or-die for Elon, [has become.] It’s not about, is this company going to sell a lot of cars? It’s about this vision for remaking society. Or at least, that’s what they’re being sold. extraction.body: The major artificial intelligence companies’ prime directive to literally bulldoze AI infrastructure into states with minimal regulation has produced citizen-led, bipartisan demands for local and national moratoriums on data center siting. While the Trump administration is doing everything it can to facilitate the only capital spending with a pulse in the economy, these calls for moratoriums are growing, and connecting with local successes in blocking data center construction. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) recently called for a national moratorium on the construction of data centers that are “powering this unregulated sprint to develop and deploy AI.” Sanders did credit “the transformative power of AI and robotics” before calling out Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Peter Thiel, and Bill Gates with a simple question: “Are these multibillionaires staying up nights worrying about what AI and robotics will do to the working families of our country and the world?” The answer would be mostly no. Over 230 organizations across the 50 states signed on to a letter to members of Congress organized by Food & Water Watch, a national advocacy group, also calling for a national moratorium on data center siting and construction. The letter characterized generative AI and crypto as generational threats. But it’s the local rejections of data centers—in places as varied as Chandler, Arizona , and Leesburg, Indiana —that should have the tech oligarchs worried. These results demonstrate that Americans are beginning to grasp the downsides of inserting AI into every facet of daily life. This mushrooming grassroots backlash promises to dominate American politics in 2026. The fallout from siting these gargantuan facilities near human habitats continues to convulse communities. Residential ratepayers are already grappling with electricity price spikes and see data centers as a major driver of the pain. Power demand from data centers will hit 106 gigawatts by 2035 , according to an analysis from BloombergNEF. A Yale Clean Energy Forum report estimates that data centers could take up as much as 12 percent of total U.S. power consumption by 2028, a higher demand than all manufacturing of steel, aluminum, and other high-intensity manufactured goods combined. “Electricity is the new price of eggs,” one industry analyst told The New York Times , and if you’re concerned about electricity, you have to be concerned about data centers. Since 2019, at least 40 states—both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms. Data centers are also guzzling city-sized amounts of water. By 2028, they’ll require up to 720 billion gallons of water every year to keep servers cool—usage would fill one million Olympic-size swimming pools or furnish water for the interior-home uses of 18.5 million American households. In Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the largest concentration of data centers in the region that represents the world’s largest data hub, data center expansions have collided with the climate crisis, leading to scrambles from local government to address the “ negative impacts on neighborhoods .” While the county wants to find environmental solutions that would reduce the burden on residents while still building the data centers, local elections in Loudoun County and throughout Virginia in November saw candidates who rejected data centers emerging victorious. Even residents in the fresh water–rich Great Lakes states have raised questions about increased data center usage. Illinois also has one of the highest concentrations of data centers in the country, and local officials and environmentalists have raised alarms that siting decisions don’t always take into consideration how local drinking water needs can clash with data center cooling demands. Georgia, Alabama, and Florida have actually had “ water wars .” In April, a federal judge ruled against Alabama in a dispute with Georgia over Army Corps of Engineers water allocations to metro Atlanta from Lake Allatoona, a northwest Georgia reservoir. Data center projects could complicate those interstate dynamics. NPR affiliate WABE reported that Chattahoochee Riverkeeper, which monitors the river running from North Georgia through Atlanta to Florida, tracks water usage plans for new data centers in the region. One facility , Coweta County’s Project Sail, would use nearly ten million gallons daily, which adds up to one-third of the county’s daily usage from the river. DATA CENTER DEVELOPERS have been exceptionally skilled at persuading local leaders of their value to communities by touting gains like temporary construction jobs. (There are few on-site permanent jobs.) Unlike what’s transpired in Northern Virginia, where county officials hand out tax credits but still haul in millions in tax revenues, some recent data center projects are steering away from generous agreements with local communities. Instead, project officials focus on tax credits, obscure the details, force officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), and never divulge their supernova clients to the public. Most residents are hard-pressed to fight corporate secrecy. The New York Times recently spotlighted Doña Ana County, New Mexico, a predominantly Latino community of 15,000. The data center developer for Project Jupiter, a multibillion-dollar component of the $500 billion SoftBank- and OpenAI-led Stargate Project, got to know the locals, but the underlying clients remained unknown because county officials had signed NDAs. Residents only found out after the project moved forward that the heavy hitters included OpenAI and Oracle. Instead of property tax revenues, the county will see a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) program, which essentially allow companies to decide how much—or how little—money they’re willing to offer a community. But this trick isn’t having much staying power. Data Center Watch, coordinated by 10a Labs, an applied research and technology company specializing in AI security, reports that in the second quarter of 2025, data center opponents slowed the roll or thwarted projects totaling about $100 billion—more than the total of every quarter since 2023. In one three-month period, 20 projects fell through. That includes a project in Chandler, a Phoenix suburb, where Arizona’s former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema personally lobbied at local meetings for a 422,000-square-foot data center plan operated by Active Infrastructure, a hyperscale data center developer. In the end, the Chandler City Council voted against the data center unanimously . In rural Leesburg, Indiana, the town council refused to rezone land for industrial use to build a data center on 554 acres. “I’m really just trying to speak out for the future of agriculture, and passing a data center is not the future of agriculture,” said one local resident. The possibility that a facility might be rejected has affected data center financing. In Michigan, Blue Owl Capital, a private credit firm, pulled out of a $10 billion data center deal with Oracle amid “shifting market sentiment around enormous AI spending” and concerns that “the Saline Township site … might face delays.” Elsewhere in Michigan, data center opponents rallied in Lansing last week and called for “ no secret deals ” between local governments, utilities, and data center developers. At the gathering, Attorney General Dana Nessel demanded that the state’s public utility commission step back from fast-tracking a major utility project to power the Saline Township project. Anthony Hudson, a Republican gubernatorial candidate who attended the protest, mostly agreed with Nessel. A pair of state lawmakers, one a Democrat and the other a Republican, have teamed up to propose reversing tax breaks for large data center facilities. But residents want a statewide moratorium. SINCE 2019, AT LEAST 40 STATES —both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms. Unfortunately, federal regulation has lagged miles behind the internet revolution. The Senate did manage to stave off , by a vote of 99-to-1, a White House–endorsed attempt to prohibit states from passing AI regulations for ten years. The prohibition on state AI regulation came up again in the annual defense policy bill and was again beaten back. But even though that proposal generated outrage, the major overstep into state regulatory authority hasn’t motivated Republicans to fill in the blanks. President Trump has seized on that inertia to issue more than half a dozen AI executive orders this year, the latest coming in mid-December complete with plans for a litigation task force and an annual evaluation of state laws determined to obliterate any opposition to AI usage or data center expansion. The Brennan Center has labeled that move “little more than political theater.” Executive orders do not invest the federal government with the powers to file lawsuits. So federal officials cannot “directly enforce” the order through court action. “To challenge a state AI regulation in court,” writes Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security in the center’s elections and government program, “the department would need to base the lawsuit on a federal statute or constitutional provision—not simply on the executive order itself.” Combine data center moratorium drama with the gutting of the Affordable Care Act, the nothing-to-see-here response to the affordability crisis, and extortionate trade tactics, and the White House and congressional Republicans have set themselves and everyone else up for a very dismal New Year. extraction.body: Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebecca Bellan, and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one-year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms of how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried. It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step. Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc. And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. But we’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them. And that’s because, a lot of time, the [technological] ability’s not there, and in part because they’re just not explaining it well. I wrote a story last week about how it’s been a year since we’ve really heard Tesla beating its own drum about building towards what it originally was calling “sustainable abundance” and is now “amazing abundance” as its mission statement. It’s just wild to me that we’re a year into that, and the company still doesn’t have a very good definition of it, especially considering that they released this whole multi-page PDF laying it out when they announced this, and even Tesla’s biggest fans criticized Elon Musk and Tesla for how unspecific it was. It read like LLM nonsense. Anthony: One of the things this has made me think about is just the narrative and this sense that for a while, it really felt like it was being pushed down our throats — this idea of, “This is inevitable, this AI-driven future, and get on board or you’re just going to be left behind.” Obviously that future is barreling ahead in a lot of ways, but in a few key ways, there have been these obstacles. What I’ve really liked about that is this sense of “No, you actually have to make the case for it.” You can’t just say, “This is the future, shut up.” And then specifically about Tesla and the abundance thing, what was shocking to me is not so much that they haven’t come up with a definition of abundance, but that that was a promise that they were making in the first place. I think [that] speaks to how strange our relationship to Tesla, and particularly the people who are invested and ride-or-die for Elon, [has become.] It’s not about, is this company going to sell a lot of cars? It’s about this vision for remaking society. Or at least, that’s what they’re being sold. extraction.body: The major artificial intelligence companies’ prime directive to literally bulldoze AI infrastructure into states with minimal regulation has produced citizen-led, bipartisan demands for local and national moratoriums on data center siting. While the Trump administration is doing everything it can to facilitate the only capital spending with a pulse in the economy, these calls for moratoriums are growing, and connecting with local successes in blocking data center construction. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) recently called for a national moratorium on the construction of data centers that are “powering this unregulated sprint to develop and deploy AI.” Sanders did credit “the transformative power of AI and robotics” before calling out Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Peter Thiel, and Bill Gates with a simple question: “Are these multibillionaires staying up nights worrying about what AI and robotics will do to the working families of our country and the world?” The answer would be mostly no. Over 230 organizations across the 50 states signed on to a letter to members of Congress organized by Food & Water Watch, a national advocacy group, also calling for a national moratorium on data center siting and construction. The letter characterized generative AI and crypto as generational threats. But it’s the local rejections of data centers—in places as varied as Chandler, Arizona , and Leesburg, Indiana —that should have the tech oligarchs worried. These results demonstrate that Americans are beginning to grasp the downsides of inserting AI into every facet of daily life. This mushrooming grassroots backlash promises to dominate American politics in 2026. The fallout from siting these gargantuan facilities near human habitats continues to convulse communities. Residential ratepayers are already grappling with electricity price spikes and see data centers as a major driver of the pain. Power demand from data centers will hit 106 gigawatts by 2035 , according to an analysis from BloombergNEF. A Yale Clean Energy Forum report estimates that data centers could take up as much as 12 percent of total U.S. power consumption by 2028, a higher demand than all manufacturing of steel, aluminum, and other high-intensity manufactured goods combined. “Electricity is the new price of eggs,” one industry analyst told The New York Times , and if you’re concerned about electricity, you have to be concerned about data centers. Since 2019, at least 40 states—both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms. Data centers are also guzzling city-sized amounts of water. By 2028, they’ll require up to 720 billion gallons of water every year to keep servers cool—usage would fill one million Olympic-size swimming pools or furnish water for the interior-home uses of 18.5 million American households. In Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the largest concentration of data centers in the region that represents the world’s largest data hub, data center expansions have collided with the climate crisis, leading to scrambles from local government to address the “ negative impacts on neighborhoods .” While the county wants to find environmental solutions that would reduce the burden on residents while still building the data centers, local elections in Loudoun County and throughout Virginia in November saw candidates who rejected data centers emerging victorious. Even residents in the fresh water–rich Great Lakes states have raised questions about increased data center usage. Illinois also has one of the highest concentrations of data centers in the country, and local officials and environmentalists have raised alarms that siting decisions don’t always take into consideration how local drinking water needs can clash with data center cooling demands. Georgia, Alabama, and Florida have actually had “ water wars .” In April, a federal judge ruled against Alabama in a dispute with Georgia over Army Corps of Engineers water allocations to metro Atlanta from Lake Allatoona, a northwest Georgia reservoir. Data center projects could complicate those interstate dynamics. NPR affiliate WABE reported that Chattahoochee Riverkeeper, which monitors the river running from North Georgia through Atlanta to Florida, tracks water usage plans for new data centers in the region. One facility , Coweta County’s Project Sail, would use nearly ten million gallons daily, which adds up to one-third of the county’s daily usage from the river. DATA CENTER DEVELOPERS have been exceptionally skilled at persuading local leaders of their value to communities by touting gains like temporary construction jobs. (There are few on-site permanent jobs.) Unlike what’s transpired in Northern Virginia, where county officials hand out tax credits but still haul in millions in tax revenues, some recent data center projects are steering away from generous agreements with local communities. Instead, project officials focus on tax credits, obscure the details, force officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), and never divulge their supernova clients to the public. Most residents are hard-pressed to fight corporate secrecy. The New York Times recently spotlighted Doña Ana County, New Mexico, a predominantly Latino community of 15,000. The data center developer for Project Jupiter, a multibillion-dollar component of the $500 billion SoftBank- and OpenAI-led Stargate Project, got to know the locals, but the underlying clients remained unknown because county officials had signed NDAs. Residents only found out after the project moved forward that the heavy hitters included OpenAI and Oracle. Instead of property tax revenues, the county will see a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) program, which essentially allow companies to decide how much—or how little—money they’re willing to offer a community. But this trick isn’t having much staying power. Data Center Watch, coordinated by 10a Labs, an applied research and technology company specializing in AI security, reports that in the second quarter of 2025, data center opponents slowed the roll or thwarted projects totaling about $100 billion—more than the total of every quarter since 2023. In one three-month period, 20 projects fell through. That includes a project in Chandler, a Phoenix suburb, where Arizona’s former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema personally lobbied at local meetings for a 422,000-square-foot data center plan operated by Active Infrastructure, a hyperscale data center developer. In the end, the Chandler City Council voted against the data center unanimously . In rural Leesburg, Indiana, the town council refused to rezone land for industrial use to build a data center on 554 acres. “I’m really just trying to speak out for the future of agriculture, and passing a data center is not the future of agriculture,” said one local resident. The possibility that a facility might be rejected has affected data center financing. In Michigan, Blue Owl Capital, a private credit firm, pulled out of a $10 billion data center deal with Oracle amid “shifting market sentiment around enormous AI spending” and concerns that “the Saline Township site … might face delays.” Elsewhere in Michigan, data center opponents rallied in Lansing last week and called for “ no secret deals ” between local governments, utilities, and data center developers. At the gathering, Attorney General Dana Nessel demanded that the state’s public utility commission step back from fast-tracking a major utility project to power the Saline Township project. Anthony Hudson, a Republican gubernatorial candidate who attended the protest, mostly agreed with Nessel. A pair of state lawmakers, one a Democrat and the other a Republican, have teamed up to propose reversing tax breaks for large data center facilities. But residents want a statewide moratorium. SINCE 2019, AT LEAST 40 STATES —both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms. Unfortunately, federal regulation has lagged miles behind the internet revolution. The Senate did manage to stave off , by a vote of 99-to-1, a White House–endorsed attempt to prohibit states from passing AI regulations for ten years. The prohibition on state AI regulation came up again in the annual defense policy bill and was again beaten back. But even though that proposal generated outrage, the major overstep into state regulatory authority hasn’t motivated Republicans to fill in the blanks. President Trump has seized on that inertia to issue more than half a dozen AI executive orders this year, the latest coming in mid-December complete with plans for a litigation task force and an annual evaluation of state laws determined to obliterate any opposition to AI usage or data center expansion. The Brennan Center has labeled that move “little more than political theater.” Executive orders do not invest the federal government with the powers to file lawsuits. So federal officials cannot “directly enforce” the order through court action. “To challenge a state AI regulation in court,” writes Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security in the center’s elections and government program, “the department would need to base the lawsuit on a federal statute or constitutional provision—not simply on the executive order itself.” Combine data center moratorium drama with the gutting of the Affordable Care Act, the nothing-to-see-here response to the affordability crisis, and extortionate trade tactics, and the White House and congressional Republicans have set themselves and everyone else up for a very dismal New Year. But despite their best efforts, local initiatives to stop the plowing over of homes and farms and businesses with giant warehouses of servers and chips will continue—and they’re starting to have an impact on the AI transition. The reason we can write these stories—stories that are orienting and informing rather than fear-inducing—is because of you. We removed programmatic ads from our site in April , which means that we don’t chase clicks for ad dollars. We don’t have a paywall, which means that everyone, regardless of their ability to pay, can access our work for free. We don’t have content partnerships with AI giants . We’re in our fall fundraising drive, and we need to raise $100,000 to hit our budget. We’re a nonprofit newsroom whose ability to write and report these stories depends on our readers.
