passages: The major artificial intelligence companies’ prime directive to literally bulldoze AI infrastructure into states with minimal regulation has produced citizen-led, bipartisan demands for local and national moratoriums on data center siting. While the Trump administration is doing everything it can to facilitate the only capital spending with a pulse in the economy, these calls for moratoriums are growing, and connecting with local successes in blocking data center construction.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) recently called for a national moratorium on the construction of data centers that are “powering this unregulated sprint to develop and deploy AI.” Sanders did credit “the transformative power of AI and robotics” before calling out Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Peter Thiel, and Bill Gates with a simple question: “Are these multibillionaires staying up nights worrying about what AI and robotics will do to the working families of our country and the world?” The answer would be mostly no.

Over 230 organizations across the 50 states signed on to a letter to members of Congress organized by Food & Water Watch, a national advocacy group, also calling for a national moratorium on data center siting and construction. The letter characterized generative AI and crypto as generational threats.

But it’s the local rejections of data centers—in places as varied as Chandler, Arizona , and Leesburg, Indiana —that should have the tech oligarchs worried. These results demonstrate that Americans are beginning to grasp the downsides of inserting AI into every facet of daily life. This mushrooming grassroots backlash promises to dominate American politics in 2026.

The fallout from siting these gargantuan facilities near human habitats continues to convulse communities. Residential ratepayers are already grappling with electricity price spikes and see data centers as a major driver of the pain. Power demand from data centers will hit 106 gigawatts by 2035 , according to an analysis from BloombergNEF. A Yale Clean Energy Forum report estimates that data centers could take up as much as 12 percent of total U.S. power consumption by 2028, a higher demand than all manufacturing of steel, aluminum, and other high-intensity manufactured goods combined. “Electricity is the new price of eggs,” one industry analyst told The New York Times , and if you’re concerned about electricity, you have to be concerned about data centers.
Since 2019, at least 40 states—both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms.

Data centers are also guzzling city-sized amounts of water. By 2028, they’ll require up to 720 billion gallons of water every year to keep servers cool—usage would fill one million Olympic-size swimming pools or furnish water for the interior-home uses of 18.5 million American households.

In Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the largest concentration of data centers in the region that represents the world’s largest data hub, data center expansions have collided with the climate crisis, leading to scrambles from local government to address the “ negative impacts on neighborhoods .” While the county wants to find environmental solutions that would reduce the burden on residents while still building the data centers, local elections in Loudoun County and throughout Virginia in November saw candidates who rejected data centers emerging victorious.

Even residents in the fresh water–rich Great Lakes states have raised questions about increased data center usage. Illinois also has one of the highest concentrations of data centers in the country, and local officials and environmentalists have raised alarms that siting decisions don’t always take into consideration how local drinking water needs can clash with data center cooling demands.

Georgia, Alabama, and Florida have actually had “ water wars .” In April, a federal judge ruled against Alabama in a dispute with Georgia over Army Corps of Engineers water allocations to metro Atlanta from Lake Allatoona, a northwest Georgia reservoir. Data center projects could complicate those interstate dynamics. NPR affiliate WABE reported that Chattahoochee Riverkeeper, which monitors the river running from North Georgia through Atlanta to Florida, tracks water usage plans for new data centers in the region. One facility , Coweta County’s Project Sail, would use nearly ten million gallons daily, which adds up to one-third of the county’s daily usage from the river.

DATA CENTER DEVELOPERS have been exceptionally skilled at persuading local leaders of their value to communities by touting gains like temporary construction jobs. (There are few on-site permanent jobs.) Unlike what’s transpired in Northern Virginia, where county officials hand out tax credits but still haul in millions in tax revenues, some recent data center projects are steering away from generous agreements with local communities. Instead, project officials focus on tax credits, obscure the details, force officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), and never divulge their supernova clients to the public.

Most residents are hard-pressed to fight corporate secrecy. The New York Times recently spotlighted Doña Ana County, New Mexico, a predominantly Latino community of 15,000. The data center developer for Project Jupiter, a multibillion-dollar component of the $500 billion SoftBank- and OpenAI-led Stargate Project, got to know the locals, but the underlying clients remained unknown because county officials had signed NDAs. Residents only found out after the project moved forward that the heavy hitters included OpenAI and Oracle.

Instead of property tax revenues, the county will see a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) program, which essentially allow companies to decide how much—or how little—money they’re willing to offer a community. But this trick isn’t having much staying power. Data Center Watch, coordinated by 10a Labs, an applied research and technology company specializing in AI security, reports that in the second quarter of 2025, data center opponents slowed the roll or thwarted projects totaling about $100 billion—more than the total of every quarter since 2023. In one three-month period, 20 projects fell through.

That includes a project in Chandler, a Phoenix suburb, where Arizona’s former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema personally lobbied at local meetings for a 422,000-square-foot data center plan operated by Active Infrastructure, a hyperscale data center developer. In the end, the Chandler City Council voted against the data center unanimously . In rural Leesburg, Indiana, the town council refused to rezone land for industrial use to build a data center on 554 acres. “I’m really just trying to speak out for the future of agriculture, and passing a data center is not the future of agriculture,” said one local resident.

The possibility that a facility might be rejected has affected data center financing. In Michigan, Blue Owl Capital, a private credit firm, pulled out of a $10 billion data center deal with Oracle amid “shifting market sentiment around enormous AI spending” and concerns that “the Saline Township site … might face delays.”

Elsewhere in Michigan, data center opponents rallied in Lansing last week and called for “ no secret deals ” between local governments, utilities, and data center developers. At the gathering, Attorney General Dana Nessel demanded that the state’s public utility commission step back from fast-tracking a major utility project to power the Saline Township project. Anthony Hudson, a Republican gubernatorial candidate who attended the protest, mostly agreed with Nessel. A pair of state lawmakers, one a Democrat and the other a Republican, have teamed up to propose reversing tax breaks for large data center facilities. But residents want a statewide moratorium.
SINCE 2019, AT LEAST 40 STATES —both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms.

Unfortunately, federal regulation has lagged miles behind the internet revolution. The Senate did manage to stave off , by a vote of 99-to-1, a White House–endorsed attempt to prohibit states from passing AI regulations for ten years. The prohibition on state AI regulation came up again in the annual defense policy bill and was again beaten back. But even though that proposal generated outrage, the major overstep into state regulatory authority hasn’t motivated Republicans to fill in the blanks.

President Trump has seized on that inertia to issue more than half a dozen AI executive orders this year, the latest coming in mid-December complete with plans for a litigation task force and an annual evaluation of state laws determined to obliterate any opposition to AI usage or data center expansion.

The Brennan Center has labeled that move “little more than political theater.” Executive orders do not invest the federal government with the powers to file lawsuits. So federal officials cannot “directly enforce” the order through court action. “To challenge a state AI regulation in court,” writes Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security in the center’s elections and government program, “the department would need to base the lawsuit on a federal statute or constitutional provision—not simply on the executive order itself.”

Combine data center moratorium drama with the gutting of the Affordable Care Act, the nothing-to-see-here response to the affordability crisis, and extortionate trade tactics, and the White House and congressional Republicans have set themselves and everyone else up for a very dismal New Year. But despite their best efforts, local initiatives to stop the plowing over of homes and farms and businesses with giant warehouses of servers and chips will continue—and they’re starting to have an impact on the AI transition.

extraction.body: Apple's "Welcome Home" product launch is happening tomorrow. As the name suggests, Apple is going to debut new home accessories, including the long-rumored home hub. Below, we've listed all the rumors we know about the three devices Apple is set to introduce. Apple's home hub, which will be called HomeView , is a multi-function device designed for all of a home's occupants. It's built around Siri AI, and will have an A18 chip and 8GB of RAM. Here's what rumors suggest it'll be able to do: The hub will be able to do anything you might want a home assistant device to do, from giving the next steps of a recipe to suggesting dinner ideas and creating a shopping list. It will rely heavily on ‌Siri‌ AI for voice-based input, but it will also have a 6-inch touch display. The display is square with bezels around the edges, and there are two models. One version can be mounted on the wall, and the other is attached to a half-dome speaker base with a flexible arm for adjusting tilt. The hub isn't expected to have its own App Store , but it will support Apple apps such as Safari, News, Music, Reminders, Calendar, Weather, Messages, FaceTime , Photos , and Mail. There will be a presence sensor and a camera in the hub, and it will use a variation of Face ID to determine who is nearby to show customized content. It will display information from a linked iPhone, like email messages, but only after authenticating. The sensors in the hub will be usable in HomeKit scenes and automations, so you can use it to trigger lights and other devices when a person walks into the room. The interface will be heavily widget-based so you can see information at a glance, and it's likely going to look similar to StandBy mode on the iPhone. You will be able to choose your preferred clock face or idle state, along with a home screen of widget options that you can tap to open a full app. If you have multiple hubs, they'll link together for features like multi-room music and intercom functionality. Rumors suggest that it will have better sound quality than the HomePod mini . There isn't going to be a built-in battery, and the hub will need to be connected to power via an included USB-C port. The speaker-equipped version is expected in multiple colors, including gray, silver, starlight, and rose. The wall-mounted version will be available in silver and gray. extraction.body: Apple has announced a special product launch for 13 October 2026 . Unlike its typical keynote events, this seems likely to be a coordinated drop of a video and press releases rather than a live presentation. I guess I know what I’ll be doing next Tuesday—hopefully along with getting the cast off my right hand. The announcement came from Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of Worldwide Marketing, featuring an embroidered rainbow Apple logo and the tagline “Welcome home.” YouTuber Marques Brownlee and presumably other influencers have been invited to an “Apple Experience” at Apple’s Tribeca building in New York at 9 AM Eastern. Jason Snell suggests that some members of the traditional press will get remote briefings. The star of the show is expected to be Apple’s long-anticipated touchscreen home hub, which the rumor mill initially dubbed “HomePad,” but which is now expected to be called “HomeView.” We’ll soon see what the final name is and whether the company comes up with a better name for the operating system powering it than “ HomePod Software ”—homeOS, perhaps? Apple is also expected to announce updated versions of the Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini, both with more capable processors that will support Siri AI. Mark Gurman of Bloomberg also suggests that Apple may introduce a suite of LG-made smart home accessories including a doorbell, smart lock, and thermostat. That feels weird to me, but Apple has done small things like this before , and it could indicate that new CEO John Ternus is changing how Apple does things. Every week you’ll get tech tips, in-depth reviews, and insightful news analysis for discerning Apple users. For over 36 years, we’ve published professional, member-supported tech journalism that makes you smarter. Registration confirmation will be emailed to you. extraction.body: Apple's "Welcome Home" product launch is happening tomorrow. As the name suggests, Apple is going to debut new home accessories, including the long-rumored home hub. Below, we've listed all the rumors we know about the three devices Apple is set to introduce. Apple's home hub, which will be called HomeView , is a multi-function device designed for all of a home's occupants. It's built around Siri AI, and will have an A18 chip and 8GB of RAM. Here's what rumors suggest it'll be able to do: The hub will be able to do anything you might want a home assistant device to do, from giving the next steps of a recipe to suggesting dinner ideas and creating a shopping list. It will rely heavily on ‌Siri‌ AI for voice-based input, but it will also have a 6-inch touch display. The display is square with bezels around the edges, and there are two models. One version can be mounted on the wall, and the other is attached to a half-dome speaker base with a flexible arm for adjusting tilt. The hub isn't expected to have its own App Store , but it will support Apple apps such as Safari, News, Music, Reminders, Calendar, Weather, Messages, FaceTime , Photos , and Mail. There will be a presence sensor and a camera in the hub, and it will use a variation of Face ID to determine who is nearby to show customized content. It will display information from a linked iPhone, like email messages, but only after authenticating. The sensors in the hub will be usable in HomeKit scenes and automations, so you can use it to trigger lights and other devices when a person walks into the room. The interface will be heavily widget-based so you can see information at a glance, and it's likely going to look similar to StandBy mode on the iPhone. You will be able to choose your preferred clock face or idle state, along with a home screen of widget options that you can tap to open a full app. If you have multiple hubs, they'll link together for features like multi-room music and intercom functionality. Rumors suggest that it will have better sound quality than the HomePod mini . There isn't going to be a built-in battery, and the hub will need to be connected to power via an included USB-C port. The speaker-equipped version is expected in multiple colors, including gray, silver, starlight, and rose. The wall-mounted version will be available in silver and gray. Rumors suggest the hub could be priced somewhere around $350. Apple isn't updating the design of the Apple TV , so expect the new model to be the same boring black box. What's changing is entirely inside. The ‌Apple TV‌ 4K is going to get a lot more powerful so it can support ‌Siri‌ AI, offering many of the same ‌Siri‌ features that are available on iPhone and iPad in iOS and iPadOS 27 . We're expecting an A19 with 8GB of RAM, along with Apple's N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. The A19 will bring a major upgrade in performance, both for ‌Siri‌ and for gaming. It has ray tracing, mesh shading, and other features that will improve gameplay graphics. There will be a new ‌Siri‌ Remote with an included speaker to make it easier to find, and we've seen some signs that Apple is working on its own gaming controller under the Beats brand , but there's no word on whether it's ready to launch. Apple will likely emphasize ‌Siri‌ AI and gaming capabilities when introducing the ‌Apple TV‌. Apple raised the price of the current ‌Apple TV‌ to $199 in June, and the new model will be at least that expensive with the processor and RAM upgrades. Like the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K, the ‌HomePod mini‌ isn't going to get a new design, but it will have internal upgrades that make it more capable. It's going to get an upgraded S10 chip, second-generation UWB for features like Handoff, and the N1 networking chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. You'll need a nearby AI-capable device for ‌Siri‌ AI processing because the HomePod probably won't be able to handle much on-device, but smarter ‌Siri‌ should make for a better experience. ‌Siri‌ AI on ‌HomePod mini‌ will have the context of ‌Siri‌ interactions on other devices, and it's likely conversations will be saved to a connected iPhone's ‌Siri‌ app. ‌Siri‌ AI can answer follow-up questions, handle multi-request queries, and access information from your apps. It'll be similar to having ChatGPT or Claude on a speaker. Though design updates aren't expected, the ‌HomePod mini‌ will get new colors. We're expecting white, blue, black, sage, and pink. ‌HomePod mini‌ pricing went up from $99 to $129 in June 2026, and the new model will likely be priced at $129 too. Apple worked with LG to make an LG-branded wired video doorbell, thermostat, smart deadbolt lock, temperature sensor, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera, and floodlight camera that will work with the home hub and the ‌HomeKit‌ platform. The accessories are part of an "Apple Home Collection" that will be marketed alongside the HomeView. They won't be ready until later this year at the earliest, but Apple could show them off during the announcement. There's no keynote event for the "Welcome Home" product debut, so Apple is probably going to release a video and an accompanying set of press releases. There's an NYC media event that's going to take place at 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday, October 13, and that could be when all of the announcements happen. The NYC event will let members of the media get some hands-on time with the new devices to share first impressions. Apple could begin accepting pre-orders just after the new devices launch. The ‌HomePod mini‌ and the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K are going to launch on Friday, October 30. The HomeView won't be available right away and is expected to ship to customers in mid-November . passages: Al Jazeera reported on the company team's findings.
Anthropic's report states that current models have not yet demonstrated the ability to reliably self-replicate on the smart TV used in testing.
At the same time, the researchers consider it likely that a model combining sufficient compactness and power for this will emerge by the end of 2026.
Data centers may be obvious valuable targets for AI worms, but internet-connected household devices could also potentially have sufficient computing resources for self-replication.

Researchers at Anthropic said that small artificial intelligence models could within several months become powerful enough to copy themselves independently across internet-of-things devices in homes and small businesses.
This includes smart TVs, refrigerators, ovens and lawn mowers, which would not require a data center for such proliferation.
Separately, Anthropic reported progress in countering distillation attacks — the unauthorized use of advanced models to train cheaper and less capable systems.
The company said that the measures it introduced reduced illegal data extraction by 90–99%.

passages: Anthropic, the creator of the Claude family of AI models, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions, sent outside regular business hours, about the finding’s safety implications.

“Computer worms are not new, but an AI worm could do something traditional malware cannot: reason about unfamiliar devices, adapt when its approach fails, and continue spreading without a human operator,” Yampolskiy told Al Jazeera.

Anthropic’s frontier red team, which ran experiments using multiple US- and Chinese-developed AI models, said such self-replicating AI would be “challenging to shut down” due to the lack of a centralised host.

Small artificial intelligence models could soon begin self-replicating on everyday consumer products such as smart TVs and fridges, without needing a data centre, according to researchers at AI giant Anthropic.

Although no current AI model proved to be both powerful and small enough to self-replicate reliably on a smart TV used in testing, the trend in development makes the emergence of such a model likely by the end of 2026, the researchers said.

Anthropic and other leading US tech firms last month joined a non-binding accord pledging stronger internal safeguards and engagement with external auditors, drawing a mixed response from experts, many of whom criticised the voluntary nature of the pact.

“Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place,” researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman said.
Anthropic’s report comes as the risks of AI escaping human control are under scrutiny following a slew of incidents of models engaging in unsanctioned malign behaviour, including cyberattacks.

In a separate announcement on Monday, Anthropic said it had made substantial progress preventing so-called distillation attacks, which involve the unsanctioned use of cutting-edge AI to train cheaper, less capable models.

Anthropic and its chief rival OpenAI have called on the international community to coordinate a slowdown in AI development to minimise catastrophic risks, a suggestion that has had little buy-in from the United States and China, the two leading AI powers.
Roman V Yampolskiy, an AI and cybersecurity expert at the University of Louisville, described Anthropic’s findings as a significant development.

extraction.body: US tech giant says small AI models may soon be capable of self-replication without access to a data centre. Small artificial intelligence models could soon begin self-replicating on everyday consumer products such as smart TVs and fridges, without needing a data centre, according to researchers at AI giant Anthropic. In a report released on Monday, the researchers said small AI models “may be months away from being capable enough” to copy themselves on internet of things (IoT) devices used in homes and small businesses. Anthropic’s frontier red team, which ran experiments using multiple US- and Chinese-developed AI models, said such self-replicating AI would be “challenging to shut down” due to the lack of a centralised host. While data centres would be “a clear, high-value target” for AI worms, internet-connected devices like smart TVs, fridges, ovens and lawnmowers could soon also provide sufficient computing power for self-replication, the research team said. Although no current AI model proved to be both powerful and small enough to self-replicate reliably on a smart TV used in testing, the trend in development makes the emergence of such a model likely by the end of 2026, the researchers said. “Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place,” researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman said. The researchers said they anticipated the future would be “awash with agents running on all types of hardware”, including some that “aren’t under human control”. “While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute,” they said. Anthropic, the creator of the Claude family of AI models, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions, sent outside regular business hours, about the finding’s safety implications. Anthropic’s report comes as the risks of AI escaping human control are under scrutiny following a slew of incidents of models engaging in unsanctioned malign behaviour, including cyberattacks. Anthropic and its chief rival OpenAI have called on the international community to coordinate a slowdown in AI development to minimise catastrophic risks, a suggestion that has had little buy-in from the United States and China, the two leading AI powers. Many AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement, where models learn to improve themselves, as a critical tipping point that could lead to catastrophic harm for humanity. Roman V Yampolskiy, an AI and cybersecurity expert at the University of Louisville, described Anthropic’s findings as a significant development. “Computer worms are not new, but an AI worm could do something traditional malware cannot: reason about unfamiliar devices, adapt when its approach fails, and continue spreading without a human operator,” Yampolskiy told Al Jazeera. “Today, this is not an existential threat. But the trajectory is concerning,” Yampolskiy said. “Once autonomous replication is combined with strong hacking, persistence, and strategic reasoning, shutting such a system down becomes much harder because there may be no single server or organisation controlling it.” Anthropic and other leading US tech firms last month joined a non-binding accord pledging stronger internal safeguards and engagement with external auditors, drawing a mixed response from experts, many of whom criticised the voluntary nature of the pact. In a separate announcement on Monday, Anthropic said it had made substantial progress preventing so-called distillation attacks, which involve the unsanctioned use of cutting-edge AI to train cheaper, less capable models. The San Francisco-based firm, which has accused Chinese competitors DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax of “industrial-scale” efforts to copy Claude, said the measures it introduced had reduced the illicit extraction of data by 90-99 percent.

The researchers said they anticipated the future would be “awash with agents running on all types of hardware”, including some that “aren’t under human control”. “While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute,” they said. Anthropic, the creator of the Claude family of AI models, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions, sent outside regular business hours, about the finding’s safety implications. Many AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement, where models learn to improve themselves, as a critical tipping point that could lead to catastrophic harm for humanity. In a separate announcement on Monday, Anthropic said it had made substantial progress preventing so-called distillation attacks, which involve the unsanctioned use of cutting-edge AI to train cheaper, less capable models. sources.title: Binance weighs adding Hong Kong, Korean, Taiwanese and Brazilian stocks, says co-CEO Teng - Crypto Briefing
passages: Binance built its empire on Bitcoin and altcoins.

Now it wants a piece of Samsung-and-chipmaker territory too. \n The exchange is considering giving users exposure to stocks from Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and Brazil, co-CEO Richard Teng told Fortune at TOKEN2049 in Singapore.

The idea is part of a broader push to turn the world’s largest crypto exchange into a platform where users can trade nearly everything. 
 

 Teng framed the move as defensive as much as ambitious.
Teng succeeded Changpeng Zhao in 2023 and became co-CEO in December 2025.
His background in regulatory environments is often cited as an asset for Binance as it moves into products that sit closer to traditional finance.
He described the strategy as a way to make Binance less dependent on any single market’s mood, and he pointed squarely at customer requests.
That same month, Binance launched bStocks, a product offering tokenized equities and ETFs on BNB Chain.
Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based tokens designed to track the price of a traditional share.
Think of them as a digital mirror of a stock that lives on a crypto network instead of a brokerage ledger.
For perspective on scale, Binance processed $34 trillion in trading volume for 300 million users in the previous year.
Against that backdrop, a $3 billion global tokenized stock market looks small.
For now, Binance’s equity ambitions are centered on US stocks.
In June 2026, the exchange rolled out direct trading for more than 7,000 US stocks and ETFs, aimed at users outside the US.

extraction.body: Binance is considering offering exposure to stocks from markets including Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and Brazil as the world’s largest crypto exchange pushes beyond digital assets and seeks to become an all-in-one trading platform , co-CEO Richard Teng told Fortune . “We are weatherproofing ourselves,” Teng said on the sidelines of TOKEN2049 in Singapore. “A lot of our users say: ‘Hey, I want to have exposure to, let’s say, the top 10 Hong Kong stocks, top 10 Korean counters, top 10 Taiwanese, Brazilian counters.’ We’re looking at what our users demand and giving them that.” In 2026, Binance introduced trading in tokenized U.S. stocks and commodity derivatives, including precious metals and oil. The exchange also rolled out pre-IPO perpetual futures contracts settled in USDT, a U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoin, giving traders the ability to speculate on the expected valuation of private companies like Anthropic. Sitting behind this shift is a slump in digital asset prices . Bitcoin and other cryptocurrency prices remain far below the highs reached in October 2025. Coinbase, for example, posted a net loss of $359.5 million in Q2 2026, its third consecutive quarterly net loss, as transaction revenue declined. Several cryptocurrency exchanges, including Binance, are transforming themselves from apps devoted to coins like Bitcoin and Ethereum into platforms that can handle different asset classes . Coinbase rolled out traditional stock trading, perpetual futures, and prediction markets on its platform last December as part of its push to become an “everything exchange.” OKX last week revealed plans to both offer tokenized shares in dozens of U.S. companies (through a joint venture with Intercontinental Exchange), as well as launch a new app for U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoins . Traditional financial companies are embracing digital assets, while crypto platforms must accept clearer rules to attract institutional money . “The first 3% of [crypto] adopters didn’t need certainty, and they didn’t want certainty,” Teng said. “But for crypto to go mainstream, we need not just retail investors, but also sophisticated institutions that want clear rules and regulations they can operate within.” Teng casts tokenized stocks and round-the-clock trading as ways to give investors outside major financial centers greater access to global markets . “Many people are still constrained by the geography that they are born in,” Teng said, pointing to how those born in emerging markets in Africa or Latin America may still lack access to U.S. stocks, despite the U.S. being the world’s largest capital market. “If we tokenize U.S. stocks, these people can get exposure to companies around the world they may not have had access to previously.” Today, though many more individuals are banked, roughly 1.3 billion adults globally still lack access to a formal bank account, according to a 2025 World Bank report. Binance, therefore, acts as a so-called shadow bank for savings, yield generation, and cross-border payments, while allowing access to global stocks with low entry thresholds. Later this month, Binance will roll out Binance AI Pro, an AI-powered crypto trading assistant that automates market analysis, strategy execution, and position management. Teng expects more trading to shift to AI agents as investors grow more comfortable setting the parameters that guide them. “It has been a great leveler,” he said. “But the nature of trading will be different.” Binance tapped Teng to serve as its CEO in November 2023, after founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao came under regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. after failing to register as a money-transmitting business and breaching sanctions laws. Following the criminal plea, Binance paid $4.3 billion in penalties and forfeitures, while Zhao personally paid a $50 million fine and served a four-month prison sentence . (He was later pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump) Teng started his career on the traditional side of the finance sector , with roles at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the country’s central bank, and the Singapore Exchange. He credits his time at both those institutions for his perspectives on risk and growth. “If you look at many different regulatory agencies around the world, the key focus is just to mitigate risk, but if you do that to the extreme, that means very minimal or no growth,” Teng explains. At MAS, Teng said he had the dual task of both regulating and growing the financial services sector. “It’s not only about looking at the risk dimension of the ecosystem, but also how you mitigate and manage it in order to support growth,” he adds. Teng was first exposed to the world of blockchain and cryptocurrencies in 2017 during a visit to the U.S. when he was serving as CEO of the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of the Abu Dhabi Global Market, an international finance center in the United Arab Emirates. Teng grew to believe that cryptocurrencies could broaden financial access in emerging markets. “I was blessed to be born and bred in Singapore, where we had access to multiple banks and investment platforms, but many people around the world were not as fortunate.” Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

extraction.body: Binance is considering offering exposure to stocks from markets including Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and Brazil as the world’s largest crypto exchange pushes beyond digital assets and seeks to become an all-in-one trading platform , co-CEO Richard Teng told Fortune . “We are weatherproofing ourselves,” Teng said on the sidelines of TOKEN2049 in Singapore. “A lot of our users say: ‘Hey, I want to have exposure to, let’s say, the top 10 Hong Kong stocks, top 10 Korean counters, top 10 Taiwanese, Brazilian counters.’ We’re looking at what our users demand and giving them that.” In 2026, Binance introduced trading in tokenized U.S. stocks and commodity derivatives, including precious metals and oil. The exchange also rolled out pre-IPO perpetual futures contracts settled in USDT, a U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoin, giving traders the ability to speculate on the expected valuation of private companies like Anthropic. Sitting behind this shift is a slump in digital asset prices . Bitcoin and other cryptocurrency prices remain far below the highs reached in October 2025. Coinbase, for example, posted a net loss of $359.5 million in Q2 2026, its third consecutive quarterly net loss, as transaction revenue declined. Several cryptocurrency exchanges, including Binance, are transforming themselves from apps devoted to coins like Bitcoin and Ethereum into platforms that can handle different asset classes . Coinbase rolled out traditional stock trading, perpetual futures, and prediction markets on its platform last December as part of its push to become an “everything exchange.” OKX last week revealed plans to both offer tokenized shares in dozens of U.S. companies (through a joint venture with Intercontinental Exchange), as well as launch a new app for U.S.-dollar-linked stablecoins . Traditional financial companies are embracing digital assets, while crypto platforms must accept clearer rules to attract institutional money . “The first 3% of [crypto] adopters didn’t need certainty, and they didn’t want certainty,” Teng said. “But for crypto to go mainstream, we need not just retail investors, but also sophisticated institutions that want clear rules and regulations they can operate within.” Teng casts tokenized stocks and round-the-clock trading as ways to give investors outside major financial centers greater access to global markets . “Many people are still constrained by the geography that they are born in,” Teng said, pointing to how those born in emerging markets in Africa or Latin America may still lack access to U.S. stocks, despite the U.S. being the world’s largest capital market. “If we tokenize U.S. stocks, these people can get exposure to companies around the world they may not have had access to previously.” Today, though many more individuals are banked, roughly 1.3 billion adults globally still lack access to a formal bank account, according to a 2025 World Bank report. Binance, therefore, acts as a so-called shadow bank for savings, yield generation, and cross-border payments, while allowing access to global stocks with low entry thresholds. Later this month, Binance will roll out Binance AI Pro, an AI-powered crypto trading assistant that automates market analysis, strategy execution, and position management. Teng expects more trading to shift to AI agents as investors grow more comfortable setting the parameters that guide them. “It has been a great leveler,” he said. “But the nature of trading will be different.” Binance tapped Teng to serve as its CEO in November 2023, after founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao came under regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. after failing to register as a money-transmitting business and breaching sanctions laws. Following the criminal plea, Binance paid $4.3 billion in penalties and forfeitures, while Zhao personally paid a $50 million fine and served a four-month prison sentence . (He was later pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump) Teng started his career on the traditional side of the finance sector , with roles at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the country’s central bank, and the Singapore Exchange. He credits his time at both those institutions for his perspectives on risk and growth. “If you look at many different regulatory agencies around the world, the key focus is just to mitigate risk, but if you do that to the extreme, that means very minimal or no growth,” Teng explains. At MAS, Teng said he had the dual task of both regulating and growing the financial services sector. “It’s not only about looking at the risk dimension of the ecosystem, but also how you mitigate and manage it in order to support growth,” he adds. Teng was first exposed to the world of blockchain and cryptocurrencies in 2017 during a visit to the U.S. when he was serving as CEO of the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of the Abu Dhabi Global Market, an international finance center in the United Arab Emirates. Teng grew to believe that cryptocurrencies could broaden financial access in emerging markets. “I was blessed to be born and bred in Singapore, where we had access to multiple banks and investment platforms, but many people around the world were not as fortunate.” Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

Traditional financial companies are embracing digital assets, while crypto platforms must accept clearer rules to attract institutional money . “The first 3% of [crypto] adopters didn’t need certainty, and they didn’t want certainty,” Teng said. “But for crypto to go mainstream, we need not just retail investors, but also sophisticated institutions that want clear rules and regulations they can operate within.”
Teng casts tokenized stocks and round-the-clock trading as ways to give investors outside major financial centers greater access to global markets .

“Many people are still constrained by the geography that they are born in,” Teng said, pointing to how those born in emerging markets in Africa or Latin America may still lack access to U.S. stocks, despite the U.S. being the world’s largest capital market. “If we tokenize U.S. stocks, these people can get exposure to companies around the world they may not have had access to previously.”

Today, though many more individuals are banked, roughly 1.3 billion adults globally still lack access to a formal bank account, according to a 2025 World Bank report. Binance, therefore, acts as a so-called shadow bank for savings, yield generation, and cross-border payments, while allowing access to global stocks with low entry thresholds.
Later this month, Binance will roll out Binance AI Pro, an AI-powered crypto trading assistant that automates market analysis, strategy execution, and position management.

Teng expects more trading to shift to AI agents as investors grow more comfortable setting the parameters that guide them. “It has been a great leveler,” he said. “But the nature of trading will be different.”

Binance tapped Teng to serve as its CEO in November 2023, after founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao came under regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. after failing to register as a money-transmitting business and breaching sanctions laws. Following the criminal plea, Binance paid $4.3 billion in penalties and forfeitures, while Zhao personally paid a $50 million fine and served a four-month prison sentence . (He was later pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump)

Teng started his career on the traditional side of the finance sector , with roles at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the country’s central bank, and the Singapore Exchange. He credits his time at both those institutions for his perspectives on risk and growth.

“If you look at many different regulatory agencies around the world, the key focus is just to mitigate risk, but if you do that to the extreme, that means very minimal or no growth,” Teng explains. At MAS, Teng said he had the dual task of both regulating and growing the financial services sector. “It’s not only about looking at the risk dimension of the ecosystem, but also how you mitigate and manage it in order to support growth,” he adds.

Teng was first exposed to the world of blockchain and cryptocurrencies in 2017 during a visit to the U.S. when he was serving as CEO of the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of the Abu Dhabi Global Market, an international finance center in the United Arab Emirates.

Teng grew to believe that cryptocurrencies could broaden financial access in emerging markets. “I was blessed to be born and bred in Singapore, where we had access to multiple banks and investment platforms, but many people around the world were not as fortunate.”
Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

facts.text: Binance built its empire on Bitcoin and altcoins.

Now it wants a piece of Samsung-and-chipmaker territory too. \n The exchange is considering giving users exposure to stocks from Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and Brazil, co-CEO Richard Teng told Fortune at TOKEN2049 in Singapore.

The idea is part of a broader push to turn the world’s largest crypto exchange into a platform where users can trade nearly everything. 
 

 Teng framed the move as defensive as much as ambitious.
Teng succeeded Changpeng Zhao in 2023 and became co-CEO in December 2025.
His background in regulatory environments is often cited as an asset for Binance as it moves into products that sit closer to traditional finance.
He described the strategy as a way to make Binance less dependent on any single market’s mood, and he pointed squarely at customer requests.
That same month, Binance launched bStocks, a product offering tokenized equities and ETFs on BNB Chain.

Against that backdrop, a $3 billion global tokenized stock market looks small.
For now, Binance’s equity ambitions are centered on US stocks.
In June 2026, the exchange rolled out direct trading for more than 7,000 US stocks and ETFs, aimed at users outside the US.

sources.title: Blast Shuts Down the Ethereum Layer 2 Network That Once Held $2.3 Billion - Startup Fortune
passages: Blast, the Ethereum layer 2 that once held $2.3 billion and became the face of 2024's airdrop-farming boom, is shutting down because it can no longer pay its own bills.

Research from Yellow and BlockEden.xyz on the 2026 Ethereum L2 sector found that the top three networks by TVL - Base, Arbitrum, and Optimism - now control roughly 80% of all sequencer fee revenue across tracked chains, based on Dune Analytics data.

Starknet's zkLend and the L2 project Kinto both shut down in 2025 after their own exploits and funding problems, and The Block's 2026 Layer-2 Outlook flagged most mid-tier rollups as unlikely to survive the next twelve months.
The team behind Blast announced the wind-down on October 2, telling users the chain now costs more to run than it earns and that there's no credible path back to profitability.
According to Unchained, Blast's chain revenue over the prior 24 hours came to $110.
That's the number that ended it: a network built to process billions in deposits, reduced to earning less than a night's take at a corner store.
Tieshun Roquerre, known as Pacman, the founder of NFT marketplace Blur, opened deposits for Blast in November 2023, months before the chain itself existed.

By the time Blast launched, CoinDesk reported TVL near $2.27 billion, making it one of the largest L2s in the Ethereum ecosystem overnight, built almost entirely on the promise of a token airdrop that hadn't happened yet.
Frankly, this was the most predictable outcome in crypto.
Points programmes don't build users, they rent them, and the rent always comes due.

After that, anyone still holding assets on the chain will need to interact directly with Blast's bridge contracts on Ethereum mainnet - a clunkier and riskier process than clicking a button in an app.
Switchboard, a core Solana price oracle, announced on September 19 that it's shutting down entirely, with services ending September 25.
CoinDesk reported that as of Friday, DeFi apps on Blast held about $32 million in total value locked, a decline of nearly 99% from the February 2024 peak.
Blast, for all its early buzz, never built that layer.

extraction.body: Chain revenue had fallen to just $110 over 24 hours before the shutdown, with five keyholders controlling Blast's bridge contracts and three able to pause withdrawals at will. About $51 million remains bridged, including $46.6 million staked with Lido. Blast, the Ethereum layer 2 that once held $2.3 billion and became the face of 2024's airdrop-farming boom, is shutting down because it can no longer pay its own bills. The team behind Blast announced the wind-down on October 2, telling users the chain now costs more to run than it earns and that there's no credible path back to profitability. According to Unchained, Blast's chain revenue over the prior 24 hours came to $110. That's the number that ended it: a network built to process billions in deposits, reduced to earning less than a night's take at a corner store. Users have until October 26 to withdraw funds through Blast's normal interface. After that, anyone still holding assets on the chain will need to interact directly with Blast's bridge contracts on Ethereum mainnet - a clunkier and riskier process than clicking a button in an app. Decrypt reported that roughly $51 million remains bridged into Blast's contracts, and $46.6 million of that is staked ETH sitting with Lido. Blast has to unwind that Lido position first, a process expected to take about a week, before the standard seven-day withdrawal window can even start shrinking toward 24 hours. There's a governance wrinkle worth sitting with. Unchained also reported that five keyholders control Blast's bridge contracts, and any three of them can alter those contracts or pause withdrawals outright. The chain's fraud-proof system, the mechanism meant to let anyone challenge a bad transaction record, reportedly never fully worked, leaving open the risk that a malicious proposer could finalise an invalid state. None of that caused the shutdown. But it's the kind of detail that explains why an L2 built on trust assumptions, not just revenue assumptions, struggles once the hype that justified the trust is gone. Blast's rise was fast and loud. Tieshun Roquerre, known as Pacman, the founder of NFT marketplace Blur, opened deposits for Blast in November 2023, months before the chain itself existed. Users sent ETH and stablecoins into a contract that racked up points, with withdrawals locked until mainnet launched on February 29, 2024. That structure - deposit now, get rewarded later - pulled in money fast: TVL hit $230 million within 48 hours of the unveiling, crossed $720 million by early December 2023, and topped $2 billion just before mainnet went live. By the time Blast launched, CoinDesk reported TVL near $2.27 billion, making it one of the largest L2s in the Ethereum ecosystem overnight, built almost entirely on the promise of a token airdrop that hadn't happened yet. Switchboard, a core Solana price oracle, announced on September 19 that it's shutting down entirely, with services ending September 25. Kamino, Jito and Drift now have six days to migrate to Pyth Network or RedStone or risk broken price feeds. - switchboard oracle shutdown Solana lending protocols - Kamino Drift price feed migration deadline The BLAST token launched in June 2024. And then, as is the pattern with nearly every points-farming chain, the money that showed up for the airdrop left right after it. CoinDesk reported that as of Friday, DeFi apps on Blast held about $32 million in total value locked, a decline of nearly 99% from the February 2024 peak. The token itself dropped another 19% on news of the shutdown and now sits roughly 98% below its launch price. Frankly, this was the most predictable outcome in crypto. Points programmes don't build users, they rent them, and the rent always comes due. Blast offered native yield on deposited ETH and stablecoins as its core pitch - a genuinely clever idea for a layer 2 - but the yield and the points together attracted capital that was never going to stay once the harvest was over. Blast isn't an isolated casualty. Research from Yellow and BlockEden.xyz on the 2026 Ethereum L2 sector found that the top three networks by TVL - Base, Arbitrum, and Optimism - now control roughly 80% of all sequencer fee revenue across tracked chains, based on Dune Analytics data. Everything else is fighting over scraps. Starknet's zkLend and the L2 project Kinto both shut down in 2025 after their own exploits and funding problems, and The Block's 2026 Layer-2 Outlook flagged most mid-tier rollups as unlikely to survive the next twelve months. The mechanism is the same every time. A rollup launches, dangles a points programme or a native yield feature, and watches TVL spike as farmers chase an airdrop rather than any real use for the chain. Once the token lists and the farmers cash out, what's left is sequencer and infrastructure costs that nobody's actual usage can cover. Base and Arbitrum survive this cycle because they have real applications and real transaction volume underneath the number. Blast, for all its early buzz, never built that layer. It had a yield mechanic and a points programme, and when both stopped mattering, so did the chain. For builders and investors watching the L2 space, the lesson isn't subtle: TVL inflated by farming incentives is not demand, it's a loan against future attention, and the bill always comes due faster than the token unlock schedule suggests. Blast raised that loan about as successfully as any L2 ever has. passages: Blur, once the largest marketplace for trading Ethereum NFTs, is shutting down its website next month after trading activity collapsed more than 99% from its peak, marking the second major retreat in ten days for projects built by crypto entrepreneur Tieshun Roquerre.
The strategy helped Blur capture more than 70% of Ethereum NFT trading volume in March 2023, when activity on the platform reached approximately $1.43 billion, DefiLlama data shows
Blur’s underlying smart contracts will remain operational on Ethereum, meaning the shutdown does not eliminate the blockchain-based trading system.
BLUR tokenholders will retain control of its fee switch — a mechanism that allows them to vote on whether the marketplace should start charging trading fees.
But Blur's marketplace generated no revenue from transaction fees for all that trading activity.

However, the figure does not establish whether Blur earned money from its lending service or other activities.

The marketplace said Monday that its website will close on Nov. 12, while its NFT lending service, Blend, will stop arranging new loans. coreStoryFacts.text: Blast, the Ethereum layer 2 that once held $2.3 billion and became the face of 2024's airdrop-farming boom, is shutting down because it can no longer pay its own bills.

Research from Yellow and BlockEden.xyz on the 2026 Ethereum L2 sector found that the top three networks by TVL - Base, Arbitrum, and Optimism - now control roughly 80% of all sequencer fee revenue across tracked chains, based on Dune Analytics data.

Starknet's zkLend and the L2 project Kinto both shut down in 2025 after their own exploits and funding problems, and The Block's 2026 Layer-2 Outlook flagged most mid-tier rollups as unlikely to survive the next twelve months.
The team behind Blast announced the wind-down on October 2, telling users the chain now costs more to run than it earns and that there's no credible path back to profitability.
According to Unchained, Blast's chain revenue over the prior 24 hours came to $110.
That's the number that ended it: a network built to process billions in deposits, reduced to earning less than a night's take at a corner store.
Tieshun Roquerre, known as Pacman, the founder of NFT marketplace Blur, opened deposits for Blast in November 2023, months before the chain itself existed.

By the time Blast launched, CoinDesk reported TVL near $2.27 billion, making it one of the largest L2s in the Ethereum ecosystem overnight, built almost entirely on the promise of a token airdrop that hadn't happened yet.
Frankly, this was the most predictable outcome in crypto.
Points programmes don't build users, they rent them, and the rent always comes due.

After that, anyone still holding assets on the chain will need to interact directly with Blast's bridge contracts on Ethereum mainnet - a clunkier and riskier process than clicking a button in an app.
Switchboard, a core Solana price oracle, announced on September 19 that it's shutting down entirely, with services ending September 25.
CoinDesk reported that as of Friday, DeFi apps on Blast held about $32 million in total value locked, a decline of nearly 99% from the February 2024 peak.
Blast, for all its early buzz, never built that layer.

However, the figure does not establish whether Blur earned money from its lending service or other activities.

passages: Blur, once the largest marketplace for trading Ethereum NFTs, is shutting down its website next month after trading activity collapsed more than 99% from its peak, marking the second major retreat in ten days for projects built by crypto entrepreneur Tieshun Roquerre.
The strategy helped Blur capture more than 70% of Ethereum NFT trading volume in March 2023, when activity on the platform reached approximately $1.43 billion, DefiLlama data shows
Blur’s underlying smart contracts will remain operational on Ethereum, meaning the shutdown does not eliminate the blockchain-based trading system.
BLUR tokenholders will retain control of its fee switch — a mechanism that allows them to vote on whether the marketplace should start charging trading fees.
But Blur's marketplace generated no revenue from transaction fees for all that trading activity.
The platform charged traders nothing, and Token Terminal records $0 in protocol revenue over the past three years, despite billions of dollars in NFT trades.
However, the figure does not establish whether Blur earned money from its lending service or other activities.

passages: BigBear.ai focuses on decision intelligence for government agencies, while Cerebras Systems builds massive wafer-scale processors to power generative AI.
Comparing them allows you to decide whether a niche software provider or a hardware challenger fits better in your portfolio as AI adoption reaches a mature phase in 2026.
Investors looking for exposure to the expanding artificial intelligence market often weigh hardware against software.
In its latest annual report, filed in early 2026, BigBear.ai details how it provides software that helps federal agencies and defense intelligence groups make better decisions.
The company focuses on global supply chains and national security, using a specialized workforce that often holds high-level security clearances.
Because the U.S. government is a major customer accounting for a large portion of revenue, customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.
Of the two, I would buy Cerebras Systems stock.
© 1995 - 2026 The Motley Fool . All rights reserved.
Cerebras Systems must outpace larger rivals to maintain its momentum in the competitive semiconductor market.

The company faces stiff competition from major players such as Amazon ( AMZN -1.10% ) , which develops its own internal AI chips, although the e-commerce giant also formed a partnership with Cerebras in 2026.
Rapid technological changes mean that today's hardware can quickly become obsolete, and its negative shareholder equity indicates a balance sheet where total liabilities outweigh book value.
BigBear.ai's a year-over-year revenue decline in 2025 is not an encouraging sign amid the rapid rise of AI.
BigBear.ai has to prove it can continue to expand revenue to instill confidence that its offerings are gaining traction with customers.
Its primary product is a wafer-scale system that integrates many processors on a single silicon chip to increase processing speed.
The company serves various industries, including medical research and energy, providing both systems and cloud-based services.
The company reported sales of $180.1 million in the second quarter, up an impressive 74% from 2025.
This demonstrates strong customer demand for its unique wafer-scale architecture.
BigBear.ai faces several operational hurdles, including a material class action lawsuit and the need to restate multiple years of financial statements.
These governance concerns are coupled with widening net losses and competitive pressure in the defense sector.
The company also recorded significant non-cash charges for the impairment of assets, and recent insider stock sales have added to investor concerns.

passages: Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack.
The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice.
Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027.
The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.
Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation.
CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor.
And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.
Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie.
But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline.
Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 .

It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.
The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs.
Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.
Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients.
And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google .
"Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.
But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.

Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests. Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google . The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic. But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft. For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD . Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade." Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 . It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models. Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline. "We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said. Microsoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs. "We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have," Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well." Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company. In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares. Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said. Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies. extraction.body: Help Net Security newsletters : Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – subscribe here! Cloud security platforms turn every failed rule into a finding, and those findings pile up in queues sorted by severity. Research from Sola Security tested what happens to that order when each finding gets checked against the environment where it lives. The researchers, Leon Goldberg and Gal Engelberg, built an AI agent that re-grades findings raised by third-party cloud security platforms. They ran it on 9,967 HIGH findings from two commercial platforms in eight production environments, and the agent changed the grade of 75.1% of them. Most moved down (58.5%), and 16.6% moved up. The severity on a cloud finding comes from the rule that raised it. Each of 599 vendor rules issued exactly one severity over 99,073 failing findings, regardless of the resource or environment involved. “A static severity reflects the risk of the condition in general,” the researchers wrote, and “a queue ordered by it is ordered by the general case.” “A rule carries the context its author can encode once for every environment,” they noted. “The context that decides what the condition is worth in a given environment lies elsewhere.” That includes whether the flagged resource is attached to anything and whether a workload runs on it. Scoring standards reserve a place for this context. CVSS includes environmental metrics that adjust a base score to a particular deployment, and NIST risk assessment guidance ties likelihood to the controls in place. “A static severity leaves that place empty,” the researchers observed. For each finding, the agent forms a theory of how an attacker would exploit the problem, then collects evidence from the resource’s configuration, the resources connected to it, and data held by other security products. Under the agent’s evidence policy, “raising a severity needs more evidence than lowering it.” Lowering a grade requires an observed property that offsets the specific way the failure would be exploited. Raising one requires evidence that the condition is worse in that environment, along with a check for firewalls, allowlists or other plausible guardrails in the path. Everything else keeps the vendor grade. Six recurring patterns accounted for the findings whose deciding facts could be checked through cloud APIs . The largest, at 32.3%, involved inert resources, attached to nothing or orphaned. Downgrades also came from resources unreachable from the internet, missing live services, narrow source restrictions and account-level blocks. One pattern, public exposure confirmed in the environment, mainly raised severity. Of 138 rules, 62 produced findings that the agent downgraded in some cases and upgraded in others. For 57 of those rules, both outcomes occurred within a single environment. A security group rule, for instance, was lowered when the group fronted only internal load balancers and raised when the environment showed a path from the internet. About half of the verdicts (49.0%) rested on evidence from outside the flagged resource, from connected resources in the asset graph or from another product’s data. “Outside evidence concentrates in attenuations, where showing a finding safe means ruling out every path to it,” the researchers explained. “The rule-severity gap is large in production, and closing it requires evidence from the whole environment,” they concluded. To test whether the agent’s verdicts rested on solid ground, the researchers ran read-only probes on eight AWS accounts, re-reading the deciding facts directly from the cloud provider and leaving the agent’s own data out of the loop. For the verdicts the probes could settle, the live environment matched the agent’s facts 99.4% of the time. When every finding the probes could not check was counted as wrong, the figure dropped to 81.8%. The probes tested the facts behind the verdicts, and whether the revised severity ratings were the right ones is a question the study left open. The authors draw a line between an AI reading findings and an AI acting on them. “Verified, environment-specific reading of each finding is a precondition for acting on findings autonomously,” Goldberg and Engelberg argued. “Reading and acting differ in blast radius, reversibility, and authorization,” they cautioned, adding that “this study measures reading only.” The work covers one system’s verdicts on the HIGH queue of two platforms, and 92% of the re-graded findings were on AWS. Live verification covered one platform and five resource types, and it tested the deciding fact behind each verdict, leaving the final grade unchecked. Findings that started at MEDIUM or LOW fell outside the scope. The study also lacks incident data, so it leaves open whether upgraded findings are more likely to be exploited, or downgraded findings less likely, than their vendor grade implies. Recall, meaning the deciding facts the agent missed, went unmeasured.

One pattern, public exposure confirmed in the environment, mainly raised severity.

Of 138 rules, 62 produced findings that the agent downgraded in some cases and upgraded in others. For 57 of those rules, both outcomes occurred within a single environment. A security group rule, for instance, was lowered when the group fronted only internal load balancers and raised when the environment showed a path from the internet.

To test whether the agent’s verdicts rested on solid ground, the researchers ran read-only probes on eight AWS accounts, re-reading the deciding facts directly from the cloud provider and leaving the agent’s own data out of the loop. For the verdicts the probes could settle, the live environment matched the agent’s facts 99.4% of the time. “Verified, environment-specific reading of each finding is a precondition for acting on findings autonomously,” Goldberg and Engelberg argued. “Reading and acting differ in blast radius, reversibility, and authorization,” they cautioned, adding that “this study measures reading only.”

The work covers one system’s verdicts on the HIGH queue of two platforms, and 92% of the re-graded findings were on AWS. Live verification covered one platform and five resource types, and it tested the deciding fact behind each verdict, leaving the final grade unchecked.

Findings that started at MEDIUM or LOW fell outside the scope. The study also lacks incident data, so it leaves open whether upgraded findings are more likely to be exploited, or downgraded findings less likely, than their vendor grade implies. passages: The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official.
Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6.
sources.body: The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official. Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6.

extraction.body: The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official. The tracker sits smack-dab between the recently launched Fitbit Air and the more powerful Google Pixel Watch 5 in the company’s current wearable lineup. Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6. Much of the Edge’s specs were previously leaked, but the tracker has a 46 percent larger OLED display compared to the Charge 6, a physical side button, and is a smidge thicker at 11.5mm. The tracker uses the same proprietary charger as the Air, and can also get about a day’s worth of battery in five minutes. (A full charge takes 90 minutes.) For health tracking, the Edge has an EKG sensor for atrial fibrillation detection, a skin temperature sensor, SpO2 and optical heart rate sensors, plus your typical motion tracking sensors. The Edge doesn’t have a mic or speaker, so you can’t take calls from the wrist even though you can see who’s calling on the screen. The latter is a bit disappointing, given that the Edge essentially replaces the Charge 6 and is $20 more expensive at $179.99. The new Fitbit offers improved automatic workout tracking and GPS compared to the Charge 6. The former is a revised motion model that’ll also come to the Air. Google says the new model means auto activity tracking is twice as accurate and supports over 100 activities. The Edge’s GPS tracking is also purportedly 40 percent more accurate — though it’s not using the same software-based post-processing update that Google introduced with the Pixel Watch 5. This increased accuracy mostly comes from on-device improvements to the Edge. Feature-wise, the device is meant for people who want glanceable information, with some but not all the bells and whistles of a smartwatch. The Edge borrows much of the Pixel Watch’s design language as far as widgets and user interface go. It’s not running Wear OS, though; this is a redesigned Fitbit OS. The Edge will launch with several types of straps so you can adjust the style to fit various occasions, including metal links to give it more of a jewelry-like feel. (Speaking of jewelry-like styling, the Air is also getting a new metal mesh strap that costs $69.99 and is available October 27th.) As with the Air and Pixel Watch 5, there’ll be a Stephen Curry edition of the Edge that will cost $219.99.

Much of the Edge’s specs were previously leaked, but the tracker has a 46 percent larger OLED display compared to the Charge 6, a physical side button, and is a smidge thicker at 11.5mm. The tracker uses the same proprietary charger as the Air, and can also get about a day’s worth of battery in five minutes. (A full charge takes 90 minutes.) For health tracking, the Edge has an EKG sensor for atrial fibrillation detection, a skin temperature sensor, SpO2 and optical heart rate sensors, plus your typical motion tracking sensors. The Edge doesn’t have a mic or speaker, so you can’t take calls from the wrist even though you can see who’s calling on the screen. The latter is a bit disappointing, given that the Edge essentially replaces the Charge 6 and is $20 more expensive at $179.99. The new Fitbit offers improved automatic workout tracking and GPS compared to the Charge 6. The former is a revised motion model that’ll also come to the Air. Google says the new model means auto activity tracking is twice as accurate and supports over 100 activities. The Edge’s GPS tracking is also purportedly 40 percent more accurate — though it’s not using the same software-based post-processing update that Google introduced with the Pixel Watch 5. This increased accuracy mostly comes from on-device improvements to the Edge. Feature-wise, the device is meant for people who want glanceable information, with some but not all the bells and whistles of a smartwatch. The Edge borrows much of the Pixel Watch’s design language as far as widgets and user interface go. It’s not running Wear OS, though; this is a redesigned Fitbit OS. The Edge will launch with several types of straps so you can adjust the style to fit various occasions, including metal links to give it more of a jewelry-like feel. (Speaking of jewelry-like styling, the Air is also getting a new metal mesh strap that costs $69.99 and is available October 27th.) As with the Air and Pixel Watch 5, there’ll be a Stephen Curry edition of the Edge that will cost $219.99.
