Applications that route requests, select agent actions, or assign policy outcomes often need scores over a fixed set of choices instead of free-form text. Deploying these decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure. This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX , vLLM-Omni – Part 1 , and vLLM-Omni – Part 2 . In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI InvokeEndpoint . You then extend the same runtime with SemIf , formerly OpenJev, which returns probabilities over declared options without decoding an answer token. The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options. Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options. Figure 1: Run the AWS DLC for llama.cpp or the SemIf child image on CPU or GPU, depending on the API and latency requirements of your workload For the standard path, package the model as model.tar.gz in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference the published DLC image directly. The container finds the first .gguf file under /opt/ml/model , maps POST /invocations to llama-server at /v1/chat/completions , and passes SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables to llama.cpp arguments. The llama-server HTTP API doesn’t expose the final-position logits and state operations that SemIf uses. The structured-decision path therefore uses AWS CodeBuild to build a child image and store it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . The child image keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries while replacing its entry point with a SageMaker-compatible adapter. The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema. Send a messages array with role and content , plus generation controls such as max_tokens and stream : The response returns option_ids , probabilities , and raw option_logits in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. With stable option IDs, your application can apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing generated prose. SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application-defined outcomes from unstructured state. Other implementations include Jev , TypeSafe’s decision model and /v1/systemone API; Kev , a model server designed for TypeSafe API compatibility; and Strands Decider 2B , a purpose-built model for agent workflows with calibrated outputs. Use this pattern when your application defines the allowed choices at request time and needs a model to interpret unstructured context. Examples include routing a case to a queue, extracting one value from a known set, assigning an incident priority, checking a policy outcome, or selecting an agent action. Keep authorization and deterministic business rules outside the model, and validate model probabilities before treating them as operational confidence. Use the standard SageMaker AI text-generation path when you need OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint . The SageMaker AI image maps POST /invocations to the llama-server /v1/chat/completions endpoint. Build a child image only when your application needs behavior that this interface doesn’t provide, such as SemIf’s direct logits and state access. Removing answer-token generation doesn’t remove model inference. The model still processes the complete state, question, and option descriptions before SemIf reads the final logits. Keep prompts focused, and evaluate the selected model with labeled decisions from your application before production use. The following benchmark applies to the SemIf extension, not the text-generation endpoint. Model size, quantization, prompt length, runtime, and CPU thread count affect each decision. To quantify these trade-offs, we sent the same 231 public JevBench tasks serially to one CPU endpoint and one GPU endpoint. Compared with the CPU configuration, the GPU endpoint was 4.9 times faster at p50 and 32.2 times faster at p95. The sample uses the SageMaker AI instance pools feature to list compatible GPU instance types in priority order, so SageMaker can select an alternative when the first preference isn’t available. The pool ordered g6e , g6 , g5 , then g4dn . SageMaker selected ml.g6e.xlarge , and startup logs confirmed that llama.cpp offloaded all 34 model layers to an NVIDIA L40S. The CPU and GPU images used different llama.cpp builds and produced different predictions on six hard tasks. Treat the one-answer accuracy difference as runtime variation, not evidence that GPU offload improves model quality. Smaller models reduced median latency, but the 2B and 0.8B candidates achieved 66.7 percent and 58.4 percent accuracy. The sample therefore keeps the 4B Q4_K_M model as its quality-first default. These measurements include network latency and aren’t service guarantees. Benchmark the complete model and infrastructure configuration against your own decisions. Use CPU for background, offline, or low-throughput workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and can tolerate seconds of response time. Use GPU for interactive decisions, long prompts, or workloads with tight tail-latency targets. Keep state and option descriptions concise, group decisions that share the same state into one request, and scale endpoint instances for concurrency. Shared-state scoring reuses the common prompt prefix, while the adapter returns retryable HTTP 503 responses instead of allowing an unbounded queue around its stateful llama.cpp context. The text-generation example uses the CPU DLC and a fixed CPU instance. The SemIf extension keeps CPU as the default for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and offers an optional CUDA image with ordered instance pools. Review SageMaker AI pricing before creating an endpoint. Use the following procedure to deploy the standard text-generation endpoint, then build the optional SemIf extension for structured decisions on CPU or GPU. Wait for the returned build ID to reach SUCCEEDED . The build records the source revisions and checksums in model-manifest.json and stops if the GGUF checksum differs from the validated value. Resolve a digest-pinned server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 image from the AWS DLC for llama.cpp documentation , then create the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint: Select a server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 or server-sagemaker-cuda-v1 image rather than the corresponding EC2 image. The SageMaker AI images implement the /ping and /invocations container contract and map invocation payloads to chat completions. This walkthrough supplies the GGUF model through the SageMaker AI model artifact in Amazon S3. As an alternative, you can configure SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_REPO and SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_FILE to download a GGUF file from Hugging Face when the endpoint has network egress. You don’t need a Dockerfile or an ECR repository for this path. Wait for the endpoint to enter InService , then send an OpenAI-compatible chat request: For the GPU image, provide ordered instance pools and request full model offload: Instance pools are ordered placement fallbacks, not inference load balancing. SageMaker selects one available type for the variant. Endpoint creation can take longer while SageMaker AI works through the pool. Check the startup logs for the selected GPU and a message confirming that all model layers were offloaded. The request declares stable IDs for each allowed option: The response preserves the option order and includes conditional probabilities, raw logits, token and prompt metadata, and the pinned model identity: Apply application-level thresholds and fallbacks. Don’t use a model decision as a substitute for authorization. Delete the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model: The script deletes only those explicitly named SageMaker AI resources. Delete the CodeBuild projects, ECR repository, model and source objects in Amazon S3, logs, and purpose-specific IAM roles when you no longer need them. The AWS DLC for llama.cpp gives you a managed foundation for serving decision models on SageMaker AI across CPU and GPU instances. It can load GGUF models from SageMaker AI model artifacts or a configured Hugging Face repository, then serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint without requiring a custom container. When your application needs direct logits and model state operations, you can extend the DLC with a SemIf adapter. Choose CPU for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive, and choose GPU when prompt prefill and tail latency affect the application experience. Review the code sample , AWS DLC for llama.cpp documentation , and SageMaker AI custom inference container contract to adapt the deployment for your workload.

The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options. Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options. VP Science, Google DeepMind & Chief Scientist, Google Cloud Your browser does not support the audio element. Google is using artificial intelligence to accelerate medical research, from mapping the human brain to identifying genetic diseases in under eight hours. These tools help scientists repurpose drugs, design custom enzymes, and improve cancer detection rates while reducing administrative burdens on doctors. You can explore these open-access platforms and research findings to see how technology is transforming patient care and public health outcomes globally. Google is using AI to help scientists understand diseases at a tiny, molecular level. These tools speed up drug discovery, map the human brain, and help doctors diagnose patients much faster. The technology also helps predict disease outbreaks so communities can get the care they need sooner. By sharing these tools, Google hopes to help researchers everywhere create better treatments and save more lives. Google’s health research and tools span from fundamental cellular discovery to laboratory analysis and patient impact. Over the last five years, Google teams have published 90 peer-reviewed research papers about understanding and addressing diseases, accumulating more than 90,000 citations. And building on our vision for how technology can accelerate science to improve lives , we’re collaborating with clinicians, academic institutes, and researchers to ensure discoveries make it out of the lab to benefit patients. Here is how our efforts are helping to advance medical research and public health solutions. AlphaGenome Atlas is the most comprehensive catalog of predictions for how single-letter variant changes in the human genome affect molecular biology. To effectively treat an illness, it helps to understand how it operates at the molecular, genetic, and cellular levels. Our early-stage biology models act as collaborative research tools for scientists, revealing nature's hidden mechanics and advancing medical discoveries. Visual map of proteins developed with the support of AlphaFold. New mammography screening systems can help to catch historically missed interval cancers and reduce specialist reading workloads. A medical breakthrough only matters if it can help real people. Our research demonstrates that machine learning models can help support disease detection as well as alleviate the administrative workload so providers can focus on care. Transforming health requires scientists, researchers, and institutions working hand-in-hand. That’s why we equip the science community with the advanced models and open-access platforms to fuel breakthrough research — along with the philanthropic funding and computing power they need to apply that research. Through Google.org, we’re supporting organizations like the Infectious Disease Institute at Makerere University to forecast malaria drug resistance mutations with AlphaFold and AlphaMissense, and the University of Pennsylvania, using AlphaProteo and AlphaFold to help design novel cellular therapies that can augment the treatment of solid tumors and complex diseases. In 2026, Google.org has provided over $60 million to organizations around the world that are applying advanced models to transform how we understand and treat diseases. By meeting disease at every stage, we can turn the most intractable human health challenges into actionable solutions, helping people everywhere live longer, healthier lives. Yossi Matias is Vice President, Google, and the Head of Google Research. Under Yossi’s leadership, world-class global teams are leading breakthrough research on Foundational Machine Learning & Algorithms, Computing Systems & Quantum Computing, Science, AI for Societal Impact in Health, Climate, Sustainability, Education and Cultural and Behavioral Intelligence. Yossi also leads teams advancing foundational research advancements in Generative AI, including in Factuality and Efficiency, driving real-world impact and shaping the future of technology.

extraction.body: “No more hand-written code” or AI-free art for delayed Marvel/Star Wars shooter. Epic Games is shifting to an “AI first” development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That’s according to a Bloomberg report , which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker. Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic’s Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means “no more hand-written code” and art assets “generated with full AI workflows,” according to the report. The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024 , was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report. “We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” an Epic spokesperson said in a statement. “We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media shortly after the Bloomberg story was posted. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.” Sweeney and Epic have long been bullish on what they see as an impending game development revolution spurred by AI. In an interview with IGN in June , Sweeney saw the technology resulting in games with “the possibility of infinite dialogue with a really simple setup for creators,” leading to situations where “small teams will be able to create games with immense amounts of characters and immense and interactive worlds.” Sweeney said last November that AI usage disclosure tags such as those required by Valve’s Steam platform “make no sense” because AI tools “will be involved in nearly all future production.” Epic laid off over 1,000 employees in March , citing a “downturn in Fortnite engagement” as the main reason behind the move. Months later, Fortnite Senior External Development Manager Stephanie Arnette said that “I know everyone’s biggest fear is, ‘Oh my god, AI is going to take all our jobs.’ That’s not our goal. The goal is to make us more efficient.” Last May, Epic and Disney faced some embarrassment when an AI-voiced Darth Vader character added to Fortnite started repeating curse words and uttering some baffling opinions before a hotfix was rolled out. A survey of over 2,300 game industry professionals ahead of this year’s Game Developers Conference found that 36 percent used generative AI tools as part of their jobs, including 30 percent of those at game development studios. But those AI tools were used for tasks like research and brainstorming (by 81 percent of AI-using respondents) much more than for code assistance (47 percent) and prototyping (35 percent). Epic Games is shifting to an “AI first” development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That’s according to a Bloomberg report , which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker.

Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic’s Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means “no more hand-written code” and art assets “generated with full AI workflows,” according to the report.

The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024 , was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report.
“We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” an Epic spokesperson said in a statement.

“We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media shortly after the Bloomberg story was posted. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.”

Sweeney and Epic have long been bullish on what they see as an impending game development revolution spurred by AI. In an interview with IGN in June , Sweeney saw the technology resulting in games with “the possibility of infinite dialogue with a really simple setup for creators,” leading to situations where “small teams will be able to create games with immense amounts of characters and immense and interactive worlds.”
Sweeney said last November that AI usage disclosure tags such as those required by Valve’s Steam platform “make no sense” because AI tools “will be involved in nearly all future production.”

Epic laid off over 1,000 employees in March , citing a “downturn in Fortnite engagement” as the main reason behind the move. Months later, Fortnite Senior External Development Manager Stephanie Arnette said that “I know everyone’s biggest fear is, ‘Oh my god, AI is going to take all our jobs.’ That’s not our goal. The goal is to make us more efficient.”

Last May, Epic and Disney faced some embarrassment when an AI-voiced Darth Vader character added to Fortnite started repeating curse words and uttering some baffling opinions before a hotfix was rolled out.

A survey of over 2,300 game industry professionals ahead of this year’s Game Developers Conference found that 36 percent used generative AI tools as part of their jobs, including 30 percent of those at game development studios. But those AI tools were used for tasks like research and brainstorming (by 81 percent of AI-using respondents) much more than for code assistance (47 percent) and prototyping (35 percent).

Sweeney and Epic have long been bullish on what they see as an impending game development revolution spurred by AI.
“We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media shortly after the Bloomberg story was posted.
